✅ Daily Implementation Checklist
  • Morning (30 min): Read 10-15 MCQs + review explanations. Focus on one domain per day.
  • Afternoon (45 min): Re-review questions you got wrong. Understand WHY the correct answer is correct.
  • Evening (60 min): Hands-on practice on your cluster. Apply KServe, KFP SDK, and oc commands from memory.
  • Weekend (2-3 hours): Full review of the week's topics. Run a timed mock session answering 50 questions in 90 minutes.
  • Day before exam: Review Q200 (final checklist). Practice KServe, KFP SDK, and oc commands from memory.
  • Exam day morning: Set up your environment: alias k=kubectl, export KUBECONFIG=..., verify context. Review the 5 pipeline patterns from Q200.

🏆 Skills You'll Master — Before vs After This Guide

❌ BEFORE — Common Beginner Pitfalls

  • ❌ "My Jupyter workbench won't start" — No idea where to look
  • ❌ "The model InferenceService returns 503" — Don't know about KServe
  • ❌ "I updated the model but serving still uses old version" — No model versioning
  • ❌ "The pipeline runs forever" — Never checked step logs or resource limits
  • ❌ "GPU is not detected in my workbench" — GPU Operator unknown
  • ❌ "My S3 data connection fails" — IAM and bucket policy concepts missing
  • ❌ "Model drift? What's TrustyAI?" — No monitoring plan

✅ AFTER — Skills This Guide Builds

  • ✅ Install & configure RHOAI operators, GPU acceleration, and platform governance
  • ✅ Create isolated Data Science Projects with workbenches, S3 connections, and Git
  • ✅ Deploy models via KServe (RawDeployment & Serverless) with custom runtimes
  • ✅ Build KFP pipelines with Elyra, schedule recurring runs, debug failures
  • ✅ Register models in Model Registry, manage versions, promote to production
  • ✅ Serve LLMs with vLLM/TGIS, configure quantization, streaming, and multi-LoRA
  • ✅ Monitor bias/drift with TrustyAI, track GPU metrics, and troubleshoot AI workloads

🚨 Critical Do's & Don'ts During The EX267 Exam
  • ✅ DO: Use kubectl create ... --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate YAML in seconds — never type manifests from scratch.
  • ✅ DO: Run kubectl config use-context <given-context> as the FIRST command for every task. Wrong context = 0 points.
  • ✅ DO: Use kubectl explain <resource> --recursive when you forget a field name. It's faster than searching docs.
  • ✅ DO: Test model endpoints: curl -k https://<is-url>/v1/models/<model>:predict to verify inference is working.
  • ❌ DON'T: Spend more than 7 minutes on any single task. Flag it, move on, return with fresh eyes.
  • ❌ DON'T: Forget to set the namespace. Many tasks require -n flag. Use kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns> to save typing.
  • ❌ DON'T: Leave any task blank. Even partial work (creating the project, writing partial YAML) may earn partial credit.
  • ❌ DON'T: Delete a running InferenceService without checking if pipelines depend on it — cascade failures.

📊 EX267 Exam Domains & StrategySTRATEGY

EX267 Exam Format & Preparation Strategy

Exam Name: Red Hat Certified Specialist in OpenShift AI | Exam Code: EX267 | Duration: 2 hours | Format: Performance-based (hands-on CLI + OpenShift Console tasks) | Passing Score: 68% (210/300) | Cost: $400 (includes one free retake) | Certification Validity: 3 years

4 Official Domains: Install RHOAI (20%), Data Science Projects & Workbenches (25%), Build/Deploy/Manage ML Models (30%), Create Data Science Pipelines (25%). Model building/deployment is the heaviest — focus your study time accordingly.

Exam Strategy: Read all tasks first (5 min) → Solve easy tasks first → Flag and return to hard ones → Use oc explain and kubectl --help liberally → Always verify your work. The exam provides access to Red Hat product documentation.

Your 6-cluster lab (below) mirrors real exam conditions. Use ksw to switch between clusters.

📚 Pre-Learning: AI/ML & OpenShift FoundationsF.1–F.5

🟢 Novice-Friendly: Building Your AI/ML Mental Model

F.1 What Is OpenShift AI & Why Does It Matter? — The "ML on My Laptop" problem. From Jupyter Notebook → Training → Serving → Monitoring. What is MLOps? What is GenAIOps? OpenShift AI vs DIY Kubernetes ML.

F.2 AI/ML Fundamentals — The Concepts You MUST Know — What IS a machine learning model? Training vs Inference. LLMs, RAG, embeddings. GPU vs CPU. Model formats: ONNX, PyTorch, TensorFlow. Quantization: FP16, INT8, INT4.

F.3 OpenShift AI Platform — The "Big Picture" Mental Model — OpenShift Container Platform → RHOAI Operator → Components. Data Science Project = Namespace + AI tooling. Workbenches, Pipeline Servers, Model Registry, KServe, TrustyAI.

F.4 The anihpj/jobpost AI Application Stack — Web tier (Django templates), API tier (Django REST), Database (PostgreSQL 15), Redis (Celery + cache), ML Pipeline (KFP), Model Server (KServe), RAG (LlamaStack + Milvus), Monitoring (TrustyAI + Prometheus).

F.5 Docker/Podman vs OpenShift — A Mental Bridge — Dockerfile → OCI artifact → Model Registry. docker-compose → Kubernetes YAML → OpenShift Templates. Why OpenShift AI when you can docker run Jupyter? The "Day 2" AI problem: GPU sharing, model versioning, drift detection.

If you're new to AI/ML or OpenShift: Read through F.1–F.5 before diving into Part 1. These foundations will give you the mental models needed to understand the MCQs, troubleshooting issues, and lab scenarios. The entire guide uses the anihpj/jobpost Django + AI application as its running example.

⚡ Quick-Start Cheat Codes

# Most-used EX267 commands (muscle memory)
oc get inferenceservice -n {project}
oc describe inferenceservice {name}
oc logs deploy/{name}-predictor
oc get pods -l serving.kserve.io/inferenceservice={name}
oc get servingruntime
oc get notebook -n {project}

# KFP SDK patterns
from kfp import Client
client = Client(host="https://...")
client.run_pipeline(experiment_id=..., params={...})
client.create_recurring_run(cron_expression="0 2 * * 0")

# KServe API pattern
curl -k https://{url}/v1/models/{name}:predict \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"inputs": [{"name": "x", "shape": [1,5],
       "datatype": "FP32", "data": [1,2,3,4,5]}]}'

🧠 Question-Taking Strategy

Read Q

2️⃣
Predict
Answer mentally

Find your answer

Pro tip: Cover the options with your hand. Read only the question. Form your own answer first. THEN look at options. This prevents the options from biasing your reasoning — the #1 cause of MCQ mistakes.

✅ How To Implement — Your Daily Action Plan

📋 Implementation Checklist — Turn Knowledge Into Practice
  • Step 1 (Pre-Reading): Read the Pre-Learning section (F.1-F.5) to build your AI/ML mental model. Understand what OpenShift AI IS before diving into questions.
  • Step 2 (Daily Routine): Answer 20-30 MCQs per session. Read EVERY explanation — even for correct answers. The explanations contain deeper insights not tested by the question itself.
  • Step 3 (Track Progress): Keep a scorecard. Mark questions you got wrong. Revisit them after 2 days. Target: improve from 70% → 85% → 90%+ over 4 weeks.
  • Step 4 (Hands-On): For every 10 MCQs, practice the related CLI commands on your 6-cluster lab. Use ksw to switch clusters. Type commands — don't copy-paste.
  • Step 5 (Deep Dive): For questions you get wrong, read the related section in the official Red Hat documentation. The exam gives you documentation access — practice using it.
  • Step 6 (Mock Exam): In Week 4, do a timed session: answer 50 random questions in 90 minutes. No notes, no documentation. This simulates exam pressure.
  • Step 7 (Pre-Exam): Review Q150 (GenAI capstone) and Q200 (Pipeline patterns checklist). These are your last-10-minutes cram sheets.

📦 Category 1: Install Red Hat OpenShift AI (20%)Q1-Q40

🟢 Novice-Friendly: Installing & Configuring RHOAI

This category is about getting OpenShift AI up and running on your cluster. Think of it like setting up a new smart home — you first install the hub (RHOAI Operator), configure user access (who can control what), set up specialized hardware (NVIDIA GPUs for AI acceleration), and ensure everything stays running (lifecycle management). For anihpj/jobpost, this means the AI platform that powers job-matching, resume analysis, and salary predictions is properly installed so data scientists can start building models.

Q1-Q40 40 Questions 🟢 Beginner

1.1 RHOAI Operator Installation & VerificationQ1-Q10

Install RHOAI Q1 of 200
What is the primary method for installing Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI) on an existing OpenShift cluster, and which component manages the installation lifecycle?
A) Download and run a standalone installer binary on the bootstrap node — RHOAI uses a dedicated installer outside of OpenShift's control plane
B) Clone the RHOAI Git repository and apply raw Kubernetes manifests directly with kubectl apply — no operator involvement
C) Install the RHOAI Operator from OperatorHub via an Operator Subscription, managed by the Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM)
D) Deploy RHOAI as a set of static pods placed in /etc/kubernetes/manifests on each control plane node
✅ Correct Answer: C

RHOAI is installed exclusively via the Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM) on OpenShift. You do NOT download a binary, clone a repo, or use static pods. Instead, an administrator creates a Subscription custom resource pointing to the RHOAI Operator in the Red Hat Operator catalog. The OLM then pulls the ClusterServiceVersion (CSV), deploys the operator pod in the redhat-ods-operator namespace, and creates all required CRDs (DataScienceCluster, Notebook, InferenceService, ServingRuntime, etc.). After the operator is running, you create a DataScienceCluster (DSC) CR to trigger the actual deployment of RHOAI components like the dashboard, workbenches, pipeline server, KServe, and model registry.

📝 Detailed Explanation

  │  │ Operator │       │ CSV +    │       │ + watches│       │ DSC CR   │  │
  │  │ Hub      │       │ CRDs     │       │ for DSC  │       │          │  │
  │  └──────────┘       └──────────┘       └──────────┘       └──────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 5 — DSC triggers component rollout:                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  DataScienceCluster CR (default-dsc)                              │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐               │    │
  │  │  │ Dashboard    │ │ Workbenches  │ │ Pipelines    │               │    │
  │  │  │ (odh-dash)   │ │ (Notebook CR)│ │ (DSPA CR)    │               │    │

  │  │  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐               │    │
  │  │  │ Model Serving│ │ Model Reg.   │ │ Monitoring   │               │    │
  │  │  │ (KServe)     │ │ (MR CR)      │ │ (TrustyAI)   │               │    │
  │  │  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘               │    │

  EXAM COMMANDS — What You Type on the EX267 Exam:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  # Check if the RHOAI Operator is installed
  oc get subscription -A | grep rhods
  oc get csv -A | grep rhods

  # Check operator pod status
  oc get pods -n redhat-ods-operator

  # Check the DataScienceCluster status (after creating DSC)
  oc get dsc
  oc describe dsc default-dsc

  # Verify all RHOAI components are ready
  oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications
  oc get pods -n redhat-ods-monitoring

  KEY NAMESPACES:                          KEY CRDs Created:
    redhat-ods-operator   → Operator pod      DataScienceCluster (DSC)
    redhat-ods-applications → Components      Notebook (Workbench)
    redhat-ods-monitoring → Prom/TrustyAI     InferenceService (KServe)
                                              ServingRuntime

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Before your data science team can build AI-powered job matching, salary predictions, or RAG-based job description generators, the RHOAI platform must be installed. If the operator isn't in OperatorHub, your CatalogSource may be missing. If the CSV is stuck in "Installing", the operator pod may lack permissions. If the DSC is not created, the dashboard, workbenches, and KServe won't deploy. Understanding the OLM → Subscription → CSV → Operator → DSC chain is the single most important concept for EX267 Domain 1.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: You may be asked to verify that RHOAI is properly installed by checking operator status, component health, and CRD availability. Master the commands above — they'll save you minutes on exam day.

Install RHOAI Q2 of 200
After the RHOAI Operator is installed, what CR (Custom Resource) must you create to trigger the actual deployment of RHOAI components like the dashboard, workbenches, KServe, and pipelines?
A) Create a DataScienceProject CR — the project CR automatically provisions all platform components
B) Create a DataScienceCluster (DSC) CR — this is the central resource that controls which RHOAI components are deployed and their configuration
C) Create an InferenceService CR — KServe's CR triggers a cascading deployment of the full AI platform
D) No CR is needed — the RHOAI Operator automatically deploys all components upon installation via the CSV
✅ Correct Answer: B

The DataScienceCluster (DSC) CR is the single most important resource in RHOAI. After the operator is running, creating a DSC instance (typically named default-dsc) tells the operator WHICH components to deploy and HOW to configure them. The DSC spec includes component enablement flags for: dashboard, workbenches, datasciencepipelines, kserve, modelregistry, trustyai, ray, trainingoperator, and more. Without a DSC, the operator sits idle — no dashboard, no workbenches, no model serving. Think of the DSC as the "master on/off switch" for the entire AI platform.

📝 Detailed Explanation
DataScienceCluster (DSC) — The Master Control Plane for RHOAI
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              DSC CR (DataScienceCluster) — Component Control             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  apiVersion: datasciencecluster.opendatahub.io/v1                        │
  │  kind: DataScienceCluster                                                │
  │  metadata:                                                               │
  │    name: default-dsc           ← The single DSC instance                 │
  │  spec:                                                                    │
  │    components:                                                           │
  │      dashboard:         { enabled: true }  → OpenShift AI Console       │
  │      workbenches:       { enabled: true }  → Jupyter/VS Code/RStudio    │
  │      datasciencepipelines: { enabled: true } → KFP + Argo Workflows     │
  │      kserve:            { enabled: true }  → Model InferenceService     │
  │      modelregistry:     { enabled: true }  → Model versioning & metadata│
  │      trustyai:          { enabled: true }  → Bias/Drift monitoring      │
  │      ray:               { enabled: false } → Distributed ML workloads   │
  │      trainingoperator:  { enabled: false } → PyTorch/TF training jobs   │
  │      codeflare:         { enabled: false } → Distributed compute        │
  │      kueue:             { enabled: false } → Resource quota management  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  DSC STATUS — What to check:                                             │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ $ oc describe dsc default-dsc                                     │    │
  │  │ Status:                                                            │    │
  │  │   Conditions:                                                      │    │
  │  │     - type: Ready            ← MUST be "True"                     │    │
  │  │     - type: DashboardReady   ← Component-level status              │    │
  │  │     - type: WorkbenchesReady                                       │    │
  │  │   Phase: Ready              ← Overall phase: Ready/Pending/Failed │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  COMMON MISTAKE — What students get wrong:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  ❌ "I installed the operator, why is nothing showing up?"
     → You forgot to create the DSC! Operator ≠ Platform.

  ❌ "I created the DSC but the dashboard still isn't there"
     → Check: oc get dsc -o yaml | grep -A2 dashboard
        Is dashboard.enabled: true? Is the DSC Phase: Ready?

  ❌ "I enabled KServe but InferenceService CRDs don't exist"
     → KServe requires dependencies (ServiceMesh/Serverless operators).
        Check DSC status conditions for error messages.

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: When your data science team says "the AI platform isn't working," your first check should be oc get dsc. If the DSC's workbenches component is not enabled, no one can launch Jupyter to build the job-matching model. If kserve is disabled, the salary prediction model can't be served to the jobpost API. The DSC is the single source of truth for what's running in your RHOAI platform.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Expect a task like "Enable the KServe component and verify it's ready." You'll edit the DSC (oc edit dsc default-dsc), set kserve: { enabled: true }, then check oc get dsc -o yaml | grep -A5 kserve and verify the Ready condition.

Install RHOAI Q3 of 200
After installing the RHOAI Operator via OLM, in which namespace does the operator pod run, and what command best verifies a healthy installation?
A) Namespace: redhat-ods-operator — verify with: oc get pods -n redhat-ods-operator and oc get csv -A | grep rhods
B) Namespace: openshift-operators — verify with: oc get pods -n openshift-operators | grep rhods
C) Namespace: redhat-ods-applications — verify with: oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications
D) Namespace: opendatahub — verify with: oc get pods -n opendatahub
✅ Correct Answer: A

RHOAI uses three key namespaces, and knowing which is which is critical for the EX267 exam. The operator pod runs in redhat-ods-operator — this is where the Subscription and CSV live. The application components (dashboard, workbenches, pipelines) run in redhat-ods-applications. The monitoring stack (Prometheus, TrustyAI) runs in redhat-ods-monitoring. The correct verification is to check the operator pod AND the CSV phase — a running operator pod alone doesn't guarantee a successful installation; the CSV must be in phase: Succeeded.

📝 Detailed Explanation
RHOAI Namespaces — What Runs Where
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     RHOAI NAMESPACE ARCHITECTURE                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  redhat-ods-operator (Operator namespace)                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Pod: rhods-operator-xxxxxxxxxx-xxxxx     ← THE operator pod      │    │
  │  │  Subscription: rhods-operator             ← Channel + source      │    │
  │  │  CSV: rhods-operator.v2.x.x               ← Phase MUST be Succeeded│   │
  │  │  InstallPlan: install-xxxxx               ← Approval status       │    │
  │  │  CRDs: DataScienceCluster, Notebook, etc. ← Created at install    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  redhat-ods-applications (Component namespace)                           │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Pod: odh-dashboard-xxxxxxxxxx-xxxxx      ← OpenShift AI Console  │    │
  │  │  Pod: notebook-controller-deployment-xxx  ← Workbench controller  │    │
  │  │  Pod: kserve-controller-manager-xxx       ← KServe controller     │    │
  │  │  Pod: modelregistry-operator-xxx          ← Model Registry        │    │
  │  │  Pod: ds-pipeline-xxx                     ← Pipeline server       │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  redhat-ods-monitoring (Observability namespace)                         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Pod: prometheus-xxx                       ← Metrics collection   │    │
  │  │  Pod: trustyai-service-xxx                 ← Bias/Drift detection │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  VERIFICATION CHECKLIST — Is RHOAI Healthy?
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  ✅ Operator pod Running:  oc get pods -n redhat-ods-operator
  ✅ CSV Phase Succeeded:   oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator
  ✅ DSC Phase Ready:       oc get dsc default-dsc
  ✅ Component pods Ready:  oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications
  ✅ Monitoring pods Ready: oc get pods -n redhat-ods-monitoring

  ⚠️ RED FLAGS:
    • Operator pod CrashLoopBackOff → Check logs: oc logs -n redhat-ods-operator deploy/rhods-operator
    • CSV stuck in "Installing" → Check InstallPlan: oc get installplan -n redhat-ods-operator
    • DSC Phase "Pending" → Some components failed to deploy, check DSC conditions

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: When your team reports "the AI dashboard is slow," you need to know WHERE to look. The operator in redhat-ods-operator may be fine, but a dashboard pod in redhat-ods-applications could be OOMKilled. Or model serving might be down because the KServe controller in redhat-ods-applications is CrashLoopBackOff. Knowing the namespace mapping means you can pinpoint issues in seconds instead of minutes.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: You may get a task like "Verify the RHOAI installation is healthy." Run the verification checklist above. If any pod is not Running, check its logs with oc logs. If a component is missing, check the DSC spec to see if it's enabled. This 3-namespace pattern is tested on nearly every EX267 exam.

Install RHOAI Q4 of 200
What is the purpose of the Subscription "channel" when installing the RHOAI Operator, and which channel should you use for a production EX267 exam environment?
A) The channel controls which namespace the operator deploys into — "stable" means redhat-ods-operator, "fast" means openshift-operators
B) The channel is cosmetic only — it's a label used by the OpenShift dashboard for display purposes and doesn't affect operator behavior
C) The channel controls access permissions — "stable" grants cluster-admin, "fast" grants namespace-admin to the operator's service account
D) The channel controls which version stream of the operator you receive — "stable" provides thoroughly tested releases, "fast" gives earlier access to new features, and "candidate" is pre-release
✅ Correct Answer: D

The Subscription channel determines which version stream of the operator OLM will install and keep updated. This is part of OLM's update graph — each channel represents a different upgrade path. stable: GA releases, thoroughly tested, recommended for production. fast: Earlier access to features, more frequent updates, suitable for development. candidate: Pre-release builds, may contain bugs, for testing only. For the EX267 exam, always use the channel specified in the task instructions — typically stable unless told otherwise. Changing channels after installation triggers an automatic upgrade (or downgrade) to the latest CSV in that channel.

📝 Detailed Explanation
OLM Subscription Channels — Version Streams & Update Graph
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    OLM CHANNEL ARCHITECTURE                               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Subscription: rhods-operator                                            │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │  spec:                                                           │     │
  │  │    name: rhods-operator                                          │     │
  │  │    channel: stable         ← Controls version stream             │     │
  │  │    source: redhat-operators                                      │     │
  │  │    sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace                         │     │
  │  │    installPlanApproval: Automatic  ← or Manual                   │     │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CHANNEL     VERSION     RISK        USE CASE                            │
  │  ─────────   ───────     ────        ────────                            │
  │  candidate   v2.15.0-rc  HIGH        Pre-release testing, CI validation  │
  │     │                                                                     │
  │     └──▶ fast      v2.14.0     MEDIUM      Dev/staging, early adopters  │
  │              │                                                             │
  │              └──▶ stable    v2.13.1     LOW         PRODUCTION clusters   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  REAL EX267 COMMANDS:                                                    │
  │  ───────────────────                                                     │
  │  # Check current channel                                                 │
  │  oc get subscription rhods-operator -o yaml | grep channel               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  # Change channel (triggers upgrade!)                                    │
  │  oc patch subscription rhods-operator --type=merge -p \                  │
  │    '{"spec":{"channel":"stable"}}'                                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  # Check what versions are available in each channel                     │
  │  oc get packagemanifest rhods-operator -o yaml | grep -A10 channels      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚠️  IMPORTANT: installPlanApproval                                      │
  │     • Automatic: OLM auto-approves upgrades (default, easier)            │
  │     • Manual: You must approve each upgrade (more control, exam may ask) │
  │     → Manual approval: oc patch installplan <name> --type=merge \       │
  │         -p '{"spec":{"approved":true}}'                                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: If your anihpj AI team is testing a new KServe feature available only in the fast channel, you'd switch the subscription channel — but this upgrades the ENTIRE RHOAI platform, potentially affecting existing workbenches and pipelines. Choosing stable for production ensures the job-matching model server, RAG pipeline, and salary predictor stay on thoroughly tested versions. Understanding channel switching is also how you'd plan a controlled RHOAI upgrade for the jobpost platform.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: A common task is "Switch the RHOAI Operator to the stable channel and approve the pending upgrade." The two commands you need: oc patch subscription rhods-operator --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"channel":"stable"}}' and oc patch installplan <name> --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"approved":true}}' (if Manual approval).

Install RHOAI Q5 of 200
Which of the following is a prerequisite for enabling the KServe component in the DataScienceCluster (DSC)? The KServe component will fail to become Ready without it.
A) The Red Hat OpenShift Serverless and ServiceMesh operators must be installed — KServe depends on Knative Serving and Istio for its networking and auto-scaling capabilities
B) An NVIDIA GPU Operator must be installed on at least one worker node, because KServe requires GPU acceleration for all model serving runtimes
C) An S3-compatible object storage bucket must be created and configured as a data connection before KServe can be enabled in the DSC
D) A Model Registry instance must be created first, because KServe pulls all models from the registry and cannot function without one
✅ Correct Answer: A

KServe has hard dependencies on two other OpenShift operators: Red Hat OpenShift Serverless (which provides Knative Serving) and Red Hat OpenShift ServiceMesh (which provides Istio). These are NOT automatically installed when you install RHOAI — you must install them separately BEFORE enabling KServe in the DSC. If you enable kserve: { enabled: true } without these dependencies, the DSC will show kserve: NotReady in its status conditions with an error message about missing dependencies. KServe uses Knative for its Serverless deployment mode (scale-to-zero, request-based autoscaling) and Istio for ingress networking to model endpoints.

  VERIFICATION — Check KServe Dependencies:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  # Check Serverless operator
  oc get csv -n openshift-serverless | grep serverless
  oc get pods -n knative-serving

  # Check ServiceMesh operator
  oc get csv -n openshift-operators | grep servicemesh
  oc get pods -n istio-system

  # Then check KServe in DSC
  oc get dsc default-dsc -o yaml | grep -A10 kserve

  ⚠️  SYMPTOM OF MISSING DEPENDENCIES:
      DSC status shows: "kserve: NotReady — dependency Serverless not found"
      → Install Serverless operator → Wait for CSV Succeeded → DSC auto-recovers

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: When your team wants to deploy the job-matching model or salary predictor as an InferenceService, KServe MUST be functional. If you enable KServe in the DSC without Serverless/ServiceMesh, the RHOAI operator will show KServe as NotReady, and your data scientists won't be able to deploy models. The anihpj-api won't be able to call the model endpoint for inference, breaking the AI-powered features. Always install the dependency operators first, verify they're healthy, THEN enable KServe.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: You'll likely be asked to "Enable model serving on the RHOAI platform." The correct sequence is: 1) Install Serverless & ServiceMesh operators, 2) Wait for their CSVs to reach Succeeded, 3) Edit DSC: oc edit dsc default-dsc → set kserve: { enabled: true }, 4) Verify: oc get dsc -o yaml | grep -A5 kserve shows Ready=true.

Install RHOAI Q6 of 200
The RHOAI Operator pod in redhat-ods-operator is CrashLoopBackOff. What is the FIRST command you should run to diagnose why?
A) oc delete pod -n redhat-ods-operator --all and wait for the ReplicaSet to recreate them — this resolves most operator issues
B) oc logs -n redhat-ods-operator deployment/rhods-operator --tail=50 to view the operator's recent log output and identify the error
C) oc get events -n redhat-ods-operator --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' — events always contain the root cause of operator failures
D) Reinstall the RHOAI Operator by deleting the Subscription and CSV — this is the recommended approach for operator pod failures
✅ Correct Answer: B

When an operator pod is CrashLoopBackOff, logs are always your first stop. Run oc logs -n redhat-ods-operator deployment/rhods-operator --tail=50 to see the most recent 50 lines of log output. The operator's log will tell you EXACTLY what failed — whether it's an RBAC permission issue ("forbidden"), a missing CRD dependency, a leader election failure, or an API server connectivity problem. Never delete and reinstall as a first step — you'll lose the error state and the problem will likely recur. Events (option C) are useful but often less detailed than the operator's own structured logging. Deleting pods (option A) just restarts the issue without diagnosing it.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Operator Troubleshooting Flow — CrashLoopBackOff Diagnosis
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           DIAGNOSING A CRASHING RHOAI OPERATOR — Step by Step            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1: Check pod status                                                │
  │  ───────────────────────                                                 │
  │  $ oc get pods -n redhat-ods-operator                                    │
  │  NAME                              READY   STATUS             RESTARTS    │
  │  rhods-operator-xxxxxxxxxx-xxxxx   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   12          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 2: View logs (MOST IMPORTANT!)                                     │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────                                      │
  │  $ oc logs -n redhat-ods-operator deployment/rhods-operator --tail=100   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Common log errors and what they mean:                                   │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ LOG MESSAGE                         ROOT CAUSE                    │    │
  │  │ ─────────────────────────────────   ───────────────────────       │    │
  │  │ "forbidden: cannot get resource"   → RBAC: ClusterRole missing    │    │
  │  │ "no matches for kind DSC"          → CRD not installed            │    │
  │  │ "connect: connection refused"      → API server unreachable       │    │
  │  │ "leader election: failed to renew" → Lease conflict, multi-pod    │    │
  │  │ "OOMKilled" (exit code 137)        → Memory limit too low         │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 3: Check previous crashed container logs                           │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────                              │
  │  $ oc logs -n redhat-ods-operator deployment/rhods-operator --previous   │
  │  → Shows logs from the PREVIOUS crashed instance (exit reason!)          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 4: Describe the pod for events                                     │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────                                     │
  │  $ oc describe pod -n redhat-ods-operator <pod-name>                     │
  │  → Look at "Events" section for OOMKilled, BackOff, Liveness failures    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 5: Check operator CSV status                                       │
  │  ───────────────────────────────                                         │
  │  $ oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator                                     │
  │  → Is the CSV at phase: Succeeded? If not, check the CSV's status.reason │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: If the RHOAI operator is down, EVERY AI feature breaks — the dashboard won't load, workbenches can't be created, pipelines won't run, and models can't be served. Your data science team can't access Jupyter to build the job-matching model, and the anihpj-api can't call the salary predictor. Diagnosing operator failures quickly means understanding the log-first approach: oc logs → identify error → fix root cause → verify CSV is Succeeded.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: You may face a broken RHOAI installation in the exam. The task might say "The RHOAI operator is not healthy. Fix it." Your flow: oc get pods -n redhat-ods-operator → oc logs deploy/rhods-operator --tail=100 → find the error → fix (likely RBAC, missing CRD, or image pull issue) → verify with oc get csv.

Install RHOAI Q7 of 200
You set the Subscription's installPlanApproval to "Manual". After switching the channel to "stable", the new version is not installed. What must you do?
A) Delete and recreate the Subscription — Manual approval requires the Subscription to be recreated to pick up pending upgrades
B) Run oc rollout restart deployment/rhods-operator — the operator needs a restart to detect the pending InstallPlan
C) Find the pending InstallPlan and approve it: oc get installplan -n redhat-ods-operator and oc patch installplan <name> --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"approved":true}}'
D) Wait — Manual mode means OLM waits 24 hours before applying any upgrade, regardless of your approval
✅ Correct Answer: C

When installPlanApproval: Manual is set in the Subscription, OLM will NEVER automatically apply an upgrade. It creates an InstallPlan with approved: false and waits for an administrator to explicitly approve it. You need to: (1) Find the pending InstallPlan with oc get installplan -n redhat-ods-operator, (2) Look for one with APPROVED: false, and (3) Approve it with oc patch installplan <name> --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"approved":true}}'. The OLM will then proceed with the upgrade. This mechanism gives you control over WHEN upgrades happen — critical for production environments where you want to validate new versions in staging first.

📝 Detailed Explanation
InstallPlan Approval Flow — Manual vs Automatic
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     INSTALLPLAN — Manual Approval Flow                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Subscription                                            InstallPlan      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐     creates     ┌────────────────┐  │
  │  │ spec:                           │──────────────▶  │ APPROVED: false│  │
  │  │   channel: stable               │                 │ (waiting...)   │  │
  │  │   installPlanApproval: Manual   │                 └───────┬────────┘  │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────┘                         │           │
  │                                                              │           │
  │                                          Admin approves ────┘           │
  │                                          ┌──────────────────────────┐    │
  │                                          │ $ oc get installplan     │    │
  │                                          │ NAME            APPROVED │    │
  │                                          │ install-xxxxx   false    │    │
  │                                          │                          │    │
  │                                          │ $ oc patch installplan \ │    │
  │                                          │   install-xxxxx \        │    │
  │                                          │   --type=merge \         │    │
  │                                          │   -p '{"spec":{          │    │
  │                                          │     "approved":true}}'   │    │
  │                                          └──────────┬───────────────┘    │
  │                                                     │                    │
  │                                                     ▼                    │
  │                                          ┌──────────────────────────┐    │
  │                                          │ OLM applies CSV changes  │    │
  │                                          │ Operator pod restarts    │    │
  │                                          │ New version is active!   │    │
  │                                          └──────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  AUTOMATIC vs MANUAL — When to use each:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  Automatic (default):                      Manual:
  • Dev/test environments                   • Production clusters
  • CI/CD pipelines                         • Staged rollouts
  • When you always want latest             • When you need to validate first
  • OLM auto-approves all upgrades          • You control timing of upgrades

  ⚠️  EXAM SCENARIO:
  You switch channel stable→fast but version doesn't change.
  → Check: oc get subscription rhods-operator -o yaml | grep installPlanApproval
  → If "Manual": You MUST approve the InstallPlan!

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: In production, you NEVER want RHOAI to auto-upgrade during business hours. Your data scientists might be training a model or running a pipeline when the operator restarts. Manual approval lets you schedule upgrades during maintenance windows. For the anihpj/jobpost platform, you'd approve the InstallPlan at 2 AM on Sunday, verify the DSC components all return to Ready, then confirm the job-matching model server and RAG pipeline are still functional before Monday morning.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: A classic exam task: "The RHOAI Operator is configured for Manual approval. Approve the pending upgrade." Your two commands: oc get installplan -n redhat-ods-operator to find the name, then oc patch installplan <name> --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"approved":true}}'. Verify with oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator.

Install RHOAI Q8 of 200
After installing the RHOAI Operator, how do you verify that the necessary CRDs (Custom Resource Definitions) like DataScienceCluster, Notebook, and InferenceService are properly created?
A) oc get crd | grep opendatahub — all RHOAI CRDs use the opendatahub.io API group, so this filters to show only RHOAI-specific CRDs
B) oc get crd --all-namespaces — CRDs are namespaced resources, so you must check all namespaces for RHOAI-specific CRDs
C) Look at the operator pod's environment variables — CRD names are listed in the OPERATOR_CRDS env var of the rhods-operator pod
D) Check the OpenShift AI dashboard at the "Installed Operators" page — CRDs are only visible through the console, not via CLI
✅ Correct Answer: A

CRDs are cluster-scoped resources (not namespaced), so oc get crd works without a namespace flag. RHOAI CRDs all belong to the opendatahub.io API group. Running oc get crd | grep opendatahub lists all RHOAI-specific CRDs: DataScienceCluster, DataScienceProject (DSP), Notebook, InferenceService, ServingRuntime, DataSciencePipelineApplication (DSPA), ModelRegistry, TrustyAI, and more. If CRDs are missing, the operator pod likely failed during its startup reconciliation and you should check its logs. The dashboard displays CRs (instances of CRDs), not the CRDs themselves.

📝 Detailed Explanation
RHOAI CRDs — What Gets Created at Install Time
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    RHOAI CRD INVENTORY (opendatahub.io)                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  $ oc get crd | grep opendatahub                                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │  CRD NAME                                PURPOSE                │     │
  │  │  ─────────────────────────────────────   ─────────────────────  │     │
  │  │  datascienceclusters.datasciencecluster  🏗️  Master platform    │     │
  │  │  datascienceprojects.opendatahub.io      📁  Team projects      │     │
  │  │  notebooks.kubeflow.org                   📓  Workbenches       │     │
  │  │  inferenceservices.serving.kserve.io     🚀  Model serving      │     │
  │  │  servingruntimes.serving.kserve.io       ⚙️  vLLM, OVMS, TGIS  │     │
  │  │  trainingoperators...                    🏋️  Distributed train  │     │
  │  │  datasciencepipelines...                 🔄  KFP pipelines      │     │
  │  │  modelregistries.modelregistry...        📦  Model versioning   │     │
  │  │  trustyais.trustyai.opendatahub.io       📊  Bias/Drift detect  │     │
  │  │  accelerators.accelerator...             🎮  GPU/FPGA profiles  │     │
  │  │  odhdashboards.dashboard...              🖥️  Console UI config  │     │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CRD LIFECYCLE:                                                           │
  │  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐        │
  │  │ Operator │────▶│ OLM      │────▶│ CRDs     │────▶│ You can  │        │
  │  │ installed│     │ creates  │     │ appear   │     │ oc apply │        │
  │  │          │     │ CRDs     │     │ in API   │     │ CRs!     │        │
  │  └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┘        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚠️  CRDs are CLUSTER-SCOPED — NOT namespaced!                           │
  │  → oc get crd (no -n flag needed)                                        │
  │  → If CRDs missing: operator didn't finish startup reconciliation       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Before your team can create workbenches or deploy models, the CRDs must exist. If you try oc apply -f notebook.yaml and get "no matches for kind Notebook", the Notebook CRD isn't installed — the RHOAI operator may not have finished its initial reconciliation, or it may have encountered an error during CRD creation. Always verify CRDs are present before telling your team "the AI platform is ready."

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: A task might ask you to "Verify that the RHOAI platform components are ready for use." Part of your verification should include oc get crd | grep opendatahub to ensure all CRDs exist, then check the DSC status, then check component pods. CRD verification is often the fastest way to confirm the platform installed correctly.

Install RHOAI Q9 of 200
What happens when you delete the DataScienceCluster (DSC) instance that was created after RHOAI installation?
A) Only the DSC CR is deleted — all running components (dashboard, workbenches, KServe) continue to operate because they were already deployed as standalone pods
B) The RHOAI operator reconciles the deletion and removes all platform components (dashboard, workbenches, KServe, pipelines, monitoring) — effectively uninstalling the AI platform while keeping the operator itself
C) The DSC is protected by a finalizer and cannot be deleted — you must first delete all DataScienceProjects before the DSC can be removed
D) Deleting the DSC also deletes the RHOAI Operator and Subscription — this fully uninstalls RHOAI from the cluster
✅ Correct Answer: B

The DSC is the declarative desired state — it tells the RHOAI operator "I want these components." When you delete the DSC, the operator sees "desired state = nothing" and cleans up all components: dashboard pods, workbench controllers, KServe controller, pipeline server, model registry, TrustyAI monitoring — everything. However, the RHOAI Operator itself keeps running (Subscription, CSV, operator pod remain). This means you can recreate a DSC to redeploy the platform without reinstalling the operator. The DSC may also have a finalizer that blocks deletion until its owned resources are properly cleaned up. This design follows the Kubernetes operator pattern: the operator reconciles the world to match the DSC spec, including the "empty" state.

📝 Detailed Explanation
DSC Lifecycle — Create, Modify, Delete
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              DSC RECONCILIATION LOOP — Three States                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STATE 1: CREATE DSC             STATE 2: MODIFY DSC                     │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────┐                  │
  │  │ No DSC exists       │        │ DSC exists          │                  │
  │  │ Operator is idle    │        │ You change spec     │                  │
  │  └─────────┬───────────┘        └─────────┬───────────┘                  │
  │            │                              │                               │
  │            ▼                              ▼                               │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────┐                  │
  │  │ You create DSC      │        │ kserve.enabled:     │                  │
  │  │ with components:    │        │   true→false        │                  │
  │  │  dashboard: true    │        │ Operator removes    │                  │
  │  │  workbenches: true  │        │ ONLY KServe pods    │                  │
  │  │  kserve: true       │        │                     │                  │
  │  └─────────┬───────────┘        └─────────────────────┘                  │
  │            │                                                              │
  │            ▼                                                              │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │  Operator deploys:                                               │     │
  │  │  🖥️  dashboard      → odh-dashboard pod                         │     │
  │  │  📓  workbenches     → notebook-controller pod                   │     │
  │  │  🚀  kserve          → kserve-controller pod                     │     │
  │  │  🔄  pipelines       → ds-pipeline pod                           │     │
  │  │  📦  modelregistry   → modelregistry-operator pod               │     │
  │  │  📊  trustyai        → trustyai-service pod                      │     │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STATE 3: DELETE DSC                                                     │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐                                                │
  │  │ DSC is deleted      │                                                │
  │  │ Operator sees       │                                                │
  │  │ "desired = nothing" │                                                │
  │  └─────────┬───────────┘                                                │
  │            │                                                              │
  │            ▼                                                              │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │  ❌ DELETED:           ✅ SURVIVES:                              │     │
  │  │  • Dashboard pod       • RHOAI Operator pod                      │     │
  │  │  • KServe controller   • Subscription & CSV                      │     │
  │  │  • Pipeline server     • DataScienceProjects (namespaces!)       │     │
  │  │  • Model Registry      • Inside projects: Notebooks, ISVCs       │     │
  │  │  • TrustyAI monitoring • User-created resources                  │     │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚠️  KEY INSIGHT: DSC owns PLATFORM components, NOT user resources!     │
  │     Recreate DSC → All platform services return → Projects intact.      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: If someone accidentally deletes the DSC, the dashboard and KServe controller disappear — but your data science projects and the workbenches/models inside them SURVIVE. The anihpj project namespace, its Jupyter workbenches, and deployed InferenceServices are not affected. This is because DataScienceProjects are independent CRs, not owned by the DSC. You can recreate the DSC, and once the KServe controller is back, your models will start serving again. Understanding what the DSC owns vs doesn't own prevents panic during platform incidents.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: You might get a task like "Disable the KServe component without deleting the entire platform." You edit the DSC (oc edit dsc default-dsc) and set kserve: { enabled: false }. The operator will clean up only KServe-related pods. To re-enable, set it back to true. This is safer than deleting the entire DSC.

Install RHOAI Q10 of 200
The DSC status shows "workbenches: NotReady". You check and the notebook-controller pod is CrashLoopBackOff. What is the most likely cause?
A) The DataScienceCluster CR has a YAML syntax error in the workbenches section — indentation errors cause the operator to skip deployment
B) The cluster has run out of CPU/memory resources — the notebook controller requires at least 8 CPU and 32GB RAM to start
C) The workbenches component requires an external S3 bucket to be configured before it can start — the controller checks for a DataConnection CR
D) The notebook-controller is failing due to missing RBAC permissions, an image pull error, or an incompatible version — check logs with oc logs -n redhat-ods-applications deployment/notebook-controller
✅ Correct Answer: D

When a DSC component shows NotReady, the troubleshooting flow is the same as any Kubernetes pod issue. The most common causes are: RBAC (the controller's ServiceAccount lacks permissions to create Notebook CRs or manage PVCs), Image pull errors (wrong image tag, private registry without pull secret), OOMKilled (memory limit too low for the controller), or version incompatibility (the controller image doesn't match the operator version). Use oc describe pod to check Events and oc logs to see the actual error. The controller does NOT need a pre-configured S3 bucket (option C) and has modest resource requirements (not 8 CPU/32GB — option B).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Component NotReady — Systematic Debugging Flow
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              DSC COMPONENT "NotReady" — TROUBLESHOOTING TREE             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  $ oc describe dsc default-dsc | grep -A10 Conditions                    │
  │  Conditions:                                                              │
  │    - type: WorkbenchesReady                                               │
  │      status: "False"                                                      │
  │      reason: "ComponentNotReady"                                          │
  │      message: "notebook-controller deployment not available"              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ▼ FIRST: Check the component's pods                                     │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ $ oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications | grep notebook         │    │
  │  │ notebook-controller-xxx   0/1  CrashLoopBackOff   15             │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ▼ SECOND: Check pod events (WHY is it crashing?)                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ $ oc describe pod -n redhat-ods-applications notebook-controller-xxx│  │
  │  │ Events:                                                            │    │
  │  │   Back-off restarting failed container                             │    │
  │  │   → Now check LOGS!                                                │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ▼ THIRD: Check logs                                                     │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ $ oc logs -n redhat-ods-applications deploy/notebook-controller   │    │
  │  │   --tail=50                                                        │    │
  │  │                                                                    │    │
  │  │ COMMON LOG ERROR FIXES:                                            │    │
  │  │ • "forbidden: notebooks.kubeflow.org is forbidden"                │    │
  │  │   → Fix: Check SA ClusterRole for Notebook CRD permissions        │    │
  │  │ • "dial tcp: i/o timeout" → API server unreachable                │    │
  │  │ • "ImagePullBackOff" → Fix image tag or image pull secret         │    │
  │  │ • "OOMKilled" → Increase memory limits in controller Deployment   │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: If the notebook-controller is down, your data science team can't create or manage workbenches. They can't launch Jupyter to build the job-matching model or fine-tune the salary predictor. But here's the key insight: existing running workbenches are NOT affected — only NEW workbench creation fails. The controller manages the lifecycle of Notebook CRs, but once a workbench pod is running, it operates independently. This means your team can continue working in already-launched workbenches while you fix the controller.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: For ANY DSC component NotReady: 1) Check DSC conditions for the error message, 2) Find the component's pod in redhat-ods-applications, 3) oc describe pod for events, 4) oc logs deploy/<component> for the actual error. The logs will tell you if it's RBAC, image, network, or memory — then you fix that specific issue.

1.2 Platform Governance & Access ManagementQ11-Q20

Install RHOAI Q11 of 200
What is a Data Science Project (DSP) in OpenShift AI, and how does it differ from a regular OpenShift namespace?
A) A DSP is identical to a namespace — it's just a cosmetic label in the dashboard with no technical difference
B) A DSP is an OpenShift namespace with additional RHOAI-specific annotations and resources — it creates the namespace AND configures it for AI workloads (workbenches, data connections, pipeline servers)
C) A DSP is a completely separate Kubernetes API resource that exists outside of namespaces — it manages AI resources at the cluster level
D) A DSP is only a dashboard concept — all configuration is stored in the browser's localStorage and has no Kubernetes representation
✅ Correct Answer: B

A Data Science Project (DSP) is a regular OpenShift namespace enhanced with RHOAI-specific configuration. When you create a DSP through the dashboard (or via the DataScienceProject CR), it: (1) Creates an OpenShift namespace, (2) Adds the opendatahub.io/dashboard: 'true' label so the dashboard recognizes it, (3) Creates default RBAC (admin/edit/view RoleBindings), (4) Sets up default NetworkPolicy for project isolation, and (5) Enables you to create AI-specific resources inside: Notebook workbenches, data connections (S3), pipeline servers, model servers, and storage mounts. The key insight: a DSP IS a namespace, but not all namespaces are DSPs — only labeled ones appear in the OpenShift AI dashboard.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Data Science Project — Namespace + AI Configuration
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              DATA SCIENCE PROJECT — What Makes It Special                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  REGULAR NAMESPACE          DATA SCIENCE PROJECT (DSP)                   │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │ my-app           │      │ anihpj (namespace)                    │     │
  │  │ Labels: {}       │      │ Labels:                               │     │
  │  │                  │      │   opendatahub.io/dashboard: 'true' ───┤     │
  │  │                  │      │                                       │     │
  │  │                  │      │ 🗂️  AI Resources Inside DSP:          │     │
  │  │                  │      │  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐  │     │
  │  │                  │      │  │ 📓 Notebook (Jupyter/VS Code)   │  │     │
  │  │                  │      │  │ 🔗 DataConnection (S3 bucket)   │  │     │
  │  │                  │      │  │ 🔄 Pipeline Server (KFP)        │  │     │
  │  │                  │      │  │ 🚀 InferenceService (KServe)    │  │     │
  │  │                  │      │  │ 💾 PVC (storage for notebooks)  │  │     │
  │  │                  │      │  └─────────────────────────────────┘  │     │
  │  └──────────────────┘      └──────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CREATION METHODS:                                                       │
  │  ─────────────────                                                       │
  │  Dashboard: Data Science Projects → Create project → name + description  │
  │  CLI: oc new-project anihpj                                              │
  │        oc label namespace anihpj opendatahub.io/dashboard=true           │
  │  CR:   Create a DataScienceProject CR (auto-labels namespace)            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RBAC AUTO-CONFIGURED:                                                   │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                    │
  │  Admin  → Full control (create/delete workbenches, manage pipelines)     │
  │  Edit   → Create/modify workbenches, deploy models, run pipelines        │
  │  View   → Read-only access to project resources                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your data science team needs their own isolated DSP called "anihpj" where they can launch Jupyter workbenches to build the job-matching model, create S3 connections to store training data, deploy the pipeline server for automated retraining, and serve the salary predictor via KServe — all within a single project. Without the DSP label, the workbench and pipeline options won't appear in the dashboard, even though the namespace exists.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: A common task: "Create a Data Science Project called 'ml-team' and grant user 'alice' edit access." Either use the dashboard OR do it via CLI: oc new-project ml-team && oc label namespace ml-team opendatahub.io/dashboard=true && oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit alice -n ml-team.

Install RHOAI Q12 of 200
How do you manage which users can access the OpenShift AI dashboard and what they can do within Data Science Projects?
A) RHOAI has its own built-in user database — you create users directly in the OpenShift AI dashboard under "User Management"
B) Dashboard access is controlled by a single "RHOAI Users" ConfigMap — adding a username to the list grants full platform access
C) RHOAI uses OpenShift's native RBAC — you add users to OpenShift Groups, then bind those groups to project-level Roles (admin/edit/view) and optionally cluster-level ClusterRoles for platform-wide settings
D) Access is controlled entirely through the DSC — you list allowed users in the DataScienceCluster spec.components.dashboard.allowedUsers field
✅ Correct Answer: C

RHOAI has no separate user management system — it inherits OpenShift's identity and RBAC. Users authenticate via OpenShift's configured identity provider (LDAP, OAuth, HTPasswd, etc.). Access is then controlled by OpenShift Groups + RBAC: you create groups like data-scientists and ml-admins, add users to them, then bind those groups to project-level Roles using oc adm policy add-role-to-group. For platform-wide admin settings (modifying the DSC, managing operator configuration), users need cluster-level ClusterRole bindings. RHOAI does NOT have its own user database, ConfigMap-based access, or DSC-level user lists.

📝 Detailed Explanation
RHOAI Access Control — OpenShift RBAC Integration
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 RHOAI ACCESS CONTROL ARCHITECTURE                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  IDENTITY PROVIDER (OpenShift OAuth)                                     │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  LDAP / HTPasswd / GitHub / OIDC → Authenticates users           │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │           │                                                               │
  │           ▼                                                               │
  │  OPENSHIFT GROUPS (oc get groups)                                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  data-scientists:  alice, bob, charlie                           │    │
  │  │  ml-admins:        diana, eve                                    │    │
  │  │  viewers:          frank, grace                                  │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │           │                                                               │
  │           ▼                                                               │
  │  PROJECT-LEVEL RBAC (per DSP namespace)                                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  RoleBindings in namespace "anihpj":                              │    │
  │  │    admin → Group: ml-admins    (full control of project)         │    │
  │  │    edit  → Group: data-scientists (create workbenches, deploy)   │    │
  │  │    view  → Group: viewers      (read-only)                       │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CLUSTER-LEVEL RBAC (platform management)                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  ClusterRoleBinding:                                              │    │
  │  │    cluster-admin → Group: ml-admins (modify DSC, install ops)    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  KEY COMMANDS:                                                            │
  │  ────────────                                                             │
  │  oc adm groups new data-scientists                                       │
  │  oc adm groups add-users data-scientists alice bob                       │
  │  oc adm policy add-role-to-group edit data-scientists -n anihpj          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your anihpj team has 3 data scientists (alice, bob, charlie) who need edit access to the anihpj DSP to create workbenches and deploy models, and 1 ML admin (diana) who needs admin access to manage pipelines and the model registry. Instead of binding each user individually, you create a anihpj-team group and bind it once. When a new member joins, just add them to the group — no need to touch RoleBindings.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: You may need to "Grant the data-scientists group edit access to the ml-project." Command: oc adm policy add-role-to-group edit data-scientists -n ml-project. To verify: oc auth can-i create notebooks --as=alice -n ml-project.

Install RHOAI Q13 of 200
In a Data Science Project, a user with the "Edit" role tries to delete the project's pipeline server but receives "forbidden". Why?
A) Deleting a pipeline server requires "Admin" role — the "Edit" role allows creating/modifying workbenches and deploying models, but not deleting infrastructure components like pipeline servers
B) Pipeline servers are cluster-scoped resources — they cannot be deleted from within a project, regardless of role
C) The pipeline server has a finalizer that blocks deletion until all pipeline runs are completed — this is not an RBAC issue
D) The user's token has expired — they need to re-authenticate before performing any destructive operations
✅ Correct Answer: A

The three DSP roles have distinct permission boundaries. Admin can do everything: create/delete workbenches, manage pipeline servers, change project settings, configure data connections. Edit can create and modify workbenches, deploy models, run pipelines — but CANNOT delete pipeline servers, change project configuration, or manage RBAC. View is read-only. This tiered model prevents data scientists from accidentally destroying shared infrastructure while still letting them do their work. In the EX267 exam, knowing exactly what each role can and cannot do is critical for RBAC troubleshooting tasks.

📝 Detailed Explanation
DSP Role Permissions Matrix
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    DSP ROLE PERMISSIONS — What Each Role Can Do          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ACTION                          ADMIN      EDIT       VIEW              │
  │  ─────────────────────────────   ─────      ────       ────              │
  │  Create workbench                 ✅         ✅         ❌                │
  │  Start/stop workbench             ✅         ✅         ❌                │
  │  Delete workbench                 ✅         ✅ (own)   ❌                │
  │  Create data connection (S3)      ✅         ✅         ❌                │
  │  Deploy model (InferenceService)  ✅         ✅         ❌                │
  │  Run pipeline                     ✅         ✅         ❌                │
  │  Create pipeline server           ✅         ❌ (1)     ❌                │
  │  Delete pipeline server           ✅         ❌         ❌                │
  │  Change project settings          ✅         ❌         ❌                │
  │  Manage RBAC (RoleBindings)       ✅         ❌         ❌                │
  │  View resources (describe/get)    ✅         ✅         ✅                │
  │  View logs                        ✅         ✅         ✅                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  (1) Pipeline servers are shared infrastructure — only admins manage    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  VERIFY ROLE:                                                            │
  │  ───────────                                                             │
  │  $ oc auth can-i delete datasciencepipelines --as=bob -n anihpj          │
  │  no                                                                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  $ oc get rolebinding -n anihpj                                          │
  │  NAME                 ROLE                USERS/GROUPS                   │
  │  admin                ClusterRole/admin   diana                          │
  │  edit                 ClusterRole/edit    alice, bob, charlie            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your data scientists (Edit role) should be able to launch Jupyter, train models, run pipelines, and deploy InferenceServices — but they should NOT be able to delete the shared pipeline server that the ML admin set up for automated model retraining. If alice accidentally deletes the pipeline server, the weekly job-matching model retraining breaks. The Admin/Edit/View split protects shared infrastructure while empowering individual work.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: A task might say "User bob reports he cannot create a pipeline server. Fix it." Check bob's role: oc get rolebinding -n <project>. If bob only has "edit", upgrade to "admin": oc adm policy add-role-to-user admin bob -n <project>.

Install RHOAI Q14 of 200
How do you control which applications (Jupyter, pipelines, model serving, etc.) appear in the OpenShift AI dashboard menu for users?
A) Each user customizes their own dashboard view through the Settings menu — application visibility is per-user, not centrally managed
B) Dashboard applications are controlled by individual ConfigMaps per application — you create a cm named "enable-jupyter" in each project to show the tile
C) Applications are always visible if the DSC component is enabled — you cannot hide individual dashboard tiles from users
D) Dashboard application visibility is controlled through the odh-dashboard ConfigMap in redhat-ods-applications, or via the DSC spec — administrators can enable/disable specific application tiles centrally
✅ Correct Answer: D

Dashboard customization is centrally managed through the odh-dashboard ConfigMap in the redhat-ods-applications namespace, or through the DSC spec. Administrators control which application tiles appear in the left navigation: Jupyter, TensorBoard, Pipelines, Model Serving, Model Registry, Resources, Settings, etc. This is NOT per-user — it's a platform-wide setting. If you disable "Jupyter" in the ConfigMap, NO user will see the Jupyter tile, even if workbenches are enabled in the DSC. The DSC controls whether the backend service runs; the ConfigMap controls whether the frontend tile is visible.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Dashboard Customization — ConfigMap vs DSC

  │            DASHBOARD APPLICATION VISIBILITY — Two Control Points          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  DSC (DataScienceCluster)              odh-dashboard ConfigMap            │
  │  ┌────────────────────────┐           ┌────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │ Controls: BACKEND      │           │ Controls: FRONTEND tiles   │     │
  │  │  workbenches: true     │           │  dashboard:                 │     │
  │  │  kserve: true          │           │    applications:            │     │
  │  │  pipelines: true       │           │      jupyter: enabled       │     │
