  │         │                              │      kserve: enabled       │     │
  │         │    BOTH MUST BE              │      modelRegistry: hidden │     │
  │         ├─── ENABLED FOR ─────────────┤      resources: enabled    │     │
  │         │    TILE TO APPEAR           │      settings: enabled     │     │
  │         │                              └────────────────────────────┘     │
  │  ┌──────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │  RESULT: User sees in left nav:                                  │     │
  │  │  📓 Jupyter    🔄 Pipelines    🚀 Model Serving                  │     │
  │  │  📊 Resources  ⚙️ Settings                                        │     │
  │  │  (Model Registry hidden — tile disabled in ConfigMap)            │     │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  KEY COMMANDS:                                                            │
  │  ────────────                                                             │
  │  # View current dashboard configuration                                   │
  │  oc get cm odh-dashboard-config -n redhat-ods-applications -o yaml       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  # Edit to enable/disable application tiles                              │
  │  oc edit cm odh-dashboard-config -n redhat-ods-applications              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: If your data science team only needs Jupyter workbenches and model serving for the anihpj project, you can hide the Pipelines and Model Registry tiles to simplify their dashboard. This reduces confusion — they only see what they need. Conversely, if the "Jupyter" tile is missing from the dashboard even though workbenches are enabled in the DSC, the ConfigMap may have jupyter: hidden.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: A task might say "The Jupyter tile is missing from the dashboard. Fix it." Check two places: (1) oc get dsc -o yaml | grep -A2 workbenches — is workbenches enabled? (2) oc get cm odh-dashboard-config -n redhat-ods-applications -o yaml | grep -A2 jupyter — is the tile enabled?

Install RHOAI Q15 of 200
An LDAP user cannot log into the OpenShift AI dashboard even though they can authenticate to OpenShift. What is the most likely cause?
A) The user exists in LDAP but has no RoleBinding in any Data Science Project — users need at least "view" access to a project for the dashboard to show content
B) The RHOAI dashboard has a separate authentication system — LDAP users must be manually imported into the dashboard's user database
C) The LDAP connection is configured at the OpenShift level but RHOAI requires a separate LDAP integration via the DSC spec
D) The user's LDAP group must match a group named "rhoai-users" — the dashboard only allows users from specifically named groups
✅ Correct Answer: A

RHOAI uses OpenShift's authentication — there's no separate login. But authentication ≠ authorization. A user can successfully authenticate (prove who they are) but still see an empty or inaccessible dashboard if they lack RBAC permissions on any Data Science Project. The dashboard requires at minimum view access to at least one DSP to display content. Without any project access, the dashboard loads but shows no projects. The fix is to add the user (or their LDAP group) to a project role: oc adm policy add-role-to-user view <user> -n <project> or oc adm policy add-role-to-group view <ldap-group> -n <project>.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Authentication vs Authorization in RHOAI
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              AUTHENTICATION → AUTHORIZATION → DASHBOARD                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1: AUTHENTICATION (Who are you?)                                   │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  OpenShift OAuth → LDAP / HTPasswd / GitHub / OIDC               │    │
  │  │  ✅ User "alice" authenticated successfully                       │    │
  │  │  → Alice can access the OpenShift console                         │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │           │                                                               │
  │           ▼                                                               │
  │  STEP 2: AUTHORIZATION (What can you access?)                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  RBAC Check: Does alice have ANY RoleBinding in ANY DSP?          │    │
  │  │                                                                    │    │
  │  │  ✅ alice has "edit" in namespace "anihpj"                        │    │
  │  │  → Dashboard shows "anihpj" project with Jupyter/Pipelines/etc    │    │
  │  │                                                                    │    │
  │  │  ❌ bob has NO RoleBindings in any DSP                            │    │
  │  │  → Dashboard loads but shows "No data science projects"           │    │
  │  │  → Or: Dashboard redirects to "Request access" page               │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  FIX FOR BOB:                                                            │
  │  ───────────                                                             │
  │  # Option 1: Add bob directly to the project                             │
  │  oc adm policy add-role-to-user view bob -n anihpj                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  # Option 2: Add bob's LDAP group to the project                         │
  │  oc adm policy add-role-to-group view cn=data-scientists,ou=groups \     │
  │    -n anihpj                                                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  # Verify:                                                               │
  │  oc auth can-i get notebooks --as=bob -n anihpj                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: When a new data scientist joins the anihpj team, they authenticate via corporate LDAP — that part works automatically. But until you add them (or their LDAP group) to the anihpj Data Science Project, they'll log in and see nothing. The most common support ticket: "I logged in but the dashboard is empty." The fix is always RBAC — add their group to the project.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "User 'charlie' reports they cannot see any projects in the OpenShift AI dashboard. Grant them view access to the 'ml-team' project." Command: oc adm policy add-role-to-user view charlie -n ml-team. Also check if they're in a group that already has access: oc get groups | grep charlie.

Install RHOAI Q16 of 200
An administrator wants to verify that ALL RHOAI components are healthy from the CLI without using the dashboard. What is the most comprehensive single check?
A) oc get pods --all-namespaces | grep rhods — this lists every RHOAI pod across all namespaces and is the only verification needed
B) oc describe dsc default-dsc — the DSC status.conditions show the Ready status of every enabled component, with error messages for any that failed
C) oc get csv -A | grep rhods — if the CSV is Succeeded, all components are guaranteed to be healthy
D) oc get events -n redhat-ods-applications — events always contain the current health status of every component
✅ Correct Answer: B

oc describe dsc default-dsc is the single most comprehensive health check. The DSC's status.conditions array contains individual Ready/NotReady entries for EVERY enabled component: dashboard, workbenches, datasciencepipelines, kserve, modelregistry, trustyai, and more. Each condition includes a reason and message explaining exactly what's wrong if a component is NotReady. This is far more informative than just listing pods — a pod could be Running but the component could still be degraded. Always start with the DSC status, then drill into individual pods if needed.

📝 Detailed Explanation
RHOAI Health Check — The 3-Level Verification
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            RHOAI HEALTH CHECK — From Platform to Pods                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  LEVEL 1: Operator Status (is RHOAI installed?)                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ $ oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator                               │    │
  │  │ NAME                       DISPLAY        VERSION   PHASE         │    │
  │  │ rhods-operator.v2.13.1    RHOAI Operator  2.13.1    Succeeded ✓  │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │           │                                                               │
  │           ▼                                                               │
  │  LEVEL 2: Component Status (DSC — MOST IMPORTANT!)                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ $ oc describe dsc default-dsc | grep -A3 "Conditions:"           │    │
  │  │ Conditions:                                                        │    │
  │  │   Type: Ready              Status: True   ← Platform overall     │    │
  │  │   Type: DashboardReady     Status: True   ← Dashboard            │    │
  │  │   Type: WorkbenchesReady   Status: True   ← Notebook controller   │    │
  │  │   Type: KServeReady        Status: True   ← Model serving         │    │
  │  │   Type: PipelinesReady     Status: False  ← ❌ PIPELINES DOWN!    │    │
  │  │     Message: "ds-pipeline pod CrashLoopBackOff"                    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │           │                                                               │
  │           ▼                                                               │
  │  LEVEL 3: Pod-Level Investigation (for failing components)               │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ $ oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications | grep pipeline         │    │
  │  │ ds-pipeline-xxx   0/1  CrashLoopBackOff                          │    │
  │  │                                                                    │    │
  │  │ $ oc logs -n redhat-ods-applications deploy/ds-pipeline --tail=20│    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Before a critical demo, your ML admin runs the 3-level check: CSV Succeeded → DSC all Ready → pods all Running. If the DSC shows PipelinesReady: False, the automated job-matching retraining won't run, and the model will grow stale. The DSC condition message tells you exactly which pod to investigate, saving minutes of guesswork.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: "Verify the RHOAI platform is healthy" is a common exam task. Your answer should demonstrate the 3-level check: oc get csv → oc describe dsc | grep Conditions → oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications. The DSC conditions are the most points-heavy part.

Install RHOAI Q17 of 200
What is the purpose of the odh-dashboard-config ConfigMap in the redhat-ods-applications namespace?
A) It stores user session data — each user's dashboard layout preferences and recently accessed projects are saved here
B) It contains the DSC specification — the ConfigMap is an alternative way to configure RHOAI components without using the DSC CR
C) It controls the dashboard UI configuration — which application tiles are visible, branding settings, notification banners, and feature flags that affect the user interface
D) It stores OpenShift OAuth client credentials — the dashboard uses this ConfigMap to authenticate users against the identity provider

The odh-dashboard-config ConfigMap is the centralized UI configuration for the entire OpenShift AI dashboard. Install RHOAI Q18 of 200
An administrator needs to be notified when RHOAI component health changes. How is alert/notification configuration managed in OpenShift AI?
A) RHOAI has a built-in email notification system configured through the DSC spec.notifications.email field
B) The dashboard sends browser notifications — administrators must keep the dashboard open to receive alerts
C) Notifications are configured via a separate "RHOAI Alerts" Custom Resource that sends webhooks to external systems
D) RHOAI integrates with OpenShift's monitoring stack (Prometheus + Alertmanager) — component health metrics are exposed as Prometheus metrics, and you configure Alertmanager rules for notification routing (email, Slack, PagerDuty)
✅ Correct Answer: D

RHOAI uses OpenShift's built-in monitoring stack — there is no separate notification system. Component health metrics (pod status, DSC conditions, resource usage) are exposed as Prometheus metrics in the redhat-ods-monitoring namespace. To configure alerts, you create PrometheusRule CRs to define alert conditions (e.g., "DSC component NotReady for more than 5 minutes") and configure Alertmanager for routing (email, Slack webhooks, PagerDuty). You can also create ServiceMonitor and PodMonitor CRs to scrape custom metrics from your AI workloads. The EX267 exam may test your ability to check Prometheus targets and verify metrics are being collected.

📝 Detailed Explanation
RHOAI Monitoring & Alerting Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              RHOAI MONITORING — Prometheus + Alertmanager                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  redhat-ods-monitoring namespace                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Prometheus                                                       │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │    │
  │  │  │  Metrics scraped from:                                     │    │    │
  │  │  │  • RHOAI component pods (health, resource usage)           │    │    │
  │  │  │  • DSC conditions (component Ready/NotReady)               │    │    │
  │  │  │  • KServe InferenceService (request rate, latency)         │    │    │
  │  │  │  • GPU metrics via DCGM exporter (utilization, memory)     │    │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │           │                                                               │
  │           ▼                                                               │
  │  PrometheusRule CRs → Define alert conditions                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  - alert: RHOAIComponentNotReady                                  │    │
  │  │    expr: dsc_component_ready == 0                                 │    │
  │  │    for: 5m                                                        │    │
  │  │    severity: critical                                             │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │           │                                                               │

  │  │    receivers:                                                     │    │

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: When the KServe controller goes down at 3 AM, your ML admin gets a Slack notification instead of discovering it at 9 AM when users complain the salary predictor is broken. Configure a PrometheusRule that alerts on dsc_component_ready{component="kserve"} == 0 for more than 5 minutes, routed to the #ml-ops Slack channel.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: You might be asked to "Verify that RHOAI metrics are being collected." Check Prometheus targets: oc get prometheus -n redhat-ods-monitoring and oc port-forward svc/prometheus-operated 9090 -n redhat-ods-monitoring, then browse to localhost:9090/targets.

Install RHOAI Q19 of 200
An administrator needs to configure RHOAI to use a specific default StorageClass for all workbench PVCs. Where is this configured?
A) In the DSC spec — the DSC has a devFlags or global configuration section where default platform-wide settings like StorageClass and container sizes can be specified
B) In each Data Science Project individually — each project administrator sets their own default StorageClass through the project settings
C) At the OpenShift cluster level — you set the default StorageClass annotation on the StorageClass itself, and RHOAI automatically uses the cluster default
D) In the odh-dashboard ConfigMap — StorageClass defaults are part of the dashboard UI configuration
✅ Correct Answer: A

The DSC is the central configuration hub for platform-wide settings. Beyond just enabling/disabling components, the DSC spec can include global configuration that affects all projects — such as default StorageClass for workbench PVCs, default container sizes, default notebook images, and idle timeout settings. While individual workbench creators can override these defaults, the DSC sets the platform-wide baseline. This ensures that every new workbench in every project starts with sensible, administrator-defined defaults — no need for each data scientist to remember which StorageClass to pick.

📝 Detailed Explanation
DSC — Beyond Component Toggles: Platform Defaults
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              DSC AS PLATFORM CONFIGURATION HUB                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  DSC spec — Two types of configuration:                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │  1. COMPONENT TOGGLES (what runs?)                               │     │
  │  │  components:                                                     │     │
  │  │    dashboard:    { enabled: true }                               │     │
  │  │    workbenches:  { enabled: true }                               │     │
  │  │    kserve:       { enabled: true }                               │     │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │  2. PLATFORM DEFAULTS (how things run?)                          │     │
  │  │  spec:                                                            │     │
  │  │    workbenches:                                                   │     │
  │  │      defaultStorageClass: "fast-ssd"  ← All new workbench PVCs   │     │
  │  │      defaultContainerSize: "Medium"    ← Default CPU/RAM          │     │
  │  │      idleTimeoutMinutes: 120           ← Auto-stop idle WBs       │     │
  │  │      defaultNotebookImage:             ← Default IDE image        │     │
  │  │        "quay.io/opendatahub/workbench-images:v2024a"              │     │
  │  │    kserve:                                                        │     │
  │  │      defaultServingRuntime: "ovms"     ← Default model runtime    │     │
  │  │      defaultStorageUri: "s3://models"  ← Default model location   │     │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚠️  These are DEFAULTS — users can override per workbench/model.       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You configure the DSC to use "fast-ssd" as the default StorageClass so every anihpj workbench gets fast SSD-backed PVCs automatically. You set the default container size to "Large" (8 CPU, 32GB RAM) because ML training needs more resources than standard data science work. Data scientists don't need to know about StorageClasses or container sizes — the platform defaults handle it.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Configure RHOAI to use 'gp3-csi' as the default StorageClass for all workbenches." Edit DSC: oc edit dsc default-dsc, add spec: workbenches: defaultStorageClass: "gp3-csi". Verify: create a test workbench and check its PVC: oc get pvc -n <project> -o yaml | grep storageClassName.

Install RHOAI Q20 of 200
Before enabling the TrustyAI bias-monitoring component in the DSC, what prerequisite should you verify?
A) An S3 bucket must be configured as a data connection — TrustyAI stores all bias/drift data in S3 and cannot function without it
B) The monitoring stack (Prometheus) must be operational — TrustyAI relies on Prometheus for metrics collection and the DSC's monitoring components must also be enabled
C) At least one model must be deployed via KServe — TrustyAI's initialization requires an existing InferenceService to monitor
D) A separate "TrustyAI Operator" must be installed from OperatorHub — TrustyAI is not bundled with RHOAI and requires an additional operator subscription
✅ Correct Answer: B

TrustyAI is part of RHOAI's monitoring stack and depends on Prometheus running in the redhat-ods-monitoring namespace. Before enabling TrustyAI in the DSC, verify that: (1) The monitoring namespace exists and Prometheus is running, (2) The DSC has the monitoring components enabled (some configurations tie TrustyAI to a parent monitoring flag), (3) Prometheus is successfully scraping metrics from RHOAI components. If Prometheus is down, TrustyAI will fail to initialize. TrustyAI does NOT require a separate operator subscription (it's bundled), does NOT require S3 (it uses Prometheus TSDB), and does NOT require an existing InferenceService (it can be enabled before any models are deployed).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Component Dependency Verification — Before You Enable

  │              COMPONENT DEPENDENCY MAP — Enable Order Matters              │
  │                                                                          │

  │  │  COMPONENT       DEPENDS ON              VERIFY WITH             │     │
  │  │  ─────────       ───────────             ──────────              │     │

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: When your team wants bias monitoring on the job-matching model (is the model favoring certain demographics?), you enable TrustyAI. But if Prometheus isn't running, TrustyAI fails silently. The DSC condition will show TrustyAIReady: False with a message about Prometheus connectivity. Following the pre-enable checklist prevents the "I enabled it but it's broken" support ticket.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Before enabling ANY component with dependencies, run: oc get pods -n redhat-ods-monitoring (for TrustyAI/Prometheus), oc get csv -n openshift-serverless (for KServe), oc get pods -n nvidia-gpu-operator (for GPU features). The exam expects you to verify dependencies BEFORE enabling components.

1.3 GPU & Accelerator SetupQ21-Q30

Install RHOAI Q21 of 200
What must be installed on an OpenShift cluster before any pod can request NVIDIA GPUs via nvidia.com/gpu?
A) Nothing — OpenShift automatically detects NVIDIA GPUs and makes them available as a schedulable resource on GPU-equipped nodes
B) The NVIDIA GPU Operator — it installs GPU drivers, the container toolkit, device plugin, and DCGM exporter, making nvidia.com/gpu an allocatable node resource
C) The CUDA toolkit installed directly on each worker node via yum/apt — the device plugin is built into the kubelet
D) A GPU-enabled container runtime like nvidia-container-runtime configured as the default CRI — OpenShift's default CRI-O already includes GPU support
✅ Correct Answer: B

The NVIDIA GPU Operator automates the entire GPU software stack on OpenShift. It installs and manages: (1) GPU drivers (proprietary NVIDIA kernel modules), (2) NVIDIA Container Toolkit (nvidia-container-runtime + nvidia-container-toolkit), (3) Kubernetes device plugin (advertises nvidia.com/gpu as a node resource), (4) DCGM exporter (GPU metrics for Prometheus), and (5) GPU Feature Discovery (labels nodes with GPU model, CUDA version, etc.). Without the GPU Operator, nodes will show nvidia.com/gpu: 0 even if physical GPUs are installed. The operator is installed via Helm or OLM from the NVIDIA OperatorHub catalog.

📝 Detailed Explanation
NVIDIA GPU Operator — What It Installs
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 NVIDIA GPU OPERATOR — Component Stack                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  GPU Operator (nvidia-gpu-operator namespace)                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐   │    │
  │  │  │ Driver          │  │ Container       │  │ Device Plugin   │   │    │
  │  │  │ (DaemonSet)     │  │ Toolkit         │  │ (DaemonSet)     │   │    │
  │  │  │                 │  │ (DaemonSet)     │  │                 │   │    │
  │  │  │ Installs NVIDIA │  │ Configures CRI  │  │ Advertises      │   │    │
  │  │  │ kernel modules  │  │ for GPU access  │  │ nvidia.com/gpu  │   │    │
  │  │  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘   │    │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐                        │    │
  │  │  │ DCGM Exporter   │  │ GPU Feature     │                        │    │
  │  │  │ (DaemonSet)     │  │ Discovery (Job) │                        │    │
  │  │  │                 │  │                 │                        │    │
  │  │  │ GPU metrics →   │  │ Labels nodes:   │                        │    │
  │  │  │ Prometheus      │  │ GPU model, CUDA │                        │    │
  │  │  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘                        │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  INSTALLATION:                                                           │
  │  ────────────                                                            │
  │  1. Label GPU nodes: oc label node <node> nvidia.com/gpu.present=true   │
  │  2. Install via OperatorHub or Helm chart                                │
  │  3. Create ClusterPolicy CR (auto-detects GPU model)                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  VERIFICATION:                                                           │
  │  ────────────                                                            │
  │  $ oc get pods -n nvidia-gpu-operator                                    │
  │  $ oc describe node <gpu-node> | grep nvidia.com/gpu                     │
  │  nvidia.com/gpu:  4    ← 4 GPUs available!                               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The job-matching model uses a sentence transformer that requires GPU acceleration for training and inference. Without the GPU Operator, the anihpj training pipeline would run on CPU — taking hours instead of minutes. The salary prediction model running on KServe would have unacceptable latency without GPU inference. Every AI workload in anihpj depends on GPU availability managed by this operator.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Enable GPU support on the cluster." Steps: (1) Verify node has GPU: oc describe node | grep -i nvidia, (2) Install GPU Operator via OperatorHub, (3) Create ClusterPolicy, (4) Verify: oc describe node | grep nvidia.com/gpu shows allocatable GPUs > 0.

Install RHOAI Q22 of 200
A GPU node shows nvidia.com/gpu: 4, but a workbench requesting 2 GPUs stays Pending with "0/4 nodes available: 4 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu". Why?
A) Other workloads are already using all 4 GPUs — the node shows 4 total GPUs but 0 allocatable; check actual allocatable count and running GPU pod requests
B) The workbench must use the nvidia.com/mig-1g.5gb resource type — nvidia.com/gpu is deprecated and no longer supported for new workloads
C) The GPU node is cordoned — all GPU nodes are automatically cordoned after GPU Operator installation to prevent scheduling
D) Workbenches cannot use GPUs directly — you must create an AccelerationProfile first, and workbenches request GPUs through the profile, not nvidia.com/gpu
✅ Correct Answer: A

The GPU count shown by oc describe node | grep nvidia.com/gpu shows BOTH Capacity AND Allocatable. The node has 4 GPUs total, but if other pods (or the GPU Operator's own DaemonSet pods) are already using those GPUs, the allocatable count drops. Run oc describe node <node> | grep -A5 "Allocated resources" to see GPU requests vs limits. If 4 GPUs are allocated, a pod requesting 2 more gets 0. The fix is either to free up GPUs by stopping other workloads, reduce GPU requests on existing pods, or add more GPU nodes to the cluster. MIG profiles, cordoning, and AccelerationProfile requirements are not the cause here.

📝 Detailed Explanation
GPU Allocation — Capacity vs Allocatable vs Requested
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  GPU RESOURCE ACCOUNTING                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  $ oc describe node gpu-worker-1 | grep -A10 "Allocated"                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Allocated resources:                                                    │
  │    (Total limits may be over 100%)                                       │
  │    Resource        Requests      Limits                                   │
  │    ────────        ────────      ──────                                   │
  │    cpu             8000m (50%)   16000m (100%)                            │
  │    memory          32Gi (50%)    64Gi (100%)                              │
  │    nvidia.com/gpu  4 (100%)      4 (100%)    ← ALL 4 IN USE!             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  YOUR WORKBENCH REQUESTS:                                                │
  │  nvidia.com/gpu: 2                                                       │
  │  → Scheduler: "0/4 nodes available: 4 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu"       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WHAT'S USING GPUs?                                                      │
  │  ─────────────────                                                       │
  │  $ oc get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[] |   │
  │    .resources.requests."nvidia.com/gpu" != null) | .metadata.name'       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  FIX OPTIONS:                                                            │
  │  ───────────                                                             │
  │  1. Stop non-critical GPU workloads: oc delete pod <name>                │
  │  2. Reduce GPU requests on existing pods (edit deployment)               │
  │  3. Add GPU nodes to cluster                                             │
  │  4. Use GPU time-slicing (share a GPU across multiple pods)              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your team has 2 data scientists, each running a GPU workbench for model training. That's 2 GPUs in use. The KServe predictor for the salary model also uses 1 GPU. That's 3 GPUs. Then a pipeline run requests 2 GPUs for distributed training — but only 1 GPU remains free. The pipeline stays Pending. You need to either add GPU nodes or use GPU time-slicing to share GPUs across workloads.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "A workbench requesting GPUs cannot schedule. Fix it." First check: oc describe node | grep -A10 Allocated. If GPUs are fully allocated, identify consuming pods: oc get pods -A -o wide | grep <gpu-node>. Scale down non-critical workloads to free GPUs.

Install RHOAI Q23 of 200
What is GPU time-slicing in OpenShift AI, and when would you use it?
A) Time-slicing splits a GPU into isolated hardware partitions — each partition gets dedicated VRAM and compute units, enabling true multi-tenant GPU sharing
B) Time-slicing is an OpenShift scheduling policy that rotates GPU pods every 5 minutes — each pod gets exclusive GPU access for its time slice
C) Time-slicing allows multiple pods to share a single GPU by oversubscribing it — the GPU Operator's time-slicing config makes the GPU appear as N replicas, but pods share the same physical GPU without hardware isolation
D) Time-slicing automatically migrates GPU workloads between nodes to balance utilization — it's a load-balancing feature, not a GPU-sharing feature
✅ Correct Answer: C

GPU time-slicing is a software-level GPU sharing mechanism (not hardware partitioning). You configure the GPU Operator's ClusterPolicy to set a time-slicing configuration (e.g., create 4 replicas per GPU). The device plugin then reports nvidia.com/gpu: 16 instead of 4 on a 4-GPU node (4 GPUs × 4 replicas). Multiple pods can request 1 "GPU" each, but they all share the same physical GPU — there's no memory or fault isolation. This is suitable for development and light inference workloads where you want to maximize GPU utilization. For production training or LLM serving, use MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) for hardware-level isolation instead.

📝 Detailed Explanation
GPU Time-Slicing vs MIG — Sharing Strategies
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              GPU SHARING — Time-Slicing vs MIG                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  TIME-SLICING (Software, oversubscription)                               │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Physical GPU (16GB VRAM)                                         │    │
  │  │  ┌────────────┬────────────┬────────────┬────────────┐           │    │
  │  │  │ Replica 1  │ Replica 2  │ Replica 3  │ Replica 4  │           │    │
  │  │  │ (Pod A)    │ (Pod B)    │ (Pod C)    │ (Pod D)    │           │    │
  │  │  │ 16GB VRAM  │ 16GB VRAM  │ 16GB VRAM  │ 16GB VRAM  │  ← ALL    │    │
  │  │  │ (shared!)  │ (shared!)  │ (shared!)  │ (shared!)  │  SHARE    │    │
  │  │  └────────────┴────────────┴────────────┴────────────┘           │    │
  │  │  ⚠️  No memory isolation! Pod A can OOM Pod B's allocation       │    │
  │  │  ✅ Good for: Dev workbenches, light inference, Jupyter notebooks│    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) — Hardware Partitioning                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Physical GPU (A100-40GB)                                         │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────┐                      │    │
  │  │  │ MIG 2g.20gb      │ MIG 1g.10gb          │                      │    │
  │  │  │ (Pod A: training)│ (Pod B: inference)    │                      │    │
  │  │  │ 20GB isolated    │ 10GB isolated         │                      │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────┴──────────────────────┘                      │    │
  │  │  ✅ Hardware isolation! Fault in Pod A does not affect Pod B     │    │
  │  │  ✅ Good for: Production training, LLM serving, multi-tenant     │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CONFIGURATION:                                                          │
  │  ─────────────                                                           │
  │  Time-slicing: GPU Operator ClusterPolicy → timeSlicing.replicas: 4      │
  │  MIG: nvidia-smi -i 0 -mig 1  (create MIG instances on GPU 0)           │
  │       Then request: nvidia.com/mig-1g.5gb in pod spec                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: During development, 4 data scientists each need a GPU for their Jupyter workbench. Instead of buying 4 separate GPU nodes, use time-slicing to share 1 GPU across 4 workbenches. But be careful — if one person runs a large training job that consumes 14GB of the 16GB VRAM, the other 3 workbenches will crash with OOM. For production model serving, use MIG to give the KServe predictor a dedicated 10GB slice.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Configure GPU time-slicing with 4 replicas." Edit ClusterPolicy: oc edit clusterpolicy gpu-cluster-policy, add devicePlugin.config.name: time-slicing and timeSlicing.replicas: 4. Verify: oc describe node | grep nvidia.com/gpu shows 4× the original GPU count.

Install RHOAI Q24 of 200
What is an Acceleration Profile in RHOAI, and how does it help data scientists use specialized hardware?
A) An Acceleration Profile is a YAML file that data scientists write to configure their training code — it manages learning rates and batch sizes for GPU training
B) It's a dashboard UI setting that overclocks the GPU — the profile adjusts GPU clock speeds based on the workload type
C) It's an OpenShift MachineConfig that installs GPU drivers on newly provisioned nodes — the profile defines which driver version to use
D) It's a RHOAI resource that maps a friendly name to hardware requirements — data scientists select "Small GPU" or "Large GPU" from a dropdown, and the profile handles the underlying nodeSelector, tolerations, and resource requests
✅ Correct Answer: D

An Acceleration Profile is an administrator-defined abstraction that simplifies GPU access for data scientists. Instead of requiring users to know Kubernetes details like nodeSelectors, taints/tolerations, and exact resource counts, the admin creates profiles like "1-GPU-16GB" or "2-GPU-A100" that pre-configure all the underlying scheduling details. Data scientists then simply pick a profile from a dropdown when creating their workbench. The profile CR specifies: (1) which node labels to target (e.g., nvidia.com/gpu.product: A100-SXM4-40GB), (2) tolerations for GPU node taints, (3) default GPU count, and (4) description visible in the dashboard.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Acceleration Profiles — Simplifying GPU Access
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              ACCELERATION PROFILES — Admin Creates, User Selects          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ADMIN VIEW (CLI):                    USER VIEW (Dashboard):             │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐       │
  │  │ AcceleratorProfile CR:   │        │ Create Workbench:        │       │
  │  │                          │        │                          │       │
  │  │ name: small-gpu          │        │ Accelerator: [dropdown]  │       │
  │  │ displayName: "1 GPU      │        │  ▼ None                 │       │
  │  │   (16GB, T4)"            │        │    Small GPU (T4, 16GB) │       │
  │  │ enabled: true            │        │    Large GPU (A100,40GB)│       │
  │  │ tolerations:             │        │    2-GPU (A100, 80GB)  │       │
  │  │   - key: nvidia.com/gpu  │        │                          │       │
  │  │     operator: Exists     │        │ Selecting "Small GPU"    │       │
  │  │ nodeSelector:            │        │ auto-configures:         │       │
  │  │   nvidia.com/gpu.product │        │  🎮 1 GPU               │       │
  │  │     : Tesla-T4           │        │  📐 Node: GPU T4 node   │       │
  │  └──────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────┘       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WHAT THE PROFILE HANDLES AUTOMATICALLY:                                 │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────                                 │
  │  ✅ Sets nvidia.com/gpu resource request                                │
  │  ✅ Adds correct nodeSelector for GPU model                             │
  │  ✅ Adds tolerations for GPU node taints                                │
  │  ✅ Selects appropriate container size (GPU needs more CPU/RAM)         │
  │  ✅ User never sees kubectl YAML — just picks from a dropdown           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your data scientists don't need to know what a "nodeSelector" or "toleration" is. You create two profiles: "anihpj-dev-gpu" (1 T4 GPU, for development) and "anihpj-train-gpu" (2 A100 GPUs, for model training). They just pick the right profile. If you upgrade your GPU hardware, you update the profile — all existing workbenches benefit automatically on restart.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Create an Acceleration Profile for NVIDIA A100 GPUs." Create an AcceleratorProfile CR with the correct nodeSelector for nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-A100. Then verify it appears in the dashboard's accelerator dropdown.

Install RHOAI Q25 of 200
A data scientist reports "nvidia-smi works on my workbench but shows 0 GPU temperature and 0% utilization." What's happening?
A) The workbench is using GPU time-slicing — nvidia-smi shows the physical GPU but the container can't read GPU stats because time-sliced GPUs don't expose management APIs to containers
B) The GPU is faulty — zero temperature indicates the cooling fan has failed and the GPU is thermal-throttled to 0% utilization
C) The workbench has nvidia.com/gpu: 0 in its spec — the workbench was created without GPU access and nvidia-smi shows the GPU but can't use it
D) The NVIDIA drivers are not loaded — nvidia-smi is a standalone binary that shows cached data even when no drivers are present
✅ Correct Answer: A

When using GPU time-slicing, the container sees a "GPU" but it's actually a time-sliced replica. The NVIDIA device plugin, when configured with time-slicing, does NOT grant the container access to the GPU management APIs (NVML). This means nvidia-smi runs but shows 0° temperature, 0% utilization, 0W power — because the container is sandboxed from the management interface. The GPU IS being used, you just can't monitor it from inside the container. Use the DCGM exporter (cluster-level Prometheus metrics) or check node-level nvidia-smi via SSH/oc debug for actual GPU metrics. This is by design to prevent containers from interfering with each other's GPU usage on time-sliced GPUs.

📝 Detailed Explanation
GPU Monitoring — Inside Container vs Cluster-Level
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              GPU MONITORING — What Works Where                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  INSIDE CONTAINER (time-sliced GPU):                                     │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  $ nvidia-smi                                                     │    │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │    │
  │  │  │  GPU  Name        Temp   Power   Utilization               │  │    │
  │  │  │  0    Tesla-T4     N/A    N/A     0%           ← ALL N/A!  │  │    │
  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │    │
  │  │  ⚠️  NVML restricted — container can USE GPU but can't MONITOR  │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  INSIDE CONTAINER (dedicated GPU or MIG):                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  $ nvidia-smi                                                     │    │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │    │
  │  │  │  GPU  Name        Temp   Power   Utilization               │  │    │
  │  │  │  0    Tesla-T4    65°C   70W      85%          ← REAL DATA  │  │    │
  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │    │
  │  │  ✅ Full NVML access — container has exclusive or MIG GPU         │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CLUSTER-LEVEL (always works):                                           │
  │  ────────────────────────────                                            │
  │  $ oc exec -n nvidia-gpu-operator dc/dcgm-exporter -- nvidia-smi        │
  │  → DCGM exporter has full NVML access                                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  $ oc port-forward svc/dcgm-exporter 9400 -n nvidia-gpu-operator        │
  │  → Browse to localhost:9400/metrics for Prometheus GPU metrics           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your data scientist is training a model and notices nvidia-smi shows 0% GPU utilization. They panic: "My GPU isn't working!" The fix is education: time-sliced GPUs don't expose NVML to containers. Train them to use cluster-level DCGM metrics or oc debug node to check real GPU usage. Or switch to dedicated GPUs (no time-slicing) if per-container monitoring is critical.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Know the difference between time-sliced GPU monitoring (NVML restricted) and dedicated/MIG GPU monitoring (NVML available). For exam tasks about GPU verification, use node-level nvidia-smi or DCGM metrics, not in-container checks.

Install RHOAI Q26 of 200
What is MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) and which NVIDIA GPU series supports it?
A) MIG is a Kubernetes operator that manages multiple GPU vendors — it supports all NVIDIA GPUs including consumer-grade GeForce cards
B) MIG partitions a single physical GPU into multiple isolated instances with dedicated VRAM and compute — supported on A100, A30, and H100 GPUs only
C) MIG is a software scheduler that distributes GPU workloads across a cluster — it's part of the OpenShift scheduler, not an NVIDIA feature
D) MIG combines multiple physical GPUs into a single virtual GPU for large model training — it's the opposite of partitioning
✅ Correct Answer: B

MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) is a hardware-level GPU partitioning technology available on NVIDIA data center GPUs (A100, A30, H100). It splits a single physical GPU into up to 7 isolated instances, each with its own dedicated VRAM, cache, and compute cores. Each MIG instance appears as an independent GPU to the OS. Pods request specific MIG profiles like nvidia.com/mig-1g.5gb (1 compute slice, 5GB VRAM) or nvidia.com/mig-2g.10gb. Unlike time-slicing, MIG provides hardware fault isolation — a crash in one instance does not affect others. MIG is NOT available on consumer GPUs (GeForce) or older data center GPUs (T4, V100).

📝 Detailed Explanation
MIG Profiles — Hardware GPU Partitioning
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  MIG PARTITIONING — A100-40GB Example                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Physical A100 GPU (40GB, 7 compute slices, 8 memory slices)             │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  │    │
  │  │  │  MIG 3g.20gb         │  │  MIG 2g.10gb │  │ MIG 1g.5gb     │  │    │
  │  │  │                      │  │              │  │                │  │    │
  │  │  │  🏋️ Training Job     │  │  🚀 KServe   │  │  📓 Jupyter    │  │    │
  │  │  │  (PyTorch DDP)       │  │  (vLLM)      │  │  (dev)         │  │    │
  │  │  │  3 slices / 20GB     │  │  2/10GB       │  │  1/5GB         │  │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └────────────────┘  │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  ✅ Each instance is ISOLATED — separate VRAM, cache, compute     │    │
  │  │  ✅ Fault in training job does NOT crash KServe or Jupyter        │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  MIG SETUP COMMANDS:                                                     │
  │  ─────────────────                                                       │
  │  # Enable MIG mode on GPU 0                                              │
  │  nvidia-smi -i 0 -mig 1                                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  # Create MIG instances                                                  │
  │  nvidia-smi mig -cgi 9,14,5 -C                                           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  # Pod requesting MIG instance                                           │
  │  resources:                                                              │
  │    limits:                                                               │
  │      nvidia.com/mig-1g.5gb: 1                                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  MIG vs TIME-SLICING:                                                    │
  │  ───────────────────                                                     │
  │  MIG:         Hardware isolation, dedicated VRAM, A100/A30/H100 only     │
  │  Time-slicing: Software sharing, shared VRAM, works on any NVIDIA GPU    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You have one A100 GPU node for the anihpj platform. You need to run: (1) KServe with vLLM for real-time salary prediction (needs 10GB), (2) a training job for the job-matching model (needs 20GB), and (3) a dev Jupyter workbench (needs 5GB). MIG lets you partition the single A100 into 3g.20gb + 2g.10gb + 1g.5gb — all three workloads run simultaneously with guaranteed VRAM.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: MIG vs time-slicing is a common exam distinction. MIG = hardware isolation, supported on A100/H100. Time-slicing = software oversubscription, works on any GPU. If the task says "ensure GPU workloads are isolated from each other," the answer is MIG.

Install RHOAI Q27 of 200
The DCGM exporter is deployed by the GPU Operator. What does DCGM stand for and what metrics does it provide?
A) Docker Container GPU Monitor — provides container-level GPU allocation counts and Docker runtime GPU statistics
B) Distributed CUDA Grid Manager — provides multi-node GPU orchestration metrics for distributed training jobs
C) Data Center GPU Manager — provides Prometheus metrics for GPU utilization, memory usage, temperature, power draw, ECC errors, and PCIe throughput
D) Device Control GPU Module — provides low-level GPU driver health checks and firmware version reporting
✅ Correct Answer: C

DCGM (Data Center GPU Manager) is NVIDIA's monitoring toolkit for data center GPUs. The GPU Operator deploys DCGM Exporter as a DaemonSet that exposes GPU metrics in Prometheus format. Key metrics include: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL (GPU utilization %), DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED (framebuffer memory used), DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP (temperature), DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE (power draw in watts), DCGM_FI_DEV_ECC_ERRORS (memory error count), and DCGM_FI_DEV_PCIE_TX_THROUGHPUT (PCIe bandwidth). These metrics are scraped by Prometheus and can be visualized in Grafana dashboards or used for alerting (e.g., "GPU temperature > 85°C").

📝 Detailed Explanation
DCGM Exporter — GPU Metrics Pipeline

  │  │  │ GPU      │     │ (collects    │     │ (DaemonSet pod)  │      │    │
  │  │  │ Driver   │     │  metrics)    │     │ :9400/metrics    │      │    │
  │  │  └──────────┘     └──────────────┘     └────────┬─────────┘      │    │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────┘    │
  │                                                     │                     │
  │  KEY DCGM METRICS:                                  │ Prometheus scrapes │
  │  ─────────────────                                  ▼                     │
  │  • DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL        → GPU % busy        ┌──────────────┐     │
  │  • DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED         → VRAM used (MiB)   │ Prometheus   │     │
  │  • DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP        → Temperature (°C)  │ (redhat-ods- │     │
  │  • DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE     → Power (Watts)     │  monitoring) │     │
  │  • DCGM_FI_DEV_ECC_ERRORS      → Memory errors     └──────┬───────┘     │
  │  • DCGM_FI_DEV_PCIE_TX_BYTES   → PCIe throughput           │             │
  │                                                             ▼             │
  │  VERIFY DCGM:                                      ┌──────────────┐     │
  │  ───────────                                       │ Grafana      │     │

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You set up a Grafana dashboard showing GPU utilization for your A100 node. When the job-matching training pipeline runs, you see GPU utilization spike to 95%. When it's idle, it drops to 5%. You also set up an alert: if GPU temperature exceeds 80°C for 10 minutes, notify the #ml-ops Slack channel. Without DCGM, you're blind to GPU health and utilization.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Verify that GPU metrics are being collected." Check: (1) DCGM pod running: oc get pods -n nvidia-gpu-operator | grep dcgm, (2) ServiceMonitor exists: oc get servicemonitor -n nvidia-gpu-operator, (3) Prometheus targets: check Prometheus UI for DCGM target being UP.

Install RHOAI Q28 of 200
A GPU node has the taint nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule. What must a workbench have to schedule on this node?
A) A toleration matching the taint key and effect — the workbench (or its Acceleration Profile) must include a toleration for nvidia.com/gpu with operator: Exists and effect: NoSchedule
B) The workbench must use the privileged security context — GPU access requires privileged: true regardless of taint configuration
C) The node's taint must be removed — GPU taints are incompatible with workbenches; you must untaint the node for AI workloads
D) The workbench must specify a nodeSelector with nvidia.com/gpu=true — nodeSelectors override taints automatically
✅ Correct Answer: A

The taint nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule is added by the GPU Operator to GPU nodes. Its purpose is to prevent non-GPU workloads from scheduling on expensive GPU nodes. Only pods with a matching toleration can land on these nodes. Workbenches (and any GPU workload) must include a toleration like: tolerations: [{key: "nvidia.com/gpu", operator: "Exists", effect: "NoSchedule"}]. Without this toleration, even pods requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 will fail to schedule because the taint check happens BEFORE resource evaluation. Acceleration Profiles typically include this toleration automatically.

📝 Detailed Explanation
GPU Taints & Tolerations — Protecting GPU Nodes
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              GPU NODE TAINT — Gatekeeper for Expensive Hardware           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  GPU Node: taint nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  Pod WITHOUT toleration:                   ❌ REJECTED             │    │
  │  │  ┌────────────────────────┐                                      │    │
  │  │  │ anihpj-api pod         │  → Scheduler: "node has taint        │    │
  │  │  │ (no GPU needed)        │     nvidia.com/gpu, no toleration"   │    │
  │  │  └────────────────────────┘                                      │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  Pod WITH toleration:                        ✅ SCHEDULED          │    │
  │  │  ┌────────────────────────┐                                      │    │
  │  │  │ Workbench pod          │  → Scheduler: "pod tolerates         │    │
  │  │  │ tolerations:           │     nvidia.com/gpu taint"             │    │
  │  │  │   - key: nvidia.com/gpu│                                      │    │
  │  │  │     operator: Exists   │  Then checks: nvidia.com/gpu         │    │
  │  │  │     effect: NoSchedule │  resource available? → YES → Run!    │    │
  │  │  └────────────────────────┘                                      │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WHY THIS IS IMPORTANT:                                                  │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                   │
  │  Without taints: Non-GPU pods (web servers, databases) could land on     │
  │  expensive GPU nodes, wasting $30K+ hardware on simple HTTP serving.      │
  │  With taints: Only AI workloads use the GPU nodes.                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your anihpj Django web pods and PostgreSQL database should NEVER run on the expensive A100 GPU node. The GPU Operator's taint ensures only AI workloads (workbenches, KServe predictors, training jobs) land on GPU nodes. If a data scientist's workbench won't start, check: does it have the GPU toleration? Acceleration Profiles should handle this automatically.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "A workbench requesting GPUs cannot schedule on GPU nodes." Check taints: oc describe node <gpu-node> | grep Taints. If the taint exists, verify the workbench has matching toleration. Fix by adding toleration to workbench spec or using an Acceleration Profile that includes it.

Install RHOAI Q29 of 200
What is the ClusterPolicy CR created by the NVIDIA GPU Operator, and what happens if you delete it?
A) ClusterPolicy is a read-only status object — it displays GPU information but deleting it has no effect on the GPU software stack
B) ClusterPolicy is a network policy for GPU-to-GPU communication — deleting it breaks NCCL communication between GPU pods
C) ClusterPolicy is a backup of the GPU configuration — you can safely delete and recreate it without affecting running GPU workloads
D) ClusterPolicy is the central configuration CR for the GPU Operator — it controls driver version, toolkit, device plugin, MIG, time-slicing, and DCGM; deleting it triggers cleanup of all GPU Operator components
✅ Correct Answer: D

The ClusterPolicy is the single CR that configures everything the GPU Operator manages. It's similar to the DSC for RHOAI — one CR controls the entire subsystem. The ClusterPolicy spec includes: driver configuration (version, repository), toolkit settings, device plugin config (time-slicing replicas), MIG settings (enabled/disabled, profiles), DCGM exporter config, GPU Feature Discovery labels, and node selection (which nodes the operator should manage). Deleting the ClusterPolicy triggers the GPU Operator to clean up ALL its components — drivers, toolkit, device plugin, DCGM — effectively uninstalling GPU support. This is a destructive operation.

📝 Detailed Explanation
ClusterPolicy — The GPU Operator's Control Center
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              ClusterPolicy CR — One CR to Rule All GPUs                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  apiVersion: nvidia.com/v1                                               │
  │  kind: ClusterPolicy                                                     │
  │  metadata:                                                               │
  │    name: gpu-cluster-policy                                              │
  │  spec:                                                                    │
  │    driver:                                                               │
  │      enabled: true                                                       │
  │      version: "550.54.15"           ← GPU driver version                │
  │    toolkit:                                                              │
  │      enabled: true                                                       │
  │    devicePlugin:                                                         │
  │      enabled: true                                                       │
  │      config:                                                             │
  │        name: time-slicing-config    ← Time-slicing enabled              │
  │        default: "4"                 ← 4 replicas per GPU                │
  │    mig:                                                                  │
  │      strategy: mixed                ← MIG mode: single, mixed, none     │
  │    dcgm:                                                                 │
  │      enabled: true                                                       │
  │    gpuFeatureDiscovery:                                                  │
  │      enabled: true                                                       │
  │    operator:                                                             │
  │      defaultRuntime: crio                                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚠️  DELETE ClusterPolicy = ALL GPU components cleaned up               │
  │  ⚠️  Running GPU pods will keep their GPU allocation until restart      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The ClusterPolicy is how you configure GPU time-slicing for your anihpj dev workbenches. Edit the ClusterPolicy, set time-slicing replicas: 4, and suddenly your single GPU node can host 4 concurrent Jupyter workbenches. But be careful — changing the driver version in the ClusterPolicy triggers a rolling update of the GPU driver DaemonSet, which may briefly disrupt running GPU workloads.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Enable GPU time-slicing with 2 replicas per GPU." Edit ClusterPolicy: oc edit clusterpolicy gpu-cluster-policy, add/update devicePlugin.config.name: time-slicing-config and devicePlugin.config.default: "2". Verify: node now shows 2× GPU count.

Install RHOAI Q30 of 200
A data scientist reports "CUDA out of memory" when training a model on a GPU workbench. The GPU has 16GB VRAM. What are valid solutions?
A) Only solution: upgrade to a GPU with more VRAM — 16GB is insufficient for any modern ML training workload
B) Reduce batch size, use gradient checkpointing, enable mixed precision (FP16), or use a smaller model variant — these techniques reduce VRAM usage without hardware changes
C) Increase the container's memory limit — CUDA OOM is caused by the container memory limit, not the GPU VRAM
D) Disable GPU time-slicing — time-sliced GPUs report incorrect VRAM availability and always cause OOM errors
✅ Correct Answer: B

"CUDA out of memory" means the GPU's VRAM is full. The model, its parameters, optimizer states, and the current batch of data all need to fit in VRAM. Solutions without hardware changes: (1) Reduce batch size — smaller batches = less activation memory. (2) Gradient checkpointing — trades compute for memory by recomputing activations instead of storing them. (3) Mixed precision (FP16) — uses half-precision floats, nearly halving memory usage. (4) Gradient accumulation — simulate larger batches by accumulating gradients over multiple forward passes. (5) Use a smaller model — switch from Llama-13B to Llama-7B, or use a distilled variant. If these don't help, then consider: MIG with a larger profile, model quantization (INT8/INT4), or upgrading to a GPU with more VRAM.

📝 Detailed Explanation
GPU VRAM — What's Using Your Memory
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              GPU VRAM BREAKDOWN (16GB Total)                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Model Weights:       ████████████  4.0 GB  (Llama-7B FP16)     │    │
  │  │  Optimizer States:    ██████████    3.5 GB  (AdamW)              │    │
  │  │  Activations:         ████████████  4.5 GB  (batch_size=16)     │    │
  │  │  Gradients:           ██████████    3.5 GB                       │    │
  │  │  CUDA Context:        ██            0.5 GB                       │    │
  │  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────                      │    │
  │  │  TOTAL:               ████████████████████████████████  16.0 GB  │    │
  │  │                       ⚠️  AT LIMIT! Any increase → OOM          │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  FIXES (in order of impact):                                             │
  │  ───────────────────────────                                              │
  │  1. batch_size: 16 → 8         Saves: ~2.5 GB activations               │
  │  2. Enable FP16 mixed precision Saves: ~2.0 GB (half-precision weights)  │
  │  3. Gradient checkpointing      Saves: ~4.5 GB (recompute activations)   │
  │  4. Gradient accumulation       Simulates batch=16 with batch=4×4 steps  │
  │  5. INT8 quantization           Saves: ~2.0 GB model weights             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  VERIFY GPU MEMORY:                                                      │
  │  ─────────────────                                                       │
  │  $ nvidia-smi                                                            │
  │  |  GPU  Name        |  Memory-Usage |                                    │
  │  |  0    Tesla-T4    |  15234MiB / 16384MiB |   ← 93% used!             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your data scientist is fine-tuning a sentence transformer on 16GB GPU for the job-matching model with batch_size=32 and gets OOM. The fix: reduce batch_size to 8 and enable FP16. Training still converges (just takes more steps) and fits within 16GB. If they need larger batches for training stability, use gradient accumulation: batch_size=8 with 4 accumulation steps = effective batch_size=32.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: You may get a practical task: "A training job fails with CUDA OOM. Fix it." The expected solution is reducing batch size in the pipeline step configuration or training script. The exam tests your understanding that this is a GPU VRAM issue, not a CPU memory issue.

1.4 Platform Lifecycle & Day 2 OperationsQ31-Q40

Install RHOAI Q31 of 200
You need to upgrade the RHOAI Operator from version 2.10 to 2.13. What is the correct upgrade sequence?
A) Delete the operator pod — OLM automatically upgrades to the latest version when the pod restarts
B) Delete and recreate the Subscription with the new channel — this is the only way to trigger an operator upgrade
C) Patch the Subscription's channel to the desired version's channel — OLM detects the change, creates a new InstallPlan, and (if approval is Automatic) applies the upgrade
D) Run oc adm upgrade rhoai —version=2.13 — this is the dedicated RHOAI upgrade command built into the oc CLI
✅ Correct Answer: C

Operator upgrades in OpenShift follow the OLM pattern. To upgrade RHOAI: (1) Check available channels: oc get packagemanifest rhods-operator -o yaml | grep -A10 channels. (2) Patch the Subscription to the new channel: oc patch subscription rhods-operator --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"channel":"stable-2.13"}}'. (3) OLM detects the channel change and creates a new InstallPlan with the updated CSV. (4) If installPlanApproval: Automatic, OLM auto-applies the upgrade. If Manual, you approve the InstallPlan. (5) The operator pod restarts with the new version. (6) The DSC may need updating if the new version deprecates or adds components. Never delete the operator pod as an upgrade method — that just restarts the same version.

📝 Detailed Explanation
RHOAI Operator Upgrade Sequence
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              RHOAI UPGRADE — Step by Step                                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1: Check current version & available channels                      │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                            │
  │  $ oc get subscription rhods-operator -o yaml | grep channel             │
  │  channel: stable-2.10                                                    │
  │  $ oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator                                     │
  │  rhods-operator.v2.10.0    Succeeded                                     │
  │                                                                          │
