Install RHOAI Q32 of 200
How do you backup RHOAI configuration and Data Science Projects for disaster recovery?
A) RHOAI has a built-in backup feature in the dashboard — go to Settings → Backup → Download to export all configuration
B) You only need to backup etcd — since all RHOAI configuration is stored in etcd, a standard etcd snapshot covers everything
C) Backup is not supported — RHOAI resources must be manually recreated after a disaster; there is no automated backup mechanism
D) Use OADP (OpenShift API for Data Protection) — create Backup CRs targeting RHOAI resources by label/namespace, store backups in S3-compatible storage, and restore with Restore CRs
✅ Correct Answer: D

OADP (OpenShift API for Data Protection) is the recommended backup solution for OpenShift, including RHOAI resources. You install the OADP Operator, configure a DataProtectionApplication CR with S3-compatible storage (AWS S3, MinIO), then create Backup CRs that target specific resources. For RHOAI, you'd backup: (1) Labeled Data Science Project namespaces (opendatahub.io/dashboard=true), (2) The DSC CR, (3) DataScienceProject CRs, (4) Workbench Notebook CRs, (5) DataConnection secrets, (6) Pipeline server configurations. OADP uses Velero under the hood. Restore is done via Restore CRs. An etcd snapshot alone is NOT sufficient — it backs up the entire cluster state, not portable project-level backups.

📝 Detailed Explanation
RHOAI Backup & Restore with OADP
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              OADP BACKUP WORKFLOW FOR RHOAI                               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  INSTALL & CONFIGURE:                                                    │
  │  ───────────────────                                                     │
  │  1. Install OADP Operator from OperatorHub                               │
  │  2. Create DataProtectionApplication CR:                                 │
  │     configuration:                                                        │
  │       velero:                                                             │
  │         defaultPlugins: [csi, openshift]                                  │
  │       backupLocations:                                                    │
  │         - velero:                                                         │
  │             provider: aws                                                 │
  │             bucket: rhoai-backups                                         │
  │             region: us-east-1                                             │
  │             credential: cloud-credentials                                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CREATE BACKUP:                                                          │
  │  ─────────────                                                           │
  │  apiVersion: velero.io/v1                                                │
  │  kind: Backup                                                             │
  │  metadata:                                                                │
  │    name: rhoai-weekly-backup                                              │
  │  spec:                                                                    │
  │    includedNamespaces:                                                    │
  │      - anihpj                    ← Data Science Project                  │
  │      - ml-experiments                                                    │
  │    labelSelector:                                                         │
  │      opendatahub.io/dashboard: true                                       │
  │    storageLocation: default                                               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RESTORE:                                                                │
  │  ───────                                                                  │
  │  apiVersion: velero.io/v1                                                │
  │  kind: Restore                                                            │
  │  metadata:                                                                │
  │    name: rhoai-restore                                                    │
  │  spec:                                                                    │
  │    backupName: rhoai-weekly-backup                                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You set up a weekly OADP backup of the anihpj Data Science Project. If a disaster corrupts the cluster, you restore: the anihpj namespace, workbenches, S3 data connections, pipeline server config, model registry entries, and Notebook CRs. Your data scientists can resume work within hours instead of days. The actual training data in S3 is backed up separately via S3 replication.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Backup the 'anihpj' Data Science Project." Install OADP Operator → create DataProtectionApplication → create Backup CR with includedNamespaces: [anihpj]. Verify with: oc get backup -n openshift-adp.

Install RHOAI Q33 of 200
After a RHOAI Operator upgrade, the DSC shows workbenches: NotReady. What is the most likely cause?
A) The new operator version requires updated component images that are still being pulled, or the notebook-controller deployment needs a rollout restart to pick up new configuration
B) Upgrading the operator automatically deletes all workbenches — they must be recreated after every upgrade
C) The DSC must be deleted and recreated after every operator upgrade — the old DSC is incompatible with new operator versions
D) RHOAI operator upgrades require cluster downtime — all components show NotReady until the cluster is rebooted
✅ Correct Answer: A

After an operator upgrade, component pods may need to restart with updated images or configurations. The operator's new CSV references newer component images that must be pulled, which can take time depending on image size and network speed. Additionally, the notebook-controller deployment may still be running the old image — it needs a rollout restart. The DSC will auto-reconcile: the operator detects the old pod versions and gradually replaces them. If a component stays NotReady for more than a few minutes, check: oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications | grep notebook — is the image pull stuck? oc describe pod for events. You may need to manually trigger oc rollout restart deploy/notebook-controller if auto-reconciliation stalls.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Post-Upgrade Health Verification
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              POST-UPGRADE RECOVERY CHECKLIST                               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  IMMEDIATELY AFTER UPGRADE:                                              │
  │  ──────────────────────────                                               │
  │  ✅ Check operator CSV: oc get csv -n redhat-ods-operator                │
  │     → Should show new version Succeeded                                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⏳ Wait for components to reconcile (may take 2-5 minutes):             │
  │  $ watch oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications                          │
  │  → New pods should appear with updated image tags                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ✅ Check DSC conditions:                                                │
  │  $ oc describe dsc default-dsc | grep -A2 Conditions                     │
  │  → Each component should transition to Ready                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ❌ If component STAYS NotReady (>5 min):                                │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────                                  │
  │  1. Check pod: oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications | grep <comp>    │
  │  2. Check logs: oc logs deploy/<component> --tail=50                   │
  │  3. Check events: oc describe pod <pod>                                 │
  │  4. If ImagePullBackOff → Check image registry, pull secret              │
  │  5. If CrashLoop → Check RBAC, config, dependencies                     │
  │  6. Manual restart: oc rollout restart deploy/<component>               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ✅ Verify user workloads survive:                                       │
  │  $ oc get notebooks -n anihpj                                           │
  │  → Running workbenches should NOT be affected by operator upgrade       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: After upgrading RHOAI on Sunday at 2 AM, you check at 2:10 AM — the dashboard is back, but workbenches show NotReady. The notebook-controller is pulling a new image over a slow connection. You wait 3 minutes, the image finishes pulling, the pod starts, and the DSC transitions to Ready. Meanwhile, alice's Jupyter workbench that was already running continues uninterrupted — she never noticed the upgrade.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "After an upgrade, the KServe component is NotReady. Fix it." Check: oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications | grep kserve. If pods are CrashLoopBackOff, check logs. If pods have old image tags, do oc rollout restart deploy/kserve-controller-manager.

Install RHOAI Q34 of 200
How do you install RHOAI in a disconnected (air-gapped) OpenShift cluster with no internet access?
A) RHOAI cannot be installed in disconnected environments — it requires internet access to pull container images and validate subscriptions
B) Mirror all RHOAI images to a private registry, create ImageContentSourcePolicy (ICSP) or ImageDigestMirrorSet (IDMS) to redirect image pulls, and configure the operator catalog for the disconnected registry
C) Download the RHOAI offline installer package from the Red Hat Customer Portal and run the install script — it handles all disconnected configuration automatically
D) Set the DSC to disconnected mode — the DSC has a spec.deploymentMode: disconnected field that disables all external image pulls
✅ Correct Answer: B

Disconnected installations require three steps: (1) Mirror images: Use oc mirror or skopeo to copy all RHOAI-related images (operator, components, workbench images, serving runtimes) from Red Hat's registries to your private registry. (2) Configure image pull redirection: Create an ImageDigestMirrorSet (IDMS) or ImageContentSourcePolicy (ICSP) that tells OpenShift "when a pod requests image from registry.redhat.io, pull from my-registry.local instead." (3) Configure the catalog: Create a CatalogSource pointing to your mirrored operator catalog index. RHOAI supports disconnected installations — it's a tested scenario for air-gapped environments.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Disconnected RHOAI Installation

  │              DISCONNECTED INSTALLATION — Image Mirroring                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  EXTERNAL (Internet)                INTERNAL (Air-gapped)                 │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐            ┌────────────────────────────┐       │
  │  │ registry.redhat.io │  ──mirror──▶  │ my-registry.local:5000    │       │
  │  │ registry.access... │            │                            │       │
  │  │ quay.io/opendatahub│            │ Mirror all images:         │       │
  │  └────────────────────┘            │  • Operator images         │       │
  │                                     │  • Component images        │       │
  │                                     │  • Workbench images        │       │
  │                                     │  • Serving runtimes        │       │
  │                                     │  • GPU Operator images     │       │
  │                                     └────────────────────────────┘       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  IMAGE REDIRECTION (IDMS):                                               │
  │  ─────────────────────────                                               │
  │  apiVersion: config.openshift.io/v1                                      │
  │  kind: ImageDigestMirrorSet                                              │
  │  metadata:                                                                │
  │    name: rhoai-mirror                                                     │
  │  spec:                                                                    │
  │    imageDigestMirrors:                                                    │
  │      - source: registry.redhat.io                                         │
  │        mirrors:                                                           │
  │          - my-registry.local:5000/redhat                                  │
  │      - source: quay.io/opendatahub                                        │
  │        mirrors:                                                           │
  │          - my-registry.local:5000/opendatahub                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CATALOG SOURCE (Mirrored):                                              │
  │  ──────────────────────────                                               │
  │  apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1                               │
  │  kind: CatalogSource                                                      │
  │  spec:                                                                    │
  │    sourceType: grpc                                                       │
  │    image: my-registry.local:5000/redhat/redhat-operator-index:v4.14      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your company's production OpenShift cluster is in a secure air-gapped environment (government/military/finance). You mirror all anihpj-related images to the internal registry, configure IDMS, and install RHOAI from the mirrored catalog. Data scientists use the platform normally — they never know it's air-gapped because all images are served locally.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Configure the cluster to use a mirror registry for RHOAI images." Create an IDMS CR mapping source registries to your mirror. Verify: oc get idms and check that image pulls succeed from the mirror.

Install RHOAI Q35 of 200
What is the purpose of the redhat-ods-monitoring namespace and its Prometheus instance?
A) It stores RHOAI audit logs — the Prometheus instance collects API server audit events for security compliance
B) It monitors the underlying OpenShift nodes only — the Prometheus instance is a clone of the cluster monitoring Prometheus, dedicated to hardware metrics
C) It provides RHOAI-specific monitoring — Prometheus scrapes component health metrics, InferenceService performance, GPU utilization (via DCGM), and TrustyAI bias/drift data for the RHOAI platform
D) It's a backup monitoring namespace — it activates only when the main cluster monitoring Prometheus fails
✅ Correct Answer: C

The redhat-ods-monitoring namespace contains RHOAI's dedicated monitoring stack — a separate Prometheus instance specifically for AI/ML workloads. This is NOT the same as OpenShift's cluster monitoring. It scrapes: DSC component health metrics, KServe InferenceService metrics (request rate, latency, error rate), GPU metrics from DCGM exporter, pipeline run metrics, and TrustyAI bias/drift metrics. This separation ensures that AI monitoring doesn't interfere with cluster monitoring and allows RHOAI-specific retention policies and alerting rules. The Prometheus is deployed as part of the DSC reconciliation when monitoring-related components are enabled.

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You create a Grafana dashboard that queries the RHOAI Prometheus. It shows: KServe request latency for the salary predictor (p95 < 50ms), GPU utilization during training (85%), and pipeline success rate (98%). When the pipeline success rate drops below 90%, an alert fires. This monitoring is separate from cluster monitoring — the SRE team's Prometheus doesn't get flooded with AI-specific metrics.

Install RHOAI Q36 of 200
What is telemetry in RHOAI, and how can an administrator control it?
A) Telemetry sends anonymous usage data to Red Hat — administrators can view what's collected and enable/disable it via the DSC spec or a dedicated ConfigMap
B) Telemetry is a monitoring feature that sends GPU metrics to NVIDIA's cloud — it's managed through the GPU Operator's ClusterPolicy
C) Telemetry tracks user behavior within the dashboard — it's a per-user opt-in feature controlled through individual user settings
D) Telemetry is always enabled and cannot be disabled — it's a mandatory part of the Red Hat subscription agreement
✅ Correct Answer: A

RHOAI collects anonymous usage telemetry to help Red Hat understand how the platform is used — which components are enabled, how many workbenches are created, pipeline usage patterns, etc. No personal data, notebook contents, or model data is collected. Administrators can: (1) View exactly what data is collected via Red Hat documentation, (2) Disable telemetry by setting spec.telemetry.enabled: false in the DSC, or (3) Use a dedicated ConfigMap to fine-tune telemetry settings. In disconnected environments, telemetry is automatically disabled since there's no internet connectivity. Telemetry data helps Red Hat prioritize bug fixes and feature development based on real usage patterns.

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your company has a strict "no data leaves our network" policy. You disable RHOAI telemetry via the DSC. The platform works identically — no features are gated behind telemetry. If you later move to a connected environment for a Red Hat support case, you can temporarily enable it to give Red Hat diagnostics.

Install RHOAI Q37 of 200
What happens to existing workbenches and InferenceServices during a RHOAI operator upgrade?
A) All workbenches are stopped and must be manually restarted — the operator upgrade causes a mandatory restart of all user workloads
B) Only workbenches running on GPU nodes are affected — CPU-only workloads continue uninterrupted
C) The upgrade requires draining all nodes — every workload, including workbenches and model servers, is terminated
D) Running workbenches and InferenceServices are NOT affected — the operator manages platform components, not user workloads; existing pods continue running throughout the upgrade
✅ Correct Answer: D

This is one of the most important operational guarantees of the RHOAI architecture. The operator manages platform components (dashboard, controllers, pipeline server infrastructure), NOT user workloads (workbench pods, InferenceService pods, pipeline run pods). When the operator upgrades: the operator pod restarts with the new version, platform controllers may restart, and the DSC may update component configurations. But user-created pods — Jupyter workbenches, running pipeline steps, active KServe predictors — keep running uninterrupted. They are managed by their own controllers and are not owned by the operator pod lifecycle. This design enables zero-downtime platform upgrades.

📝 Detailed Explanation
What's Affected During RHOAI Upgrade
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              OPERATOR UPGRADE — Impact Analysis                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  PLATFORM COMPONENTS (Restart — BRIEF DOWNTIME):                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  ⚠️  RESTARTS:                                                    │    │
  │  │  • RHOAI Operator pod (redhat-ods-operator)  ← Upgrades itself   │    │
  │  │  • Dashboard (odh-dashboard)                  ← ~30 sec downtime  │    │
  │  │  • Notebook controller                        ← WBs can't be      │    │
  │  │  • KServe controller                          ← created during    │    │
  │  │  • Pipeline server                            ← restart window    │    │
  │  │  • Model Registry operator                                        │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  USER WORKLOADS (UNINTERRUPTED — ZERO DOWNTIME):                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  ✅ CONTINUES RUNNING:                                             │    │
  │  │  • Jupyter workbench pods (anihpj workspace)                      │    │
  │  │  • VS Code workbench pods                                          │    │
  │  │  • KServe InferenceService predictors (salary model serving)      │    │
  │  │  • Running pipeline steps (training job in progress)              │    │
  │  │  • Model Registry database pods                                    │    │
  │  │  • Data connection Secret mounts                                    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚠️  DURING THE RESTART WINDOW (~1-2 min):                              │
  │  • New workbench creation may fail temporarily                           │
  │  • Dashboard may show "loading" briefly                                  │
  │  • Model deployment via KServe may be delayed                            │
  │  • Existing workbenches/models continue serving without interruption     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You plan the RHOAI upgrade for 2 AM Tuesday. During the upgrade, the anihpj salary prediction model continues serving API requests with zero downtime. Data scientists who left Jupyter workbenches running overnight find them still running at 8 AM. The only brief impact: no one can create NEW workbenches for about 2 minutes. This is why you schedule upgrades during low-activity windows.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: A common misconception tested in the exam is that operator upgrades force workload restarts. The correct answer is always: "user workloads are unaffected during operator upgrades." Platform component controllers may briefly restart, but running pods continue.

Install RHOAI Q38 of 200
You need to check whether any RHOAI components have pending security vulnerabilities. How do you do this?
A) RHOAI includes a built-in vulnerability scanner — go to Settings → Security → CVEs in the dashboard
B) Use OpenShift's built-in image vulnerability scanning or external tools like Trivy/Grype to scan RHOAI component images in their namespaces — check the Container Security tab in the OpenShift console
C) Red Hat automatically patches all RHOAI images — there's no need to check for vulnerabilities as they're resolved before release
D) Subscribe to the Red Hat Security Advisory (RHSA) mailing list for RHOAI — vulnerabilities are announced via email only
✅ Correct Answer: B

RHOAI images are regular container images and are subject to the same security scanning as any other workload. OpenShift's built-in Container Security feature (powered by Quay Clair) scans images in all namespaces, including redhat-ods-operator, redhat-ods-applications, and redhat-ods-monitoring. You can also use external tools: Trivy (trivy image <image>), Grype, or the Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security (ACS) for enterprise-grade vulnerability management. The OpenShift console Developer perspective → Advanced → Container Security shows all vulnerabilities across the cluster. Red Hat DOES patch images, but you still need to upgrade to the patched version.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Image Vulnerability Scanning for RHOAI

  │              SCANNING RHOAI IMAGES FOR CVEs                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  OPENSHIFT BUILT-IN (Container Security):                                │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────                                 │
  │  Developer Console → Advanced → Container Security                        │
  │  Shows CVE counts per namespace per deployment                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CLI APPROACH:                                                            │
  │  ────────────                                                             │
  │  # Get current RHOAI component images                                     │
  │  $ oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications -o json | \                    │
  │    jq '.items[].spec.containers[].image'                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  # Scan with Trivy                                                        │
  │  $ trivy image quay.io/opendatahub/odh-dashboard:v2.13                   │
  │  → Shows: CVE-2024-xxxx (HIGH), CVE-2024-yyyy (CRITICAL)                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  # Scan all images in a namespace                                         │
  │  $ for img in $(oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications -o json | \       │
  │    jq -r '.items[].spec.containers[].image' | sort -u); do               │
  │    echo "Scanning: $img"; trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL $img      │
  │    done                                                                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WHAT TO DO WITH RESULTS:                                                 │
  │  ─────────────────────────                                                │
  │  • Check Red Hat's advisory for patches                                   │
  │  • Upgrade RHOAI to a version that includes the fix                       │
  │  • For critical CVEs: apply workaround or upgrade immediately             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your security team runs weekly Trivy scans on all namespaces. They flag a HIGH CVE in the odh-dashboard image. You check the RHOAI release notes: version 2.13.1 patches this CVE. You schedule an operator upgrade to 2.13.1 for the next maintenance window. The CVE is resolved, and the security team is satisfied.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Check if RHOAI components have any HIGH or CRITICAL CVEs." Use OpenShift Container Security in the console, or CLI: oc get images and check the ImageStream tags for vulnerability annotations.

Install RHOAI Q39 of 200
The DSC is accidentally deleted. All RHOAI components disappear. What is the recovery procedure?
A) Reinstall the RHOAI operator from scratch — deleting the DSC requires a complete reinstallation of the operator and all its CRDs
B) Restore from the latest OADP backup — there is no way to recover a deleted DSC without a backup
C) Simply recreate the DSC — the operator is still running (only the DSC was deleted, not the operator), so creating a new DSC triggers redeployment of all enabled components, and existing Data Science Projects and their resources survive
D) Wait 5 minutes — the DSC has a self-healing mechanism and will automatically recreate itself from the operator's internal state
✅ Correct Answer: C

Deleting the DSC is recoverable and does NOT require operator reinstallation. The operator, Subscription, and CSV remain intact — only the DSC CR was deleted. To recover: (1) Recreate the DSC with the same component configuration, (2) The operator detects the new DSC and begins reconciliation, (3) All enabled components are redeployed, (4) Existing Data Science Projects (namespaces) were never deleted because they are independent CRs, not owned by the DSC, (5) User workbenches, InferenceServices, and pipeline configs inside those projects also survived. The recovery time is typically 2-5 minutes — the time it takes for all component pods to be redeployed and become Ready.

📝 Detailed Explanation
DSC Deletion Recovery — What Survives, What Needs Recreation
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              DSC ACCIDENTAL DELETION — RECOVERY PLAN                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SURVIVES (No action needed):                                            │
  │  ────────────────────────────                                              │
  │  ✅ RHOAI Operator pod (redhat-ods-operator)                              │
  │  ✅ Subscription & CSV                                                   │
  │  ✅ All CRDs (DataScienceCluster, Notebook, InferenceService, etc.)      │
  │  ✅ ALL Data Science Projects (anihpj, ml-experiments, etc.)             │
  │  ✅ Workbenches INSIDE projects (Notebook CRs + pods)                    │
  │  ✅ InferenceServices (KServe model deployments)                         │
  │  ✅ Pipeline configurations and run history                              │
  │  ✅ Data connections (S3 secrets)                                        │
  │  ✅ PVCs and stored data                                                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  MUST BE RECREATED (Platform components):                                │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────                                  │
  │  ⚠️  Dashboard pod                                                       │
  │  ⚠️  Notebook controller pod                                             │
  │  ⚠️  KServe controller pod                                               │
  │  ⚠️  Pipeline server pod                                                 │
  │  ⚠️  Model Registry operator pod                                         │
  │  ⚠️  TrustyAI monitoring pod                                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RECOVERY COMMAND:                                                       │
  │  ────────────────                                                         │
  │  $ oc apply -f dsc.yaml             ← Recreate DSC                      │
  │  $ oc describe dsc default-dsc      ← Wait for Phase: Ready              │
  │  $ oc get pods -n redhat-ods-applications  ← Verify pods Running         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: A junior admin accidentally runs oc delete dsc default-dsc during a cleanup exercise. Panic ensues — the dashboard goes down, the pipeline server disappears. But you stay calm: the anihpj project and alice's Jupyter workbench are still running. You recreate the DSC from the saved YAML (or from memory of the component config). Within 3 minutes, the dashboard is back, the KServe controller is running, and models are serving again. Crisis averted in under 5 minutes.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Always keep a backup of your DSC YAML: oc get dsc default-dsc -o yaml > dsc-backup.yaml. In the exam, if you accidentally delete the DSC, just recreate it. The operator handles the rest.

Install RHOAI Q40 of 200
You need to completely uninstall RHOAI from the cluster. What is the correct sequence?
A) Delete the DSC first → Delete Data Science Projects → Delete the Subscription (which removes CSV and operator pod) → Delete operator CRDs → Clean up namespaces (redhat-ods-*)
B) Delete the Subscription first — OLM cascades the deletion and automatically removes the DSC, projects, and all resources
C) Run oc delete project --all in the redhat-ods namespaces — namespace deletion cascades and removes everything
D) There is no supported uninstall procedure — RHOAI is designed to be permanent once installed on a cluster
✅ Correct Answer: A

The correct uninstall sequence follows the dependency chain in reverse: (1) Delete DSC — this removes all platform components (dashboard, controllers, etc.) while keeping user projects intact. (2) Delete Data Science Projects — remove project namespaces and their AI resources (workbenches, InferenceServices, pipelines). (3) Delete the Subscription — OLM then removes the CSV, operator pod, and InstallPlan. (4) Manually delete CRDs — OLM by default does NOT delete CRDs when uninstalling (to prevent data loss). (5) Delete RHOAI namespaces — redhat-ods-operator, redhat-ods-applications, redhat-ods-monitoring. Following this order ensures clean cleanup without orphaned resources.

📝 Detailed Explanation
RHOAI Uninstall Sequence
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              COMPLETE RHOAI UNINSTALL — Step by Step                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1: Delete DSC (stops all platform components)                      │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────                        │
  │  $ oc delete dsc default-dsc                                              │
  │  → Wait for platform pods to terminate                                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 2: Delete Data Science Projects (user data)                         │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────                          │
  │  $ oc delete project anihpj ml-experiments                                │
  │  → This deletes workbenches, InferenceServices, pipeline configs          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 3: Delete Subscription (removes operator)                           │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────                            │
  │  $ oc delete subscription rhods-operator                                  │
  │  → OLM removes CSV, operator pod, InstallPlan                             │
  │  ⚠️  CRDs are NOT deleted automatically!                                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 4: Delete CRDs (manual cleanup)                                    │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────                                     │
  │  $ oc get crd | grep opendatahub | awk '{print $1}' | \                  │
  │    xargs oc delete crd                                                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 5: Delete RHOAI namespaces                                          │
  │  ───────────────────────────────                                           │
  │  $ oc delete namespace redhat-ods-operator                                │
  │  $ oc delete namespace redhat-ods-applications                            │
  │  $ oc delete namespace redhat-ods-monitoring                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ✅ VERIFY: oc get pods -A | grep -E "rhods|opendatahub" (should be empty)│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You're migrating from a self-managed RHOAI on-prem to OpenShift AI on AWS. You need to cleanly uninstall from the old cluster. Following the correct sequence ensures no orphaned resources remain that could cause confusion or resource leaks. You keep backups of workbench configurations and pipeline definitions before deleting the projects.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Completely remove RHOAI from the cluster." The exam expects the correct ORDER: DSC → Projects → Subscription → CRDs → Namespaces. Deleting the Subscription first may leave orphaned components. Remember: OLM does NOT delete CRDs automatically.

📁 Category 2: Data Science Projects & Workbenches (25%)Q41-Q90

🟢 Working with Projects, Workbenches, Data Connections & Git

This category is about where data scientists do their work. Think of a Data Science Project as a dedicated lab room with keycard access (RBAC), a workbench as your desk with a powerful computer (Jupyter/VS Code + GPU), data connections as utilities (S3 storage, databases), and Git integration as the shared reference library. For anihpj/jobpost, each AI initiative (job matching, salary prediction, RAG) gets its own project with isolated workbenches, data connections, and version-controlled notebooks.

Q41-Q90 50 Questions 🟢 Beginner → 🟡 Intermediate

2.1 Project Isolation & Multi-TenancyQ41-Q50

Projects & WBs Q41 of 200
How are Data Science Projects isolated from each other in OpenShift AI?
A) Projects share all resources by default — isolation requires manually creating NetworkPolicies and RBAC rules for each project
B) Each DSP is a separate OpenShift namespace with its own RBAC, ResourceQuota, NetworkPolicy, and service accounts — network isolation and access control are namespace-scoped
C) Projects are isolated only at the dashboard UI level — the underlying Kubernetes resources are shared and accessible cross-project
D) Isolation is achieved through a separate Kubernetes cluster per project — OpenShift AI provisions a dedicated cluster for each DSP
✅ Correct Answer: B

Each DSP is a full OpenShift namespace with all the isolation that namespaces provide: (1) RBAC isolation — RoleBindings are namespace-scoped; a user with edit access in project-A has no access in project-B. (2) Resource isolation — ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges are per-namespace. (3) Network isolation — pods in different namespaces cannot communicate unless NetworkPolicies explicitly allow it. (4) Service account isolation — each project has its own default SA and can create project-specific SAs. (5) Storage isolation — PVCs are namespace-scoped. This means the anihpj team can't accidentally access or modify the ml-experiments team's workbenches, data, or models.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Project Isolation — Multi-Tenant DSP Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              DATA SCIENCE PROJECT ISOLATION                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  NAMESPACE: anihpj                    NAMESPACE: ml-experiments          │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │ RBAC:                      │      │ RBAC:                      │     │
  │  │  alice, bob: edit          │      │  charlie: admin            │     │
  │  │  diana: admin              │      │  eve: edit                 │     │
  │  │                            │      │                            │     │
  │  │ Resources:                 │      │ Resources:                 │     │
  │  │ 📓 workbench-alice (GPU)   │      │ 📓 workbench-charlie       │     │
  │  │ 📓 workbench-bob (GPU)     │      │ 🚀 inference-salary-pred   │     │
  │  │ 🔗 s3-connection-anihpj    │      │ 🔗 s3-connection-ml-data   │     │
  │  │ 🔄 pipeline-job-match      │      │ 💾 pvc-training-data       │     │
  │  │                            │      │                            │     │
  │  │ NetworkPolicy:             │      │ NetworkPolicy:             │     │
  │  │  deny-from-other-ns        │      │  deny-from-other-ns        │     │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────────┘     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ❌ alice CANNOT:                                                        │
  │  • See ml-experiments project in dashboard                               │
  │  • Access charlie's workbench                                            │
  │  • Read ml-experiments' S3 secrets                                       │
  │  • Deploy models to ml-experiments namespace                             │
  │  ✅ Network isolation: pods in anihpj can't reach pods in ml-experiments │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your organization has two AI teams: the "anihpj" team building job-matching and salary prediction, and the "ml-experiments" team prototyping new models. Both need GPU workbenches and S3 access, but neither should see the other's data, models, or notebooks. DSP namespace isolation ensures clean separation without needing separate clusters.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Ensure team-A cannot access team-B's project." Verify that team-A users have no RoleBinding in team-B's namespace. Optionally, create a NetworkPolicy in team-B's namespace denying ingress from other namespaces.

Projects & WBs Q42 of 200
A data scientist has "Edit" role in the anihpj project but can't see it in the dashboard. What's wrong?
A) The "Edit" role only grants API access — dashboard visibility requires the "View" role in addition to "Edit"
B) The dashboard caches project lists for 1 hour — the user must wait for the cache to refresh before the project appears
C) The namespace is missing the opendatahub.io/dashboard=true label — without this label, the dashboard does not recognize the namespace as a Data Science Project
D) The user needs cluster-level permissions to see any projects — project visibility requires at minimum a ClusterRole with "list namespaces"
✅ Correct Answer: C

The opendatahub.io/dashboard: 'true' label is the key that tells the OpenShift AI dashboard "this namespace is a Data Science Project — show it in the UI." Without this label, the namespace exists and RBAC works, but the dashboard filters it out. This is a common issue when creating namespaces via CLI (oc new-project) instead of through the dashboard, which auto-applies the label. Fix: oc label namespace anihpj opendatahub.io/dashboard=true. The user does not need cluster-level permissions or dual roles — Edit role is sufficient for dashboard visibility once the label is present.

📝 Detailed Explanation
DSP Dashboard Visibility — The Label Requirement

  │              WHY A PROJECT DOESN'T APPEAR IN THE DASHBOARD                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  NAMESPACE EXISTS:                 DASHBOARD SHOWS:                      │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────┐          │
  │  │ $ oc get ns anihpj       │     │                          │          │
  │  │ NAME     STATUS   AGE    │     │  Data Science Projects   │          │
  │  │ anihpj   Active   5d     │     │  ┌──────────────────┐    │          │
  │  │                          │     │  │ anihpj           │    │  ← SHOWN │
  │  │ $ oc get ns anihpj       │     │  │ (with label)     │    │          │
  │  │   --show-labels          │     │  └──────────────────┘    │          │
  │  │ NAME     LABELS          │     │  ┌──────────────────┐    │          │
  │  │ anihpj   opendatahub.io/ │     │  │                  │    │          │
  │  │          dashboard=true  │     │  └──────────────────┘    │  ← HIDDEN│
  │  └──────────────────────────┘     │  (ml-team exists but      │          │
  │                                    │   no dashboard label)     │          │
  │  NAMESPACE EXISTS (no label):     └──────────────────────────┘          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┐                                            │
  │  │ $ oc get ns ml-team      │     FIX:                                  │
  │  │ NAME      STATUS   AGE   │     ────                                   │
  │  │ ml-team   Active   2d    │     $ oc label namespace ml-team \         │

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You create the anihpj namespace via CLI for automation purposes. Your data scientist reports "I have edit access but the project isn't in the dashboard." You check: oc get ns anihpj --show-labels — no dashboard label. Fix with one command. This is the #1 cause of "missing project" support tickets.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "A project named 'ml-team' exists but doesn't appear in the dashboard. Fix it." Command: oc label namespace ml-team opendatahub.io/dashboard=true. Verify by refreshing the dashboard.

Projects & WBs Q43 of 200
How do you share a Data Science Project with a new team member?
A) Add the user (or their group) to a RoleBinding in the project namespace — use oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit newuser -n project-name
B) Share the project URL from the dashboard — the dashboard generates a shareable link that grants temporary access
C) Add the user's email to the project's "Members" list in the dashboard UI — the dashboard manages access through its own user management system
D) The project creator must transfer ownership — only the original project admin can add new members through the project settings
✅ Correct Answer: A

Project access in RHOAI is standard OpenShift RBAC. To share a project: (1) Add user to a group (optional, but recommended): oc adm groups add-users anihpj-team newuser. (2) Bind the user/group to a project role: oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit newuser -n anihpj or oc adm policy add-role-to-group edit anihpj-team -n anihpj. The user immediately sees the project in their dashboard upon next login/refresh. There is no dashboard-based "Share" button or "Members" list separate from OpenShift RBAC — the dashboard simply reads the RoleBindings in the namespace.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Sharing a DSP — RBAC in Practice
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              SHARING A DATA SCIENCE PROJECT                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  METHOD 1: Add user directly (simple, less scalable)                     │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────                        │
  │  $ oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit frank -n anihpj                   │
  │  → frank can now create workbenches, deploy models in anihpj             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  METHOD 2: Use groups (recommended for teams)                            │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────                            │
  │  $ oc adm groups new anihpj-team                                          │
  │  $ oc adm groups add-users anihpj-team alice bob charlie                 │
  │  $ oc adm policy add-role-to-group edit anihpj-team -n anihpj            │
  │  → All group members get edit access                                     │
  │  → When a new member joins: oc adm groups add-users anihpj-team diana    │
  │  → No need to touch RoleBindings!                                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  VERIFY WHO HAS ACCESS:                                                  │
  │  ───────────────────────                                                  │
  │  $ oc get rolebinding -n anihpj                                          │
  │  NAME                 ROLE                USERS/GROUPS                   │
  │  admin                ClusterRole/admin   diana                          │
  │  edit                 ClusterRole/edit    anihpj-team                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  $ oc adm policy who-can edit notebooks -n anihpj                        │
  │  → Shows all users/groups with notebook edit permissions                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: A new data scientist "grace" joins the anihpj team. Instead of binding her individually to every project, you just add her to the anihpj-team group. She immediately gets edit access to the anihpj project, all the data connections, and can launch workbenches. When she leaves, remove her from the group — one command, all access revoked.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Grant user 'henry' edit access to the 'ml-team' project." Command: oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit henry -n ml-team. Verify: oc auth can-i create notebooks --as=henry -n ml-team.

Projects & WBs Q44 of 200
What is a ResourceQuota in a Data Science Project and why would you configure one?
A) ResourceQuota limits the number of users in a project — it's used to control how many data scientists can join a team project
B) ResourceQuota limits total resource consumption (CPU, memory, GPU, PVC storage, object counts) within a namespace — it prevents one project from consuming all cluster resources and starving other projects
C) ResourceQuota defines the minimum resources for each workbench — it ensures every workbench gets at least the specified CPU and memory
D) ResourceQuota is automatically set by RHOAI based on the project's tier — you cannot manually configure quotas for DSPs
✅ Correct Answer: B

A ResourceQuota is a namespace-level constraint that limits total resource consumption. In a DSP, you can set: total CPU (e.g., 16 cores), total memory (e.g., 64Gi), total GPU count (e.g., 4 GPUs), total PVC storage (e.g., 500Gi), and object counts (max 10 workbenches, max 20 PVCs). Without quotas, one project could spawn 50 GPU workbenches and consume the entire cluster, leaving no resources for other teams. Quotas are enforced at admission — if creating a new workbench would exceed the quota, the API server rejects it. This is different from LimitRange (which sets defaults per pod) and different from user limits (which are RBAC, not quota).

📝 Detailed Explanation
ResourceQuota in Data Science Projects
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              RESOURCEQUOTA — Per-Project Resource Limits                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  PROJECT: anihpj (ResourceQuota: anihpj-quota)                           │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Resource          Used        Hard Limit    Status               │    │
  │  │  ────────          ────        ──────────    ──────               │    │
  │  │  CPU Requests      12 cores    16 cores      🟡 75% used          │    │
  │  │  Memory Requests   48 Gi       64 Gi         🟡 75% used          │    │
  │  │  GPU (nvidia.com)  3           4             🟡 75% used          │    │
  │  │  PVC Storage       200 Gi      500 Gi        🟢 40% used          │    │
  │  │  Workbench Count   5           10            🟢 50% used          │    │
  │  │  PVC Count         8           20            🟢 40% used          │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WITHOUT QUOTA:                                                          │
  │  ─────────────                                                           │
  │  ❌ Team A creates 50 workbenches → Cluster runs out of resources        │
  │  ❌ Team B cannot create any workbenches → "Platform is broken"          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WITH QUOTA:                                                             │
  │  ──────────                                                              │
  │  ✅ Each team has defined limits                                         │
  │  ✅ Team A hits their GPU quota limit → Must clean up old workbenches    │
  │  ✅ Team B always has guaranteed resources                               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your cluster has 8 GPUs shared across 3 teams. Without quotas, the anihpj team could use all 8 GPUs for training, leaving the ml-experiments team unable to run inference. You set a quota: anihpj gets 4 GPUs max, ml-experiments gets 3, and the NLP team gets 1. Everyone has guaranteed GPU access.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Limit the anihpj project to 4 GPUs and 64 Gi memory." Create a ResourceQuota CR in the anihpj namespace with hard limits for nvidia.com/gpu and memory. Verify: oc get resourcequota -n anihpj.

Projects & WBs Q45 of 200
What is a ServiceAccount in the context of a Data Science Project, and why is it important?
A) ServiceAccounts are user login accounts for the dashboard — each data scientist gets one ServiceAccount to authenticate
B) ServiceAccounts are billing accounts that track GPU usage — they're used by Red Hat to calculate subscription costs
C) ServiceAccounts are unnecessary in RHOAI — the platform manages all authentication and authorization automatically
D) ServiceAccounts are machine identities for pods — pipeline steps, KServe predictors, and workbench pods use SAs to authenticate to the API server, access S3, pull images, and interact with other services
✅ Correct Answer: D

ServiceAccounts (SAs) are pod-level identities — not for human users. Every pod in a project runs under a ServiceAccount. This is critical for RHOAI because: (1) Pipeline steps use SAs to create/delete Kubernetes resources, access S3 artifacts, and push to model registries. (2) KServe predictors use SAs to pull model images from private registries. (3) Workbench pods use SAs to access S3 data connections and interact with the Kubernetes API. (4) Custom SAs with specific RBAC permissions ensure the principle of least privilege — your pipeline SA doesn't need cluster-admin; it only needs access to its own namespace and S3.

📝 Detailed Explanation
ServiceAccounts in RHOAI — Machine Identities for Pods
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              SERVICE ACCOUNTS IN A DSP                                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  PROJECT: anihpj                                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  default SA (created automatically)                               │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                        │    │
  │  │  │ Used by: Workbench pods, basic pods  │                        │    │
  │  │  │ Permissions: Minimal (namespace only)│                        │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                        │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  pipeline-sa (custom, for pipelines)                              │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                        │    │
  │  │  │ Used by: KFP pipeline step pods      │                        │    │
  │  │  │ Permissions: Create pods, access S3  │                        │    │
  │  │  │   (bound via Role + RoleBinding)     │                        │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                        │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  kserve-sa (custom, for model serving)                            │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐                        │    │
  │  │  │ Used by: KServe predictor pods       │                        │    │
  │  │  │ Permissions: Pull images, read S3    │                        │    │
  │  │  │   (bound via Role + RoleBinding)     │                        │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                        │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CREATE SA WITH S3 ACCESS:                                               │
  │  ─────────────────────────                                                │
  │  $ oc create sa pipeline-sa -n anihpj                                    │
  │  $ oc adm policy add-role-to-user edit -z pipeline-sa -n anihpj          │
  │  $ oc create secret generic s3-creds --from-literal=...                  │
  │  $ oc secrets link pipeline-sa s3-creds -n anihpj                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The anihpj pipeline needs to read training data from S3, create pods for training steps, and push the trained model to the model registry. You create a dedicated SA called pipeline-sa with exactly these permissions — no more, no less. If the pipeline code has a bug that tries to delete other projects, the SA's limited permissions block it. This is defense in depth through least-privilege SAs.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Create a ServiceAccount for pipeline execution with S3 access." Create SA, create S3 credentials secret, link secret to SA, bind edit role to SA. The pipeline server should be configured to use this SA.

Projects & WBs Q46 of 200
A data scientist creates a workbench in the wrong project. How can they move it to the correct project?
A) Use the dashboard's "Move Workbench" feature — select the target project from a dropdown and the workbench is migrated automatically
B) Workbenches cannot be moved between projects — you must export your notebooks/data, delete the workbench in the old project, and recreate it in the new project
C) Use oc edit notebook and change the namespace field — Kubernetes supports cross-namespace resource migration natively
D) Clone the workbench from the dashboard — the clone operation creates an identical workbench in any project you specify
✅ Correct Answer: B

Notebook CRs (workbenches) are namespace-scoped and cannot be migrated between namespaces. The PVC (persistent storage) is also namespace-scoped and cannot be moved. The correct procedure: (1) Save all work — commit notebooks to Git or download files. (2) Export any important data from the workbench's PVC. (3) Delete the workbench in the wrong project. (4) Create a new workbench in the correct project. (5) Clone the Git repo or re-upload data. This is why project planning matters — create the right project BEFORE building extensive workbenches.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Workbench Migration — You Can't Move, You CAN Recreate
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              MOVING A WORKBENCH — The Correct Procedure                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WRONG PROJECT: ml-experiments           RIGHT PROJECT: anihpj           │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐          ┌────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ 📓 workbench-alice         │          │                            │  │
  │  │ 💾 pvc-alice (50Gi)        │          │                            │  │
  │  │                            │          │                            │  │
  │  │  ❌ Cannot be moved!       │          │                            │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘          └────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1: SAVE YOUR WORK                                                  │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                   │
  │  $ cd /opt/app-root/src                                                  │
  │  $ git add . && git commit -m "save before migration" && git push        │
  │  $ mc cp -r /data/ s3/anihpj-backup/ ← Backup data to S3                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 2: DELETE OLD WORKBENCH                                            │
  │  ───────────────────────────                                              │
  │  Dashboard: Stop → Delete workbench                                       │
  │  CLI: oc delete notebook workbench-alice -n ml-experiments               │
  │        oc delete pvc pvc-alice -n ml-experiments (if no longer needed)   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 3: RECREATE IN CORRECT PROJECT                                     │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────                                       │
  │  Dashboard: anihpj project → Create workbench → same config              │
  │  CLI: Create Notebook CR in anihpj namespace                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 4: RESTORE WORK                                                    │
  │  ─────────────────                                                       │
  │  $ git clone <repo-url>                                                 │
  │  $ mc cp s3/anihpj-backup/ /data/ --recursive                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice accidentally created her "salary-prediction" workbench in the wrong project. She's been working on it for a week and has trained several model versions. The fix: she commits all notebooks to the anihpj Git repository, exports model checkpoints to S3, and recreates the workbench in the correct anihpj project in 10 minutes.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Workbenches (Notebook CRs) and PVCs are namespace-scoped and CANNOT be migrated. The exam may test this directly. Always plan project structure before creating workbenches.

Projects & WBs Q47 of 200
What is a NetworkPolicy in a DSP context, and how does it protect AI workloads?
A) NetworkPolicy controls internet access for workbenches — it's used to allow/block workbenches from accessing external websites and PyPI packages
B) NetworkPolicy is a load-balancing rule for KServe — it distributes inference requests across multiple predictor replicas
C) NetworkPolicy controls pod-to-pod communication — it can restrict which pods can access the pipeline server database, model endpoints, or workbenches, enforcing defense-in-depth within and across projects
D) NetworkPolicy is automatically managed by RHOAI — administrators cannot create custom policies without breaking the platform
✅ Correct Answer: C

NetworkPolicies are Kubernetes-native firewall rules for pod traffic. In a DSP, you can create policies like: "Only workbench pods can access the pipeline server's MariaDB on port 3306," "KServe predictors can only be reached from the project's own pods and the ingress controller," or "No pods from other namespaces can access this project's resources." This is critical for securing AI workloads — you don't want an untrusted pod in another namespace accessing your model endpoint or training data. NetworkPolicies require a CNI that supports them (OpenShift's OVN-Kubernetes does by default).

📝 Detailed Explanation
NetworkPolicy — Securing AI Workload Communication
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              NETWORKPOLICY IN A DSP — Defense in Depth                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  PROJECT: anihpj                                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  Policy 1: Allow workbench → pipeline server DB (port 3306)       │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐               │    │
  │  │  │ 📓 Workbench     │──3306──▶│ 🔄 Pipeline Svr  │               │    │
  │  │  │ (app: notebook)  │  ✅     │ (app: pipeline)  │               │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────┘         └──────────────────┘               │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  Policy 2: Deny from other namespaces                             │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐               │    │
  │  │  │ 📓 Workbench     │◀──X────│ 🐛 Malicious Pod  │               │    │
  │  │  │ (ns: anihpj)     │  ❌     │ (ns: other-team) │               │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────┘         └──────────────────┘               │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  Policy 3: Allow ingress → KServe predictor (port 8080)           │    │
  │  │         ┌──────────────────┐                                      │    │
  │  │   🌐 ──▶│ 🚀 KServe Pred   │  ← Only from ingress + same ns      │    │
  │  │  ✅    │ (app: kserve)    │                                      │    │
  │  │         └──────────────────┘                                      │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The salary prediction model endpoint should only be accessible from the anihpj-api pod and the OpenShift ingress controller — not from random pods in other namespaces. A NetworkPolicy restricts ingress to the KServe predictor, preventing unauthorized access to the model. If another team's buggy pod tries to flood the model endpoint, the NetworkPolicy drops the traffic at the network level.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Ensure only pods in the anihpj namespace can access the KServe model endpoint." Create a NetworkPolicy with ingress from the same namespace with matching podSelector for the KServe predictor.

Projects & WBs Q48 of 200
What happens to a Data Science Project's resources when the project is deleted via oc delete namespace?
A) ALL resources in the namespace are deleted — workbenches (Notebook CRs + pods + PVCs), InferenceServices, pipeline configs, data connections, secrets, and the namespace itself are permanently removed
B) Only the namespace metadata is deleted — the actual pods and PVCs are orphaned and continue running as cluster-scoped resources
C) RHOAI has a safety mechanism that prevents namespace deletion if it contains active workbenches — you must stop all workbenches first
D) The namespace enters a 30-day "soft delete" state — resources can be recovered within 30 days via the dashboard's trash feature
✅ Correct Answer: A

Namespace deletion is cascading and permanent. When you delete a namespace, the Kubernetes garbage collector removes ALL resources within it: Notebook CRs, workbench pods, PVCs (and their data!), InferenceServices, pipeline configurations, data connection secrets, RoleBindings — everything. There is no "soft delete" or "trash" feature. RHOAI does NOT prevent namespace deletion if workbenches are running. This is why you should always backup important work (Git, S3) and verify before deleting a project. OADP backups can restore a deleted project if configured.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Project Deletion — Cascading & Permanent
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              PROJECT DELETION IMPACT                                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BEFORE: oc delete namespace anihpj                                      │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────                                        │
  │  anihpj/                                                                 │
  │  ├── 📓 Notebook: workbench-alice (RUNNING)                              │
  │  ├── 📓 Notebook: workbench-bob (STOPPED)                                │
  │  ├── 🚀 InferenceService: salary-predictor (RUNNING)                     │
  │  ├── 🔄 DSPA: pipeline-server                                            │
  │  ├── 💾 PVC: pvc-alice (50Gi) — Contains trained models!                 │
  │  ├── 💾 PVC: pipeline-artifacts (100Gi)                                  │
  │  ├── 🔗 Secret: s3-credentials                                           │
  │  ├── 👤 RoleBinding: anihpj-team (edit)                                  │
  │  └── ...                                                                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  AFTER: Namespace is gone. ALL of the above are DELETED PERMANENTLY.     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚠️  THERE IS NO RECYCLE BIN. NO RECOVERY (unless you have OADP backup).│
  │                                                                          │
  │  BEFORE DELETING A PROJECT:                                              │
  │  ──────────────────────────                                               │
  │  1. Notify all team members                                              │
  │  2. Commit/push all notebooks to Git                                     │
  │  3. Backup important PVC data to S3                                      │
  │  4. Export model registry metadata                                       │
  │  5. Verify OADP backup exists                                             │
  │  6. Then delete                                                           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: A well-meaning admin cleans up "old projects" and deletes what they think is an unused namespace. Unfortunately, it was the production anihpj project. All workbenches, trained models on PVCs, pipeline history, and the KServe salary predictor are gone. The only recovery is from the weekly OADP backup. This is why you implement RBAC restrictions on who can delete project namespaces.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: The exam may ask: "What happens when you delete a Data Science Project?" The answer: ALL resources in that namespace are permanently deleted. There is no undo. Always backup before deleting.

Projects & WBs Q49 of 200
How do cross-project model sharing and collaboration work in RHOAI?
A) All projects share a global model registry by default — any model registered in one project is automatically available in all others
B) Cross-project sharing requires cluster-admin intervention — only an admin can copy resources between namespaces
C) Cross-project sharing uses standard Kubernetes mechanisms — you can use S3 for shared artifacts, Model Registry with cross-namespace RBAC, or explicit NetworkPolicies allowing project-to-project communication for model endpoints
D) Projects are completely isolated and cannot share anything — each DSP is a fully air-gapped environment with no cross-project communication possible
✅ Correct Answer: C

Projects are isolated by default, but sharing is possible through explicit configuration: (1) S3 as shared storage — multiple projects can read/write to the same S3 bucket (e.g., team-A trains a model, saves to S3, team-B deploys it from S3). (2) Model Registry — with cross-namespace RBAC, project-B can read models registered by project-A. (3) NetworkPolicies — allow specific ingress from project-A to project-B's KServe endpoint. (4) Image registries — shared OCI registries let any project pull model images. The key principle: nothing is shared by default; everything requires explicit allow rules.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Cross-Project Collaboration Patterns
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              CROSS-PROJECT SHARING — Explicit, Not Automatic              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  PROJECT: model-training                  PROJECT: model-serving         │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐          ┌────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ 📓 Train workbench         │          │ 🚀 KServe Pred (vLLM)      │  │
  │  │     │                      │          │      ▲                     │  │
  │  │     │ saves to S3          │          │      │ reads from S3       │  │
  │  │     ▼                      │          │      │                     │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────┐ │          │  ┌───┴──────────────────┐  │  │
  │  │  │ S3: s3://anihpj/     │─┼──────────┼─▶│ Same bucket!         │  │  │
  │  │  │ models/v3/           │ │  ✅ S3   │  │ Read via IAM         │  │  │
  │  │  └──────────────────────┘ │  shared  │  └──────────────────────┘  │  │
  │  │                           │          │                            │  │
  │  │  NetworkPolicy:           │          │  NetworkPolicy:            │  │
  │  │  egress → model-serving   │───✅────▶│  ingress ← model-training │  │
  │  │  (port 8080)              │          │  (port 8080)              │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘          └────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SHARING MECHANISMS:                                                     │
  │  ─────────────────                                                       │
  │  • S3 buckets: Both projects use same bucket (IAM + credentials)         │
  │  • Model Registry: Cross-namespace RBAC for reading registered models    │
  │  • OCI Registry: Shared image pull secrets for model artifacts            │
  │  • NetworkPolicy: Explicit allow rules for inter-project traffic         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The "model-training" team trains the job-matching model and saves it to S3. The "model-serving" team deploys it via KServe. They're in separate projects for isolation, but share the S3 bucket for model artifacts. A NetworkPolicy allows the training team's workbench to reach the serving team's KServe endpoint for validation testing. This is the enterprise pattern: isolated development, controlled sharing.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Allow project-A to access project-B's KServe model endpoint." Create a NetworkPolicy in project-B allowing ingress from project-A's namespace labels. Verify with curl from a pod in project-A.

Projects & WBs Q50 of 200
What is the best practice for organizing Data Science Projects for a team working on multiple AI initiatives?
A) One project per team — put all workbenches, models, and pipelines for all initiatives into a single team project for simplicity
B) One project per user — each data scientist gets their own personal project; collaboration happens through shared S3 buckets
C) One project per cluster — use namespace-level sub-divisions within a single mega-project for all AI work
D) One project per AI initiative/environment — separate projects for dev/staging/prod of each initiative, with shared Git repos, S3 buckets, and model registries for controlled cross-project collaboration
✅ Correct Answer: D

The recommended pattern is one project per initiative per environment: anihpj-jobmatch-dev, anihpj-jobmatch-prod, anihpj-salary-dev, anihpj-salary-prod. This provides: (1) Environment isolation — dev experiments don't affect production model serving. (2) Resource isolation — production gets guaranteed GPU quota; dev shares the remainder. (3) RBAC granularity — interns get edit access to dev only; senior engineers get prod access. (4) Blast radius control — deleting a dev project doesn't affect production. (5) Cost tracking — resource usage is per-project, simplifying chargeback.

📝 Detailed Explanation

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your team follows this layout. Alice trains a new job-matching model in anihpj-jobmatch-dev with 2 GPUs. After validation, she registers it in the model registry and promotes it to anihpj-jobmatch-prod, where KServe deploys it with 4 dedicated GPUs. If alice accidentally deletes the dev project during cleanup, production is untouched. Interns have access to dev projects only — they can't break production.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Design a project layout for a team with dev and prod environments." The answer is separate namespaces per environment per initiative. Use RBAC to restrict prod access. Use ResourceQuotas to guarantee prod resources.

2.2 Workbench Creation & IDE ConfigurationQ51-Q62

Projects & WBs Q51 of 200
What IDE options are available when creating a workbench in OpenShift AI?
A) Only JupyterLab — OpenShift AI exclusively supports Jupyter notebooks as the workbench IDE
B) JupyterLab and RStudio — these are the only two supported data science IDEs available
C) JupyterLab, VS Code Server, RStudio, and custom images — you can select from prebuilt IDE images or bring your own custom image with any IDE
D) Any IDE that runs in a browser — you provide the URL and OpenShift AI proxies it through the workbench
✅ Correct Answer: C

OpenShift AI workbenches support multiple IDE options through prebuilt notebook images: JupyterLab (standard data science notebooks), VS Code Server (code-server for a full IDE experience), RStudio (for R-based data science), and custom images where you build your own container with any tools and IDE you need. The IDE is baked into the container image — you select the image that contains your preferred IDE when creating the workbench. You can also customize prebuilt images by extending them: add Python packages, system libraries, or configuration files via a custom Dockerfile.

Projects & WBs Q52 of 200
When creating a workbench, you select a "Container size." What does this control?
A) CPU and memory requests/limits allocated to the workbench pod — Small (1 CPU/4Gi), Medium (2 CPU/8Gi), Large (4 CPU/16Gi), X-Large (8 CPU/32Gi), with GPU options adding GPU resources
B) The disk size of the workbench's PVC — Small (10Gi), Medium (50Gi), Large (100Gi), X-Large (500Gi)
C) The number of concurrent users that can connect to the workbench — Small (1 user), Medium (5 users), Large (20 users)
D) The timeout duration before the workbench auto-stops — Small (1 hour), Medium (4 hours), Large (12 hours), X-Large (24 hours)
✅ Correct Answer: A

Container size controls the CPU and memory allocated to the workbench pod. The predefined sizes are: Small (1 CPU, 4Gi RAM), Medium (2 CPU, 8Gi RAM), Large (4 CPU, 16Gi RAM), X-Large (8 CPU, 32Gi RAM). GPU options add nvidia.com/gpu resources on top of the base size. The PVC storage size is configured separately under "Cluster storage." Container sizes are defined as defaults in the DSC but can be customized per workbench. Choosing the right size is critical — too small and the workbench OOMKills during model training; too large and you waste cluster resources.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Container Sizes — CPU/Memory Allocation
