  │  │    containers:                                                     │    │
  │  │      - image: vllm/vllm-openai:latest                             │    │
  │  │        args: ["--model", "/mnt/models", "--port", "8080"]         │    │
  │  │    supportedModelFormats:                                          │    │
  │  │      - name: pytorch                                               │    │
  │  │        version: "2"                                                │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                    │                                                      │
  │                    │ referenced by                                        │
  │                    ▼                                                      │
  │  InferenceService CR (model deployment)                                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  spec:                                                             │    │
  │  │    predictor:                                                      │    │
  │  │      model:                                                        │    │
  │  │        storageUri: "s3://models/llama-3/"                         │    │
  │  │        runtime: vllm-runtime    ← References the ServingRuntime   │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The salary predictor uses OVMS for efficient CPU inference (low cost), while the RAG LLM uses vLLM for high-throughput GPU serving. Both use the same ServingRuntime pattern but different runtimes. When vLLM releases a performance update, you update the ServingRuntime — all LLM InferenceServices benefit automatically.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Create a custom serving runtime for a PyTorch model." Create ServingRuntime CR → specify container image, ports, supported formats → create InferenceService referencing it.

Models Q95 of 200
What is the difference between RawDeployment and Serverless (Knative) deployment modes for KServe InferenceServices?
A) RawDeployment uses GPUs and Serverless uses CPUs only — the mode determines hardware allocation
B) RawDeployment creates standard Kubernetes Deployments (fixed replicas, manual scaling) while Serverless uses Knative Services (scale-to-zero, request-based autoscaling, traffic splitting for canary rollouts)
C) RawDeployment is for development only and Serverless is the only supported production mode
D) RawDeployment is faster but less secure — Serverless adds a sidecar proxy for TLS but doubles latency
✅ Correct Answer: B

KServe supports two deployment modes: RawDeployment creates a standard Kubernetes Deployment + Service — you set minReplicas for fixed pod count or use HPA for CPU/memory-based scaling. Pods run continuously. Best for: low-latency requirements (no cold start), GPU workloads (GPUs don't scale to zero well), and predictable traffic. Serverless (Knative) creates a Knative Service — supports scale-to-zero (no pods when idle), request-based autoscaling (concurrency-based), and traffic splitting for canary rollouts. Best for: sporadic inference, cost optimization, and A/B testing. The mode is set in the InferenceService: spec.predictor.mode: RawDeployment or Serverless (default).

📝 Detailed Explanation
RawDeployment vs Serverless — Deployment Modes
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RAW DEPLOYMENT                          SERVERLESS (Knative)            │
  │  ┌────────────────────────┐             ┌────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Deployment (fixed pods)│             │ Knative Service            │  │
  │  │ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐     │             │ ┌──────┐    (idle)         │  │
  │  │ │ Pod  │ │ Pod  │     │             │ │ Pod  │    ═══════        │  │
  │  │ │ (GPU)│ │ (GPU)│     │             │ │      │    0 pods         │  │
  │  │ └──────┘ └──────┘     │             │ └──────┘                   │  │
│  │  minReplicas: 2         │             │  Request arrives ─────────▶│  │
  │  │  Always running       │             │ ┌──────┐    pod spins up   │  │
  │  │  No cold start        │             │ │ Pod  │    (30s cold)     │  │
  │  └────────────────────────┘             │ └──────┘                   │  │
  │                                          │  ↔ Scale-to-zero ✓       │  │
  │  USE: Production GPU serving            │  ↔ Canary traffic % ✓     │  │
  │       Low-latency APIs                  │  ↔ Concurrency scaling ✓ │  │
  │                                          └────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │                                          USE: Bursty inference           │
  │                                               Cost optimization          │
  │                                               A/B model testing          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The salary predictor API is called hundreds of times per minute — it needs RawDeployment with 2 GPU pods always running for low latency. The RAG job description generator is used a few times per hour — it uses Serverless to scale to zero between requests, saving GPU costs.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Configure a model for production with guaranteed 2 replicas." Use RawDeployment with minReplicas: 2. For cost-sensitive sporadic inference, use Serverless (default) for scale-to-zero.

Models Q96 of 200
How do you expose a secure external endpoint for a KServe InferenceService so applications can call it?
A) KServe endpoints are automatically public — the InferenceService URL is accessible from the internet without additional configuration
B) You must manually create a NodePort Service and configure an external load balancer — KServe does not create external endpoints automatically
C) KServe creates an OpenShift Route (or Istio VirtualService) automatically — you can enable token-based authentication and TLS for secure external access; the endpoint URL is available in the InferenceService status
D) External access requires a separate API Gateway deployment — KServe models are internal-only by design
✅ Correct Answer: C

KServe automatically creates networking for InferenceServices. On OpenShift, it creates a Route (with TLS edge termination). On vanilla Kubernetes, it creates an Istio VirtualService. The endpoint URL is available at: oc get inferenceservice <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.url}'. For security, you can enable token-based authentication (ServiceAccount tokens required in request headers) and configure TLS/mTLS through ServiceMesh. The endpoint follows the KServe v1 API protocol: POST {url}/v1/models/{model}:predict with JSON payload.

📝 Detailed Explanation
KServe External Endpoint — Secure Access Pattern
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  $ oc get inferenceservice salary-predictor -n anihpj                    │
  │  NAME               URL                                   READY          │
  │  salary-predictor   https://salary-predictor-anihpj.apps.cluster.com    │
  │                                                              True        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CLIENT CALL (with auth token):                                          │
  │  ─────────────────────────────                                            │
  │  curl -k https://salary-predictor-anihpj.apps.cluster.com/v1/models/     │
  │    salary-predictor:predict \                                            │
  │    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(oc sa get-token kserve-sa -n anihpj)" \  │
  │    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \                                 │
  │    -d '{"inputs": [{"name": "features", "shape": [1,5],                 │
  │         "datatype": "FP32", "data": [5, 120000, 3, 1, 0]}]}'           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SECURITY OPTIONS:                                                       │
  │  ────────────────                                                        │
  │  • Token auth: Enable in InferenceService spec                           │
  │  • TLS: OpenShift Route auto-terminates TLS                              │
  │  • mTLS: Enable via ServiceMesh (PeerAuthentication)                     │
  │  • NetworkPolicy: Restrict ingress to specific namespaces                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The anihpj Django API needs to call the salary predictor for every job listing page. It uses the InferenceService URL with a ServiceAccount token for authentication. The endpoint is TLS-secured via OpenShift Route. Only the anihpj-api ServiceAccount has access — other services are blocked by NetworkPolicy.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Get the URL for a deployed model." Run oc get inferenceservice -n <project> -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.url}'. Test with curl using the KServe v1 predict API format.

Models Q97 of 200
How do you deploy a new version of a model using canary rollout to test it before full production traffic?
A) Update the InferenceService with a new predictor spec under canaryTrafficPercent — KServe splits traffic between the default (current) and canary (new) revisions based on the percentage you specify
B) Delete the old InferenceService and create a new one — KServe automatically performs blue-green deployment
C) Create a second InferenceService with "-v2" suffix and manually update the client code to call the new endpoint
D) Use the dashboard's "Rollout Model" button — this triggers an automated canary deployment with pre-configured traffic percentages
✅ Correct Answer: A

KServe supports canary rollouts natively. To deploy a new model version: (1) Apply the updated InferenceService with the new model storage URI and a canaryTrafficPercent field (e.g., 10). (2) KServe creates a canary revision — 10% of traffic goes to the new model, 90% stays on the current. (3) Monitor metrics — if the canary performs well, increase to 50%, then 100%. (4) When canaryTrafficPercent reaches 100, the canary becomes the default and the old revision is scaled down. This requires Serverless (Knative) mode — RawDeployment does not support canary traffic splitting.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Canary Rollout — Traffic Splitting
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 1: canaryTrafficPercent: 10                                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  🌐 Ingress ──┬── 90% ──▶ Default (v1): s3://models/job-match/v1│    │
  │  │               │                                                   │    │
  │  │               └── 10% ──▶ Canary (v2): s3://models/job-match/v2 │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 2: Verify canary health → Increase to 50%                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  🌐 Ingress ──┬── 50% ──▶ Default (v1)                           │    │
  │  │               │                                                   │    │
  │  │               └── 50% ──▶ Canary (v2)                            │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 3: Promote → canaryTrafficPercent: 100                             │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  🌐 Ingress ──── 100% ──▶ Canary (v2) now becomes default!       │    │
  │  │  Old v1 scaled to zero                                            │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The data science team trained a new job-matching model (v3) with 5% better accuracy. Instead of switching 100% of traffic immediately (risking downtime if the model has a bug), they deploy with canaryTrafficPercent: 10. For an hour, 10% of users get v3 results. Metrics show lower latency and better matches. They increase to 100%. Rollback takes one command: set canaryTrafficPercent: 0.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Deploy a new model version with 20% canary traffic." Add canaryTrafficPercent: 20 to InferenceService spec with the new model URI. Requires Serverless mode. Monitor with oc get inferenceservice to see traffic split.

Models Q98 of 200
What is the Model Registry in OpenShift AI and how does it help with model lifecycle management?
A) It's a file server that stores model weights — it's essentially a network file share for ML artifacts
B) It's a CRD-based system that registers, versions, and manages model metadata (metrics, parameters, framework, stage) — models can be promoted from Staging to Production and deployed directly via KServe
C) It's a Docker registry specifically for ML models — it extends OCI registries with model-specific metadata tags
D) It's a CI/CD pipeline that automatically retrains models on a schedule and deploys them to production
✅ Correct Answer: B

The Model Registry is a RHOAI component that provides centralized model lifecycle management. Each registered model has: (1) Versions (v1, v2, v3 with unique IDs), (2) Metadata (framework, metrics like accuracy/F1, training parameters, dataset info), (3) Stage transitions (Staging → Production → Archived), (4) Artifact location (S3 URI, OCI image reference), and (5) Deployment integration (can deploy directly to KServe from the registry). It uses CRDs (ModelRegistry, RegisteredModel, ModelVersion) and provides a REST API for querying models and versions programmatically.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Model Registry — Model Lifecycle Management
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Registered Model: job-match-model                                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Version 1 (Archived)                                             │    │
  │  │  ├── Metrics: accuracy=0.82, f1=0.79                              │    │
  │  │  ├── Framework: pytorch                                           │    │
  │  │  └── Artifact: s3://models/job-match/v1                           │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  Version 2 (Production) ← Currently serving!                      │    │
  │  │  ├── Metrics: accuracy=0.87, f1=0.85                              │    │
  │  │  ├── Framework: pytorch                                           │    │
  │  │  └── Artifact: s3://models/job-match/v2                           │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  Version 3 (Staging) ← Testing in progress                        │    │
  │  │  ├── Metrics: accuracy=0.89, f1=0.87                              │    │
  │  │  ├── Framework: pytorch                                           │    │
  │  │  └── Artifact: s3://models/job-match/v3                           │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  LIFECYCLE: Dev → Register in Staging → Validate → Promote to Production │
  │  ROLLBACK: Production → Archived (v2), Staging → Production (v3)         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The pipeline trains and registers each new model version automatically. The ML lead reviews metrics in the registry, promotes v3 from Staging to Production. KServe detects the production stage change and deploys v3 with canary rollout. If v3 underperforms, one click rolls back to v2. The registry provides full audit trail: who trained what, when, with what metrics.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Register a model and promote it to Production." Create ModelRegistry CR → register model with version, metrics, artifact URI → set stage: Staging → after validation, update stage: Production. KServe can auto-deploy from Production stage.

Models Q99 of 200
What is model quantization and when should you use it for deploying models in RHOAI?
A) Quantization compresses model files for faster download from S3 — it reduces storage costs but doesn't affect inference performance
B) Quantization is a training technique that improves model accuracy by using higher-precision numbers — it should always be enabled
C) Quantization is only for LLMs — smaller models like scikit-learn or XGBoost cannot be quantized
D) Quantization reduces model weight precision (FP32→INT8/INT4), decreasing VRAM usage by 2-4x and increasing inference speed — use it when GPU memory is limited and some accuracy loss is acceptable
✅ Correct Answer: D

Quantization converts model weights from 32-bit floating point (FP32, 4 bytes per weight) to lower precision like INT8 (1 byte) or INT4 (0.5 bytes). A 7B parameter model goes from ~28GB (FP32) to ~7GB (INT8) or ~3.5GB (INT4). This means: a model that required an A100 (40GB) can now run on a T4 (16GB). The trade-off is accuracy — quantized models typically lose 0.5-2% accuracy depending on the quantization method. Methods include: GPTQ, AWQ (activation-aware), GGUF/GGML (CPU-focused), and bitsandbytes (QLoRA fine-tuning). In RHOAI, vLLM supports AWQ-quantized models natively.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Model Quantization — Size vs Accuracy Trade-off
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LLAMA-3-8B MODEL SIZE AT DIFFERENT PRECISIONS:                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Precision    Size (VRAM)    GPU Required     Accuracy Impact            │
  │  ─────────    ───────────    ────────────     ───────────────            │
  │  FP32         28 GB          A100 (40GB)      Baseline                   │
  │  FP16         14 GB          T4 (16GB) / A10  ~0% loss                   │
  │  INT8          7 GB          T4 (16GB)         ~0.5% loss               │
  │  INT4          3.5 GB        T4 (16GB)         ~1-2% loss               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  COMMAND IN WORKBENCH:                                                   │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                   │
  │  from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig       │
  │  quant_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True)                    │
  │  model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(                           │
  │      "meta-llama/Llama-3-8B", quantization_config=quant_config          │
  │  )                                                                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  vLLM WITH AWQ (Production serving):                                     │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────                                      │
  │  ServingRuntime args: [                                                  │
  │    "--model", "/mnt/models",                                             │
  │    "--quantization", "awq"   ← Loads AWQ-quantized model                │
  │  ]                                                                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Your team wants to deploy Llama-3-8B for RAG job description generation, but you only have T4 GPUs (16GB). FP16 requires 14GB — too close to the limit. You quantize to INT8 (7GB) with AWQ. The model runs smoothly on T4 with minimal accuracy loss. Job descriptions generated by the quantized model are nearly indistinguishable from the full-precision version.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "A model OOMs on a T4 GPU. Fix it." Options: quantize (INT8/INT4), reduce batch size, use smaller model variant, or upgrade GPU. Quantization is the most efficient fix for LLM deployment.

Models Q100 of 200
How do you monitor a deployed model for data drift and bias in OpenShift AI?
A) Enable TrustyAI in the DSC, deploy a TrustyAI payload logger, and configure drift/bias metrics — TrustyAI monitors inference data distribution and alerts when drift exceeds thresholds
B) Check the InferenceService logs manually — drift patterns are visible in the predictor pod's stdout logs
C) Use the dashboard's "Model Health" tab — it automatically displays drift and bias metrics for all deployed models without configuration
D) Model monitoring requires a separate SaaS product — RHOAI does not include built-in drift or bias monitoring capabilities
✅ Correct Answer: A

TrustyAI is RHOAI's model monitoring component for bias and drift detection. Setup: (1) Enable TrustyAI in the DSC (trustyai: {enabled: true}). (2) Deploy a TrustyAI payload logger that captures inference requests/responses. (3) Configure drift metrics (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Chi-Squared, Wasserstein distance) and bias metrics (Statistical Parity Difference, Disparate Impact). (4) Set thresholds — when drift exceeds 0.1, TrustyAI fires a Prometheus alert. The dashboard shows drift over time and highlights which features are drifting. This is critical for production models — if user behavior changes (e.g., new job categories), the model's accuracy degrades silently without monitoring.

📝 Detailed Explanation
TrustyAI — Model Drift & Bias Monitoring
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TRUSTYAI MONITORING PIPELINE:                                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Inference Requests ──▶ Payload Logger ──▶ TrustyAI Service              │
  │  (input features)        (captures data)    (analyzes drift/bias)        │
  │                                                      │                    │
  │                                                      ▼                    │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  DRIFT DETECTION:                                                 │    │
  │  │  Feature: "salary_range"                                          │    │
  │  │  Training distribution: mean=$80K, std=$30K                       │    │
  │  │  Current distribution:  mean=$95K, std=$35K                       │    │
  │  │  Drift score: 0.35   ⚠️  EXCEEDS THRESHOLD (0.1)                 │    │
  │  │  → Alert: "salary_range feature is drifting!"                     │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  BIAS DETECTION:                                                  │    │
  │  │  Protected attribute: "gender"                                    │    │
  │  │  Statistical Parity Difference: -0.15                             │    │
  │  │  → Model may be biased against certain demographics               │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The salary predictor was trained on 2024 salary data. By 2026, inflation has pushed average salaries 15% higher. Without TrustyAI, the model silently becomes inaccurate — predicting lower salaries than market rate, frustrating job seekers. TrustyAI detects the drift in "salary" feature distribution and alerts the ML team: "Retrain the model with recent data."

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Enable drift monitoring for a deployed model." Enable TrustyAI in DSC → deploy payload logger → configure drift metrics with thresholds → verify: check TrustyAI dashboard or Prometheus alerts for drift scores.

3.2 KServe Model Serving ArchitectureQ101-Q114

Models Q101 of 200
What is the Predictor component in a KServe InferenceService and what configuration options does it support?
A) The Predictor is a load balancer between multiple model replicas — it distributes incoming requests
B) The Predictor is a monitoring agent that tracks prediction accuracy — it doesn't serve models directly
C) The Predictor is the core model server — it loads the model from storageUri, runs the serving runtime, handles inference requests, and supports configuration for GPU, memory, minReplicas, and runtime selection
D) The Predictor is a caching layer that stores recent predictions — it reduces latency by returning cached results
✅ Correct Answer: C

The Predictor is the only required component of an InferenceService. It handles: model loading from S3/OCI/PVC, running the specified ServingRuntime (vLLM, OVMS, TGIS), processing inference requests, and returning predictions. Configuration includes: storageUri (model location), runtime (ServingRuntime name), resources (GPU count, CPU, memory), minReplicas/maxReplicas (scaling), tolerations/nodeSelector (scheduling to GPU nodes), affinity (pod placement), and imagePullSecrets (private registries). The predictor pod is where nvidia-smi shows GPU utilization and where model weights are loaded into VRAM.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Predictor Configuration — The Core Model Server
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  InferenceService spec.predictor:                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  predictor:                                                       │    │
  │  │    model:                                                         │    │
  │  │      storageUri: "s3://anihpj-models/job-match/v3/"              │    │
  │  │      runtime: vllm-runtime        ← Which ServingRuntime         │    │
  │  │    resources:                                                     │    │
  │  │      requests:                                                   │    │
  │  │        nvidia.com/gpu: 1          ← GPU allocation               │    │
  │  │        memory: "16Gi"             ← RAM for model + overhead     │    │
  │  │    minReplicas: 2                 ← Always 2 pods running        │    │
  │  │    tolerations: [{ key: "nvidia.com/gpu", operator: "Exists" }]  │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │  THIS SINGLE BLOCK CONTROLS: Model source, hardware, scaling, placement  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The salary predictor needs 1 GPU and 2 replicas for high availability. Configured in the predictor spec, KServe ensures 2 pods always run on GPU nodes with the correct tolerations.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: The predictor is the only required InferenceService component. The model location (storageUri) and serving runtime must both be configured correctly for the model to load.

Models Q102 of 200
What is the purpose of the Transformer component in a KServe InferenceService?
A) Pre/post-processing — it transforms raw input into model-compatible format before prediction and converts model output back to user-friendly format
B) Model conversion — it converts models between formats (PyTorch→ONNX, TF→TFLite) at deployment time
C) Data augmentation — it generates additional training samples to improve model accuracy
D) Load balancing — it distributes inference requests across predictor replicas based on their current load
✅ Correct Answer: A

The Transformer is an optional sidecar that handles data transformation before and after the predictor. Common use cases: (1) Image preprocessing — resize, normalize pixels before feeding to CNN. (2) Text tokenization — convert raw text to token IDs for LLMs. (3) Feature engineering — one-hot encoding, scaling, missing value imputation. (4) Output formatting — convert model probabilities to human-readable labels, format JSON responses. This separation keeps the predictor focused on pure inference while the transformer handles data concerns. If your client already sends model-ready data, you don't need a transformer.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Transformer — Pre/Post Processing Pipeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Client sends raw data:                                                   │
  │  {"salary": 120000, "experience": 5, "title": "Senior Engineer"}         │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐                │
  │  │ Transformer  │───▶│  Predictor   │───▶│ Transformer  │                │
  │  │ (pre-process)│    │  (inference) │    │ (post-process)│               │
  │  │              │    │              │    │              │                │
  │  │ salary→log   │    │ DNN forward  │    │ prob→label   │                │
  │  │ title→embed  │    │ pass         │    │ format JSON  │                │
  │  │ scale [0,1]  │    │              │    │              │                │
  │  └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘                │
  │                                                          │                │
  │                                                          ▼                │
  │  Response: {"predicted_salary": 135000, "confidence": 0.92, "range":...}│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The salary predictor expects normalized features [0,1] range. The Django API sends raw values ($120K, 5 years). The transformer normalizes inputs, the predictor infers, and the transformer converts the normalized prediction back to dollar amounts with a confidence score.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: The Transformer is optional. Use it when your model expects pre-processed input or you need to transform output. Adding a transformer means 2 containers per pod (transformer + predictor).

Models Q106 of 200
What is the difference between RawDeployment and Serverless (Knative) deployment modes in KServe?
A) RawDeployment uses Kubernetes deployments; Serverless uses OpenShift DeploymentConfigs — they are the same thing with different names
B) RawDeployment requires manual pod scaling only; Serverless mode requires at least 10 nodes — it's for enterprise clusters only
C) RawDeployment is for CPU-only models; Serverless is required for GPU models — Knative is the only way to schedule GPU workloads
D) RawDeployment creates standard Kubernetes Deployments/Services controlled by KServe's controller; Serverless mode uses Knative Serving for scale-to-zero, request-based autoscaling, and traffic splitting — choose based on your scaling needs and Knative availability
✅ Correct Answer: D

KServe supports two deployment modes configured via spec.deploymentMode: RawDeployment (default, previously called "Serverless: None") creates standard K8s Deployments, Services, and HPA-based autoscaling. Simpler, no Knative dependency. Serverless (requires Knative Serving installed) enables scale-to-zero (no pods when idle), request-based concurrency autoscaling, traffic splitting for canary rollouts, and revision history. For production LLM serving, RawDeployment with HPA is common (GPUs shouldn't scale to zero — reloading models takes minutes). For bursty, lightweight models, Serverless Knative reduces idle costs.

📝 Detailed Explanation
RawDeployment vs Serverless (Knative)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RAWDEPLOYMENT:                     SERVERLESS (KNATIVE):                 │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────┐          │
  │  │ Deployment (KServe-     │       │ Knative Service         │          │
  │  │ controlled)             │       │   ├─ Revision (v1)      │          │
  │  │   ├─ HPA (min=1, max=5) │       │   ├─ Route (traffic)    │          │
  │  │   └─ Service            │       │   └─ Configuration      │          │
  │  └─────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────┘          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  USE RAWDEPLOYMENT WHEN:          USE SERVERLESS WHEN:                   │
  │  ✅ GPU models (warm pods)        ✅ CPU models (scale to zero)          │
  │  ✅ Always-on inference           ✅ Bursty traffic patterns             │
  │  ✅ No Knative dependency         ✅ Need traffic splitting              │
  │  ✅ Simpler troubleshooting       ✅ Pay-per-use cost model              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The salary predictor (GPU model) uses RawDeployment — always 2 replicas warm, no cold start. The job-matching embedding model (CPU, lightweight) uses Serverless — scales to zero overnight when no users browse jobs, saving compute resources.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: RawDeployment = standard K8s Deployments (simpler). Serverless = Knative (scale-to-zero, traffic splitting). Config: spec.deploymentMode. GPU models should use RawDeployment to avoid cold-start delays.

Models Q107 of 200
What is a ServingRuntime in KServe and how does it relate to model deployment?
A) It's a Python library installed in workbenches — ServingRuntimes are client-side packages for building models
B) A ServingRuntime defines the container image and configuration for a model server (OVMS, vLLM, TGIS, Triton) — the InferenceService references it by name, and the runtime's image loads and serves the model
C) It's a Kubernetes operator that manages model lifecycle — ServingRuntimes replace the KServe controller for custom model formats
D) It's a monitoring agent that tracks serving performance — ServingRuntimes collect latency and throughput metrics
✅ Correct Answer: B

ServingRuntime is a cluster-scoped CRD that defines how a specific model server runs. It specifies: the container image (e.g., quay.io/opendatahub/vllm:latest), supported model formats (PyTorch, GGUF, ONNX), resource defaults, environment variables, ports, and health check endpoints. Common built-in runtimes: OVMS (OpenVINO Model Server — optimized for Intel CPUs), vLLM (high-throughput LLM serving with PagedAttention), TGIS (Text Generation Inference Server — IBM/Red Hat's LLM server), Triton (NVIDIA's multi-framework server). Custom ServingRuntimes can be created for custom model servers or optimized configurations.

📝 Detailed Explanation
ServingRuntime → InferenceService Relationship
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SERVINGRUNTIME (Cluster Resource):                                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1alpha1                           │    │
  │  │  kind: ServingRuntime                                              │    │
  │  │  metadata:                                                         │    │
  │  │    name: vllm-runtime                                              │    │
  │  │  spec:                                                             │    │
  │  │    containers:                                                     │    │
  │  │      - image: quay.io/opendatahub/vllm:0.4.2                      │    │
  │  │        args: ["--port", "8080", "--model", "/mnt/models"]         │    │
  │  │    supportedModelFormats: [{name: pytorch}, {name: gguf}]         │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       │ referenced by                                                     │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  INFERENCESERVICE:                                                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  spec:                                                            │    │
  │  │    predictor:                                                     │    │
  │  │      model:                                                       │    │
  │  │        runtime: vllm-runtime    ← references ServingRuntime      │    │
  │  │        storageUri: s3://anihpj-models/llama-8b/                  │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The RAG LLM uses the vLLM ServingRuntime for high-throughput token generation (continuous batching, PagedAttention). The salary predictor uses OVMS ServingRuntime optimized for regression models on CPU. One cluster, multiple runtimes, each model picks the right one.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: ServingRuntime = "what server runs my model." InferenceService = "which model to serve." Know: vLLM for LLMs, OVMS for Intel CPU optimization, TGIS for IBM/Red Hat LLM stack.

Models Q108 of 200
How does KServe autoscaling work and what configuration options control it?
A) KServe uses HPA (RawDeployment) or KPA (Serverless/Knative) — configure minReplicas/maxReplicas for bounds, targetUtilization for CPU/memory thresholds, and for Knative, concurrency targets per pod
B) KServe automatically scales based on GPU utilization only — CPU and memory metrics are not used for scaling decisions
C) Autoscaling is fixed — you set replica count and KServe never changes it; there is no autoscaling in KServe
D) KServe delegates scaling to OpenShift's ClusterAutoscaler — you configure cluster-level settings, not per-model
✅ Correct Answer: A

KServe autoscaling depends on deployment mode. RawDeployment: Uses Kubernetes HPA based on CPU/memory utilization. Configure minReplicas (warm pods), maxReplicas (cost ceiling), targetUtilization (when to scale, e.g., 70% CPU). Serverless (Knative): Uses KPA (Knative Pod Autoscaler) based on concurrency. Configure containerConcurrency (max concurrent requests per pod, default 0 = unlimited), target (target concurrency to trigger scaling), scaleToZero and scaleDownDelay (how long to keep pods after last request). For GPU models, set minReplicas ≥ 1 to avoid cold starts (loading model into VRAM takes minutes).

📝 Detailed Explanation
KServe Autoscaling Configuration
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RAWDEPLOYMENT (HPA):                                                     │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  predictor:                                                       │    │
  │  │    minReplicas: 2          ← Always 2 warm pods (no cold start)  │    │
  │  │    maxReplicas: 8          ← Cost ceiling                        │    │
  │  │    scaleTarget: 70         ← CPU% threshold for scale-out        │    │
  │  │    scaleMetric: cpu        ← Scale based on CPU                  │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SERVERLESS / KNATIVE (KPA):                                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  predictor:                                                       │    │
  │  │    minReplicas: 0          ← Scale to zero when idle             │    │
  │  │    maxReplicas: 10                                                │    │
  │  │    containerConcurrency: 5 ← Max 5 concurrent requests per pod   │    │
  │  │    scaleMetric: concurrency ← Scale based on concurrent requests │    │
  │  │    scaleDownDelay: 60s     ← Wait 60s before scaling down        │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The RAG LLM uses RawDeployment with minReplicas=2 — LLMs take 2+ minutes to load into GPU VRAM, so cold starts would cause terrible user experience. The embedding model (CPU) uses Knative with minReplicas=0 — it starts in under 5 seconds, so scale-to-zero saves overnight costs.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: GPU models: minReplicas ≥ 1 always. CPU/lightweight models: minReplicas=0 with Knative for cost savings. HPA = RawDeployment, KPA = Serverless.

Models Q109 of 200
How do you perform a canary rollout when updating a model version in KServe?
A) Delete the old InferenceService and create a new one — KServe handles zero-downtime rollouts automatically
B) Update the storageUri in the existing InferenceService — KServe performs a rolling update like a standard Deployment
C) Create a new InferenceService revision and use spec.predictor.canaryTrafficPercent to gradually shift traffic — KServe splits traffic between old and new revisions
D) Use the OpenShift Route to split traffic — canary rollouts are handled at the OpenShift networking layer, not in KServe
✅ Correct Answer: C

KServe supports canary rollouts via the canaryTrafficPercent field. Process: (1) Deploy the new model as a new revision by updating the InferenceService with the new model URI. (2) Set canaryTrafficPercent: 10 to send 10% of traffic to the new revision. (3) Monitor metrics (latency, error rate, prediction quality). (4) Gradually increase: 10% → 25% → 50% → 100%. (5) When satisfied, remove the canary field to promote fully. If issues arise, set canaryTrafficPercent: 0 to instantly rollback to the old revision. This is critical for ML models where you need to validate prediction quality on live traffic before full promotion.

📝 Detailed Explanation
KServe Canary Rollout
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  MODEL V3 (CURRENT)                  MODEL V4 (NEW)                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────┐            │
  │  │ accuracy: 92%         │           │ accuracy: 94%         │            │
  │  │ latency p99: 120ms    │           │ latency p99: 115ms    │            │
  │  │ 2 replicas running    │           │ 1 replica running     │            │
  │  └──────────────────────┘           └──────────────────────┘            │
  │         ▲                                    ▲                           │
  │         │                                    │                           │
  │    ┌────┴────────────────────────────────────┴────┐                      │
  │    │         TRAFFIC SPLIT                         │                      │
  │    │                                               │                      │
  │    │  Phase 1: V4=10%, V3=90%  (1 hour)           │                      │
  │    │  Phase 2: V4=25%, V3=75%  (4 hours)          │                      │
  │    │  Phase 3: V4=50%, V3=50%  (8 hours)          │                      │
  │    │  Phase 4: V4=100%         (promote)          │                      │
  │    └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Config: canaryTrafficPercent: 25                                        │
  │  Rollback: canaryTrafficPercent: 0  (instant, all traffic back to V3)   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You train a new salary prediction model (V4) with 94% accuracy vs V3's 92%. Instead of instantly replacing V3 (risky), you canary V4 at 10% traffic. Monitor prediction quality for 1 hour. If V4's predictions are worse on real data, rollback to V3 instantly with zero impact.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: canaryTrafficPercent = gradual rollout. Set to 0 for instant rollback. Use with Knative Serverless mode for best traffic splitting. Monitor metrics during rollout.

Models Q110 of 200
What is ModelMesh and how does multi-model serving work in KServe?
A) ModelMesh is a 3D visualization tool for model architectures — it renders neural network topologies as interactive meshes
B) ModelMesh enables hosting multiple models on a single ServingRuntime pod — models share GPU/CPU resources, loaded on-demand, reducing infrastructure costs for low-traffic models
C) ModelMesh is a service mesh for models — it adds mTLS encryption between the predictor and transformer containers
D) ModelMesh replicates models across multiple clusters — it's a multi-cluster model synchronization tool like a CDN for ML models
✅ Correct Answer: B

ModelMesh is KServe's multi-model serving solution. Instead of each model having its own pod (one-to-one), ModelMesh hosts multiple models on shared ServingRuntime pods. Key benefits: (1) GPU sharing — 10 lightweight models share one GPU instead of needing 10 GPUs. (2) On-demand loading — models are loaded from S3/PVC when first requested, then cached in memory. (3) Intelligent eviction — least-used models are unloaded to free memory for active models. (4) Namespace scoping — models are isolated per namespace via ServingRuntime configuration. ModelMesh uses etcd for model state tracking and gRPC for model management API. Best for: many small models with sporadic inference requests. Not ideal for: a single large LLM that needs the entire GPU.

📝 Detailed Explanation
ModelMesh — Multi-Model Serving
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TRADITIONAL (1 Model = 1 Pod):          MODELMESH (N Models per Pod):    │
  │  ┌────────┐┌────────┐┌────────┐        ┌────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │Model A ││Model B ││Model C │        │  ServingRuntime Pod     │     │
  │  │  GPU 0 ││  GPU 1 ││  GPU 2 │        │                        │     │
  │  │ (idle) ││ (idle) ││ (idle) │        │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐ │     │
  │  └────────┘└────────┘└────────┘        │  │ A  │ │ B  │ │ C  │ │     │
  │  3 GPUs = 3 models (most idle)         │  │    │ │    │ │    │ │     │
  │                                         │  └────┘ └────┘ └────┘ │     │
  │                                         │       GPU 0            │     │
  │                                         └────────────────────────┘     │
  │                                         1 GPU = N models (efficient)     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  LOADING: On-demand — model loaded into memory on first inference        │
  │  EVICTION: LRU (Least Recently Used) — idle models unloaded automatically│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You have 5 lightweight models (job-category classifier, skill extractor, experience normalizer, location parser, salary-band predictor). Instead of 5 separate pods each using 1 GPU, ModelMesh loads all 5 onto a single GPU. When the job-category classifier gets 1000 requests per hour and the location parser gets 10, ModelMesh keeps the classifier loaded and evicts the location parser to save memory.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: ModelMesh = many models on one pod/pod group. Good for lightweight models with sporadic traffic. Not for large LLMs. Know the difference between single-model serving (one InferenceService per model) and ModelMesh multi-model serving.

Models Q111 of 200
What is the Explainer component in KServe and when would you use it?
A) The Explainer generates human-readable documentation for model APIs — it's an auto-documentation tool for InferenceServices
B) The Explainer provides model interpretability — it runs explainability algorithms (LIME, SHAP, Anchor) as a sidecar to explain individual predictions, critical for regulated industries needing to justify AI decisions
C) The Explainer debugs model loading failures — it analyzes why a model failed to load and suggests fixes
D) The Explainer is a chatbot interface that answers questions about the model — it's an LLM-powered model documentation assistant
✅ Correct Answer: B

The Explainer is an optional KServe component that adds model interpretability. It runs algorithms like LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), and Anchor to explain WHY the model made a specific prediction. For example: "This resume was ranked #1 because of 5 years Python experience (weight: 0.4) and AWS certification (weight: 0.3)." Critical for: financial services (explain loan decisions), healthcare (justify diagnoses), HR (defend hiring recommendations against bias claims). The explainer runs as a sidecar alongside the predictor. RHOAI also integrates TrustyAI for advanced bias/drift monitoring beyond basic explainability.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Explainer — Model Interpretability
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  InferenceService with Explainer:                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  spec:                                                            │    │
  │  │    predictor:          ← Serves predictions                       │    │
  │  │      model: {storageUri: "s3://...", runtime: "vllm-runtime"}    │    │
  │  │    explainer:          ← Explains WHY that prediction             │    │
  │  │      type: "Lime"                                                 │    │
  │  │      model: {storageUri: "s3://...", runtime: "ovms-runtime"}    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Example prediction explanation:                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Input: {"resume": "...Python 5yr, AWS cert, BSc Math..."}       │    │
  │  │  Prediction: "Strong Match — 92%"                                  │    │
  │  │  Explanation (LIME):                                               │    │
  │  │    ✅ "Python 5 years" → +35% (highest weight)                     │    │
  │  │    ✅ "AWS Certification" → +28%                                   │    │
  │  │    ⚠️ "BSc Math" → +15%                                            │    │
  │  │    ⚠️ "No management exp" → -14%                                   │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: When the job-matching model ranks candidates, HR needs to justify decisions. The Explainer shows exactly which skills and qualifications drove each ranking — critical for compliance with hiring regulations and defending against bias allegations.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Explainer = model interpretability (LIME, SHAP). Optional component. Use for regulated industries. RHOAI also has TrustyAI for continuous bias/drift monitoring.

Models Q112 of 200
How does KServe expose an InferenceService externally and what networking options are available?
A) KServe creates a Kubernetes Service and optionally an OpenShift Route or Knative Route — the external URL is in the InferenceService status; you can configure TLS via OpenShift's edge/re-encrypt termination
B) KServe requires a separate Ingress Controller installation — it does not integrate with OpenShift Routes natively and needs NGINX or HAProxy
C) InferenceServices are only accessible within the cluster — external access requires manually creating a NodePort Service for each model
D) KServe uses a proprietary API Gateway — all inference requests must go through the RHOAI dashboard proxy
✅ Correct Answer: A

When you create an InferenceService, KServe automatically creates a Kubernetes Service and, depending on the deployment mode, either an OpenShift Route (RawDeployment) or a Knative Route (Serverless). The external URL is available in the InferenceService status: oc get inferenceservice -o jsonpath='{.status.url}'. TLS can be configured via OpenShift Routes (edge, re-encrypt, passthrough). For internal-only communication (microservices), use the cluster-internal service name: http://{is-name}-predictor.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local. Authentication can be added via OpenShift OAuth proxy or API keys.

📝 Detailed Explanation
KServe Networking — Internal & External Access

  │  EXTERNAL ACCESS:                                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  curl -k https://salary-predictor-anihpj.apps.cluster.com/v1/    │    │
  │  │    models/salary-predictor:predict                                │    │
  │  │       │                                                            │    │
  │  │       ▼                                                            │    │
  │  │  OpenShift Route (TLS edge) ──▶ KServe Service ──▶ Predictor Pod │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  INTERNAL ACCESS (microservices):                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  # Django API calls salary predictor internally:                  │    │
  │  │  POST http://salary-predictor-predictor.anihpj.svc.cluster.local │    │
  │  │    /v1/models/salary-predictor:predict                            │    │
  │  │  # No TLS needed for in-cluster traffic                           │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  GET URL: oc get is salary-predictor -o jsonpath='{.status.url}'        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The Django API calls the salary predictor internally via cluster DNS (fast, no TLS overhead). External users access the RAG job description generator via the OpenShift Route (TLS-encrypted). Both patterns coexist on the same InferenceService.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: KServe auto-creates Service + Route. URL in InferenceService status. Internal DNS: {name}-predictor.{ns}.svc.cluster.local. TLS via OpenShift Route.

Models Q113 of 200
What happens when you delete an InferenceService — what Kubernetes resources are cleaned up?
A) Only the InferenceService CR is deleted — all pods, services, and routes remain running until manually removed
B) The InferenceService and its pods are deleted, but Services and Routes persist — they become orphaned resources
C) Nothing is deleted — KServe retains all resources for rollback purposes; you must use a separate cleanup command
D) KServe's controller handles full cleanup — deleting the InferenceService cascades to remove Deployments/Services/Routes/HPAs, but the model data in S3/PVC is NOT deleted (data storage is separate from serving infrastructure)
✅ Correct Answer: D

KServe uses owner references for cascade deletion. When you delete an InferenceService: (1) KServe controller receives the deletion event. (2) Kubernetes garbage collection deletes all owned resources: Deployment/Knative Service, Service, Route, HPA/KPA, Pods. (3) The model data in S3, PVC, or OCI registry is NOT touched — storage is independent of serving. (4) The InferenceService CR is removed from etcd. This separation means you can delete and recreate InferenceServices without re-uploading models. The model data persists in storage, ready for the next deployment.

📝 Detailed Explanation
InferenceService Lifecycle
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CREATE:                             DELETE:                              │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐             ┌────────────────────┐              │
  │  │ InferenceService   │             │ oc delete is X     │              │
  │  │        │           │             │        │           │              │
  │  │        ▼           │             │        ▼           │              │
  │  │  KServe Controller │             │  Owner Refs cascade│              │
  │  │        │           │             │        │           │              │
  │  │   ┌────┼─────┐     │             │   ┌────┼─────┐     │              │
  │  │   ▼    ▼     ▼     │             │   ▼    ▼     ▼     │              │
  │  │  Dep  Svc  Route   │             │  🗑️   🗑️   🗑️    │              │
  │  │                    │             │                    │              │
  │  │  S3/PVC untouched  │             │  S3/PVC untouched  │              │
  │  │  (model data safe) │             │  (model data safe) │              │
  │  └────────────────────┘             └────────────────────┘              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  KEY PRINCIPLE: Serving infrastructure is ephemeral. Model data is       │
  │  persistent. Delete/recreate serving without re-uploading models.        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You deploy a new model version weekly. Old InferenceService is deleted — pods, services, routes are cleaned up. But the model weights in S3 (v1, v2, v3...) remain forever, giving you a complete model version history. Rollback = just recreate InferenceService pointing to an older S3 path.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Deleting InferenceService cleans up serving infra (pods, svc, routes) via owner refs. Model data in S3/PVC/OCI is NOT deleted. Cascade deletion is automatic.

Models Q114 of 200
An InferenceService is stuck in "PredictorUnknown" state. The predictor pod shows "CrashLoopBackOff". What should you check FIRST?
A) Delete and recreate the InferenceService — KServe sometimes gets stuck and a fresh creation resolves it
B) Check if the OpenShift cluster has enough nodes — PredictorUnknown always means the cluster is out of capacity
C) Check the predictor pod logs — the most common causes are invalid storageUri (model path doesn't exist), wrong ServingRuntime (image incompatible with model format), or missing S3 credentials (access denied loading model)
D) Restart the KServe controller pod — the controller is stuck and needs a restart to reconcile the InferenceService
✅ Correct Answer: C

PredictorUnknown means KServe can't confirm the predictor is healthy. The most common root causes by frequency: (1) Invalid storageUri — S3 path doesn't exist or model files are missing. Symptom: "No such file or directory" in logs. (2) Wrong ServingRuntime — using vLLM runtime for an ONNX model (format mismatch). Symptom: "Unsupported model format" in logs. (3) Missing S3 credentials — ServiceAccount doesn't have S3 access. Symptom: "AccessDenied" or "403 Forbidden" in logs. (4) Insufficient GPU memory — model is too large for the allocated GPU. Symptom: "CUDA out of memory" in logs. Debug flow: oc get inferenceservice → check READY status → oc logs deploy/{is-name}-predictor → identify error → fix.

📝 Detailed Explanation
InferenceService Troubleshooting — PredictorUnknown
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DEBUG FLOW:                                                              │
  │  ───────────                                                              │
  │  $ oc get is salary-predictor -n anihpj                                   │
  │  NAME              URL   READY   PREV   LATEST                           │
  │  salary-predictor         False                                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  $ oc get pods -n anihpj | grep salary-predictor                         │
  │  salary-predictor-predictor-xxx   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  $ oc logs salary-predictor-predictor-xxx -n anihpj --tail=20            │
  │  → "ERROR: Failed to load model from s3://anihpj-models/v4/"            │
  │  → "botocore.exceptions.ClientError: An error occurred (404)"           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  FIX: Check if s3://anihpj-models/v4/ exists                             │
  │  $ aws s3 ls s3://anihpj-models/v4/ --endpoint https://minio.anihpj     │
  │  → No objects found → Model wasn't uploaded. Upload first.               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: After a pipeline run, the salary predictor InferenceService showed PredictorUnknown. Checking logs revealed the pipeline wrote model files to s3://anihpj-models/salary/v4/ but the InferenceService pointed to s3://anihpj-models/salary-predictor/v4/ (typo). Fixed the URI and the predictor came up healthy immediately.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: PredictorUnknown → check predictor pod logs FIRST. Most common: wrong storageUri, wrong runtime, missing S3 creds, GPU OOM. Don't delete and recreate — diagnose the actual error.

3.3 API Inference & Model EndpointsQ115-Q126

Models Q103 of 200
What API protocol does KServe use for inference requests and what is the endpoint format?
A) KServe uses a custom binary protocol over TCP sockets — endpoints are accessed via IP:PORT without HTTP
B) KServe uses GraphQL exclusively — all inference requests must be GraphQL queries with model name as the root field
C) KServe uses WebSocket connections for streaming inference — HTTP REST is not supported for latency reasons
D) KServe uses the KServe v1 REST API (HTTP POST to /v1/models/{model}:predict) and optionally gRPC — request/response format follows KServe's V2 Inference Protocol with JSON payloads
✅ Correct Answer: D

KServe follows the V2 Inference Protocol (standardized across KServe, NVIDIA Triton, TensorFlow Serving). REST endpoint: POST {base-url}/v1/models/{model-name}:predict. Request body uses JSON with inputs array specifying name, shape, datatype, and data. Response contains outputs with predictions. gRPC is also supported for high-throughput scenarios. For LLM streaming, KServe supports Server-Sent Events (SSE) with the OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions endpoint when using vLLM or TGIS runtimes. The base URL is found in the InferenceService status.
