Models Q115 of 200
How do you secure a KServe inference endpoint with authentication?
A) Add an OpenShift OAuth proxy sidecar (Service Mesh or Route annotation), use API keys via Kubernetes Secrets, or enable mTLS via Istio/Service Mesh — KServe endpoints are plain HTTP by default and need explicit security configuration
B) KServe endpoints are automatically secured with mTLS — no additional configuration is needed as Kubernetes handles all security
C) Create a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy that blocks all traffic — inference endpoints are designed to be accessed only through the RHOAI dashboard
D) Use HTTP Basic Auth credentials hardcoded in the InferenceService YAML — KServe natively supports username/password authentication
✅ Correct Answer: A

KServe endpoints are unauthenticated by default. Security must be added explicitly: (1) OpenShift OAuth Proxy — add a sidecar container that intercepts requests and validates OpenShift OAuth tokens. Configure via the Service Mesh or Route annotations. (2) API Keys — inject API keys as environment variables from Secrets; the predictor/transformer validates them in application code. (3) mTLS via Service Mesh — Istio/OpenShift Service Mesh can enforce mutual TLS between clients and the inference endpoint. (4) Token-based auth — validate JWT tokens in a custom transformer before forwarding to the predictor. Best practice: use the Service Mesh for mTLS + OAuth proxy for user auth.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Securing KServe Endpoints
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  UNAUTHENTICATED (default):            SECURED:                           │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ curl → Route → Pod │               │ curl + Bearer token →        │  │
  │  │ (anyone can call)  │               │   Route → OAuth Proxy →      │  │
  │  └────────────────────┘               │     (validate token) → Pod   │  │
  │                                        │   → Predictor                │  │
  │  SECURITY OPTIONS:                     └──────────────────────────────┘  │
  │  ────────────────                                                         │
  │  1. OAuth Proxy (OpenShift) — validates OAuth tokens                     │
  │  2. API Keys (Secret → env var) — app-level key validation               │
  │  3. Service Mesh mTLS — encrypt + authenticate at mesh layer             │
  │  4. JWT Transformer — custom auth in transformer sidecar                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The salary predictor endpoint is called by the Django API internally (no auth needed). But the RAG job description generator is exposed externally — it uses OAuth Proxy so only authenticated users can generate job descriptions. Two endpoints, different security postures.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: KServe endpoints are unauthenticated by default. Secure with OAuth proxy, API keys, or Service Mesh mTLS. No built-in auth — must be configured explicitly.

Models Q116 of 200
When should you use gRPC instead of REST for KServe inference requests?
A) gRPC should always be used — it's universally faster than REST for all inference workloads
B) REST should always be used — gRPC is deprecated in KServe v2 and only supported for legacy models
C) Use gRPC for high-throughput, low-latency scenarios (1000+ requests/sec) with binary payloads; use REST for simpler integration, debugging, and when clients don't support gRPC — both are first-class KServe protocols
D) gRPC is only for streaming responses — REST must be used for all single-request inference calls
✅ Correct Answer: C

KServe supports both REST (V2 protocol over HTTP/1.1) and gRPC (HTTP/2 with protobuf). gRPC advantages: binary serialization (smaller payloads), HTTP/2 multiplexing (multiple concurrent streams), native streaming, ~30-50% lower latency than REST for high-throughput. Use gRPC when: internal microservices communicate, you have 1000+ req/s, or you need streaming. REST advantages: simpler debugging (curl works), broader client support (any HTTP client), JSON is human-readable. Use REST when: you're testing with curl, building web frontends, or integrating with third-party systems. Both protocols are first-class — KServe does not deprecate either.

📝 Detailed Explanation
REST vs gRPC for KServe Inference
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  REST (HTTP/1.1 + JSON):              gRPC (HTTP/2 + protobuf):          │
  │  ─────────────────────                ─────────────────────────          │
  │  POST /v1/models/X:predict           rpc Predict(PredictRequest)         │
  │  Content-Type: application/json        returns (PredictResponse)         │
  │  {"inputs": [{"data": [1,2,3]}]}     PredictRequest { data: [1,2,3] }   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WHEN REST:                          WHEN gRPC:                           │
  │  ✅ curl debugging                    ✅ Internal microservices           │
  │  ✅ Web frontends                     ✅ 1000+ requests/second            │
  │  ✅ Quick prototyping                 ✅ Binary payloads (images)         │
  │  ✅ Third-party integration           ✅ Streaming responses              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The Django API uses REST (simple, debuggable). The pipeline evaluation step uses gRPC (sends 10K test samples, needs max throughput). Both protocols coexist on the same InferenceService — KServe exposes both ports automatically.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: KServe supports both REST and gRPC natively. gRPC is faster for high-throughput (binary + HTTP/2). REST is simpler for debugging. Choose based on client needs, not KServe limitations.

Models Q117 of 200
What is inference batching and how does it improve model serving performance?
A) Batching means retraining the model in batches — it has nothing to do with inference performance
B) Batching combines multiple inference requests into one API call — but it only helps when all requests are identical
C) Batching is automatic in KServe — you cannot configure or control it; it always uses optimal batch sizes
D) Batching groups multiple inference requests into a single GPU computation — it maximizes GPU utilization by processing inputs in parallel, significantly improving throughput at the cost of slightly higher per-request latency
✅ Correct Answer: D

Inference batching is a key optimization for GPU-based models. GPUs are massively parallel processors — running one inference at a time wastes most of the GPU's compute capacity. Batching sends multiple inputs together (e.g., 32 resumes at once), and the GPU processes them simultaneously. Static batching: client sends a fixed-size batch. Dynamic batching (used by vLLM, Triton): server accumulates requests over a short window (e.g., 10ms) and processes them together. Continuous batching (vLLM): for LLMs, requests are added/removed from the batch as they complete (different from static batching where all must finish together). Trade-off: batching increases throughput (more inferences/sec) but adds latency (waiting for batch to fill).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Inference Batching — GPU Utilization
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  NO BATCHING:                          WITH BATCHING:                     │
  │  ┌────────────────────────┐           ┌────────────────────────┐        │
  │  │ Req1 → GPU → Resp1     │           │ Req1 ┐                 │        │
  │  │ Req2 → GPU → Resp2     │           │ Req2 │                 │        │
  │  │ Req3 → GPU → Resp3     │           │ Req3 ├─→ GPU ─→ Resp   │        │
  │  │ Req4 → GPU → Resp4     │           │ Req4 │  (parallel)      │        │
  │  │                         │           │ Req5 │                 │        │
  │  │ GPU utilization: 25%   │           │ Req6 ┘                 │        │
  │  │ Throughput: 4 req/s     │           │                         │        │
  │  └────────────────────────┘           │ GPU utilization: 90%    │        │
  │                                        │ Throughput: 24 req/s    │        │
  │  DYNAMIC BATCHING:                    └────────────────────────┘        │
  │  ────────────────                                                         │
  │  Window: 10ms → collect requests → process together → return results     │
  │  maxBatchSize: 32 (prevents memory overflow)                             │
  │  maxQueueDelay: 50ms (max wait before processing partial batch)          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The job-matching model scores 1000 resumes per minute during peak hours. Without batching, each resume is a separate GPU call — GPU utilization is 20%. With dynamic batching (batch size 32), the GPU processes 32 resumes simultaneously — utilization jumps to 85%, and throughput increases 4x.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Batching = more throughput at slight latency cost. Dynamic batching in vLLM/Triton. Continuous batching for LLMs. maxBatchSize + maxQueueDelay control batching behavior.

Models Q125 of 200
How should you handle inference errors and implement retries when calling KServe endpoints?
A) Retry all failed requests immediately — inference errors are always transient and fixed by retrying
B) Classify errors: 4xx (client error — bad input, fix and don't retry), 5xx (server error — use exponential backoff with jitter), timeout (may retry with idempotency key) — implement circuit breaker to stop retries when the model is unhealthy
C) Don't retry inference requests — models are deterministic so retrying always gives the same result
D) Let KServe handle all retries — the InferenceService CR has built-in retry configuration that covers all error scenarios
✅ Correct Answer: B

Inference error handling requires classification: 4xx errors (400 Bad Request, 422 Unprocessable Entity) mean the input is malformed — retrying won't help, fix the input instead. 5xx errors (503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout) are transient — use exponential backoff with jitter: retry after 1s, then 2s, 4s, 8s (max 3 retries). Timeouts — the model may be overloaded; retry with idempotency key to avoid duplicate processing. Circuit breaker — after N consecutive failures, stop sending requests for a cooldown period to let the model recover. KServe does NOT handle retries — the client application must implement retry logic. Use libraries like tenacity (Python) or resilience4j (Java).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Inference Error Handling Strategy
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ERROR RESPONSE FLOW:                                                     │
  │  ────────────────────                                                     │
  │  Client Request                                                           │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Response Code?                                                    │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐        │    │
  │  │  │ 2xx (OK) │  │ 4xx      │  │ 5xx      │  │ Timeout  │        │    │
  │  │  │ ✅ Done  │  │ ❌ No    │  │ 🔄 Retry │  │ 🔄 Retry │        │    │
  │  │  │          │  │  retry   │  │  backoff │  │  w/ key  │        │    │
  │  │  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘        │    │
  │  │                                    │              │               │    │
  │  │    4xx Examples:                   ▼              ▼               │    │
  │  │    • 400: Bad JSON                Retry 1: 1s    Retry 1: 2s     │    │
  │  │    • 413: Input too large         Retry 2: 2s    Retry 2: 4s     │    │
  │  │    • 422: Invalid features        Retry 3: 4s    Retry 3: 8s     │    │
  │  │                                   → Still fail?  → Still fail?   │    │
  │  │    5xx Examples:                  → Circuit OPEN  → Circuit OPEN │    │
  │  │    • 503: No healthy pods         → Fallback      → Fallback     │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The Django API calls the salary predictor. If the predictor returns 503 (pod restarting), the API retries with exponential backoff (1s→2s→4s) instead of showing an error to the user. If the circuit breaker opens after 5 consecutive failures, the API falls back to a cached average salary estimate until the predictor recovers.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: KServe does NOT auto-retry. Client must implement retry logic. 4xx = no retry. 5xx = exponential backoff + jitter. Circuit breaker prevents cascading failures.

Models Q126 of 200
How does LLM streaming work with KServe and what is Server-Sent Events (SSE)?
A) Streaming sends the entire response at once but in compressed format — it's just gzip compression over HTTP
B) Streaming requires WebSocket connections — KServe opens a persistent WebSocket for each streaming client
C) Streaming splits the request into multiple HTTP calls — the client polls repeatedly until the full response is available
D) SSE streams tokens as they're generated over a single HTTP connection — the client receives each token immediately via event-stream, enabling real-time display like ChatGPT's typing effect; KServe supports OpenAI-compatible streaming endpoints with vLLM/TGIS runtimes
✅ Correct Answer: D

Server-Sent Events (SSE) is the standard protocol for LLM token streaming. Instead of waiting for the full response (which could take 30+ seconds for long generations), the server sends each token as it's generated. HTTP header: Content-Type: text/event-stream. Each event: data: {"token": {"text": "The"}}\n\n. The client receives tokens in real-time and displays them progressively (the "typing" effect). KServe with vLLM or TGIS runtimes supports OpenAI-compatible streaming: POST /v1/chat/completions with {"stream": true}. Key parameters: max_tokens (max output length), temperature (randomness, 0=deterministic, 1=creative), top_p (nucleus sampling), stop (stop sequences).

📝 Detailed Explanation
LLM Token Streaming via SSE
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STANDARD (non-streaming):              STREAMING (SSE):                   │
  │  ─────────────────────────              ────────────────                   │
  │  Client: POST /v1/chat/completions     Client: POST /v1/chat/completions │
  │          {"stream": false}                      {"stream": true}          │
  │  │                                      │                                │
  │  │  ⏳ Wait 15 seconds...               │  data: {"token":"The"}         │
  │  │                                      │  data: {"token":" salary"}     │
  │  ▼                                      │  data: {"token":" for"}       │
  │  {"response": "The salary for..."}      │  data: {"token":" this"}      │
  │                                          │  data: {"token":" role"}      │
  │  User waits 15s, sees full response     │  data: {"token":" is"}        │
  │                                          │  ...                           │
  │                                          │  data: [DONE]                  │
  │                                          ▼                                │
  │                                          User sees tokens appear in      │
  │                                          real-time (typing effect)        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  GENERATION PARAMETERS:                                                   │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                     │
  │  max_tokens: 256     → Max output length (controls cost)                 │
  │  temperature: 0.7    → 0=deterministic, 1=creative, >1=random           │
  │  top_p: 0.9          → Nucleus sampling (considers top 90% probability)  │
  │  stop: ["\n\n"]      → Stop generating when sequence appears             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The RAG job description generator produces 200-300 word descriptions. Without streaming: user waits 12 seconds, then sees the full description. With SSE streaming: user sees words appear in real-time starting at ~500ms — much better UX. The Django frontend uses EventSource API to render tokens as they arrive.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: SSE = token-by-token streaming over HTTP. Not WebSocket. KServe supports OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions with stream:true. vLLM/TGIS runtimes required. Key params: max_tokens, temperature, top_p.

3.4 Model Registry, Optimization & EvaluationQ127-Q138

Models Q104 of 200
What is the LLM Compressor in RHOAI and what problem does it solve?
A) It compresses training datasets to reduce storage costs — smaller datasets train faster but with the same model size
B) It optimizes LLMs through quantization (INT8/INT4), pruning (removing redundant weights), and distillation (training a smaller student model) — reducing model size and inference cost while preserving accuracy
C) It compresses inference responses for faster network transfer — reduces API response latency through gzip compression
D) It's a Kubernetes controller that compresses container images for faster pod startup on GPU nodes
✅ Correct Answer: B

LLM Compressor is RHOAI's toolkit for model optimization. It supports three techniques: (1) Quantization — reduces weight precision (FP16→INT4) for 4x VRAM savings. (2) Pruning — removes less important weights (e.g., 30% sparsity) to reduce compute. (3) Distillation — trains a smaller "student" model to mimic a larger "teacher" model. Combined, these can reduce a 70B model to ~10B with minimal quality loss. LLM Compressor integrates with vLLM for optimized serving of compressed models. This is critical for deploying large models on limited GPU hardware without sacrificing too much quality.

📝 Detailed Explanation
LLM Compressor — Model Optimization Pipeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  INPUT: Llama-3-70B (140GB, requires 4×A100)                             │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  LLM COMPRESSOR PIPELINE:                                                 │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  1. QUANTIZATION (AWQ)                                            │    │
  │  │     140GB (FP16) → 35GB (INT4)  = 4x smaller                     │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  2. PRUNING (SparseGPT)                                           │    │
  │  │     Remove 30% least important weights → 24.5GB                   │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  3. DISTILLATION                                                  │    │
  │  │     Train 8B student from 70B teacher → 8GB                       │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  OUTPUT: Optimized model runs on single T4 (16GB)!                        │
  │  Accuracy: ~95% of original (benchmarked via LMEval)                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You want to use Llama-3-70B for RAG job description generation, but you only have T4 GPUs. LLM Compressor quantizes and prunes it to fit on a single T4 with 90%+ quality retention. Job descriptions are still excellent while saving $40K in GPU costs.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: LLM Compressor is the RHOAI tool for model size optimization. It does quantization, pruning, and distillation. Use it when GPU memory is the bottleneck for LLM deployment.

Models Q105 of 200
After quantizing and deploying a model, how do you evaluate whether the optimization caused unacceptable quality degradation?
A) Use LMEval Harness to run standardized benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, HumanEval) on both the original and optimized model, then compare scores — if the optimized model's scores drop below acceptable thresholds, adjust quantization parameters or use a different method
B) Check the model's file size — if the compressed model is less than 50% of the original, quality is guaranteed to be acceptable
C) Run a single inference and compare the output manually — if the first result looks similar, the model is fine
D) Trust the quantizer's built-in quality score — quantization tools provide a guarantee that quality is preserved
✅ Correct Answer: A

LMEval Harness is the standard framework for LLM evaluation in RHOAI. It runs the model against benchmark datasets: MMLU (57 subjects, measures knowledge), HellaSwag (commonsense reasoning), HumanEval (code generation), GSM8K (math), and custom evaluation tasks you define. Process: (1) Run LMEval on the original FP16 model → get baseline scores. (2) Apply quantization/optimization. (3) Run LMEval on the optimized model → compare. If MMLU drops from 68% to 66%, that's acceptable. If it drops from 68% to 52%, the quantization is too aggressive — try INT8 instead of INT4.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Model Evaluation with LMEval Harness
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LMEVAL COMPARISON REPORT:                                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Benchmark        FP16 (Original)    INT4 (Optimized)    Delta           │
  │  ─────────        ──────────────    ────────────────    ─────           │
  │  MMLU             68.2%             66.1%              -2.1%  🟢 OK     │
  │  HellaSwag        79.5%             78.3%              -1.2%  🟢 OK     │
  │  HumanEval        42.1%             38.7%              -3.4%  🟡 WATCH  │
  │  GSM8K            55.0%             51.2%              -3.8%  🟡 WATCH  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  DECISION: INT4 is acceptable for job description generation             │
  │  (MMLU + HellaSwag are most relevant). Deploy to production.             │
  │  Monitor metrics and re-evaluate monthly.                                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Before deploying the quantized Llama-3-8B for RAG, you run LMEval. The INT4 model scores 66% on MMLU vs 68% for FP16 — a 2% drop that's acceptable for job description generation. You document the benchmark results in the Model Registry for audit trail.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Task: "Evaluate model quality after optimization." Run LMEval with lm_eval --model hf --tasks mmlu,hellaswag. Compare before/after scores. Document in Model Registry metadata.

Models Q118 of 200
What is the Model Registry in RHOAI and what problem does it solve?
A) It's a Git repository for model code — the registry stores training scripts and configuration files, similar to GitHub
B) It's a Docker image registry — models are stored as container images and the registry is just the OpenShift internal registry
C) It's a centralized catalog for versioned ML models with metadata (framework, metrics, parameters, tags), stages (Staging/Production/Archived), and deployment targets — solving model discoverability, lineage tracking, and governance
D) It's a database table that stores model predictions — the registry tracks inference results for auditing purposes
✅ Correct Answer: C

The Model Registry is RHOAI's solution to the "model sprawl" problem. Without a registry: models exist as files in S3/PVC with no metadata — "which version is in production? What accuracy does this model have? Who trained it?" The registry answers these by storing: model versions (v1, v2, v3 with unique IDs), metadata (framework, training dataset, hyperparameters, metrics like accuracy/F1), stages (Staging → Production → Archived with approval workflows), deployment targets (which InferenceServices use this model), and lineage (which pipeline run produced this model). Models stored as OCI artifacts — the registry is actually an OCI-compatible registry under the hood, so models can be pulled by any OCI-compatible tool.

Models Q119 of 200
How do model stages work (Staging → Production → Archived) and what happens during promotion?
A) Models move through stages: Staging (testing), Production (live serving), Archived (deprecated) — promotion from Staging to Production triggers deployment to registered InferenceServices, and only one version can be in Production per model at a time
B) Stages are just labels — they have no effect on deployment; moving a model to Production does not trigger any automation
C) All model versions are in Production simultaneously — stages are for organizational sorting only
D) Models automatically promote based on accuracy thresholds — no manual approval is ever needed after initial configuration
✅ Correct Answer: A

Model stages enforce governance: Staging — model is registered but not serving live traffic (testing/validation phase). Production — model is actively serving predictions; promotion to Production can trigger automatic deployment to configured InferenceServices. Only ONE version per model can be in Production at a time (prevents confusion about which model is "live"). Archived — model is deprecated but retained for audit/compliance (can't be deployed but metadata/lineage is preserved). Promotion typically requires approval (RBAC: only project admins can promote). The pipeline can register a model directly to Staging, then a human or automated approval promotes it.

If it performs well, she promotes to Production — KServe auto-deploys the new model. The old Production model is archived (kept for rollback). This gives a clear audit trail: who promoted, when, with what metrics.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Model stages: Staging → Production → Archived. Only one Production per model. Promotion can trigger deployment. Archived models retained for audit/rollback.

Models Q120 of 200
A newly deployed model in Production starts returning incorrect predictions. How do you rollback to the previous version?
A) Delete the InferenceService and recreate it from scratch with the old model URI — KServe has no built-in rollback mechanism
B) In the Model Registry, promote the previous (Archived) version back to Production — this triggers KServe to redeploy the old model; or manually update the InferenceService storageUri to point to the previous model's S3 path
C) Use oc rollout undo on the KServe deployment — Kubernetes native rollback handles model versioning automatically
D) Copy the old model files over the new ones in S3 — KServe detects the file change and reloads automatically
✅ Correct Answer: B

Model rollback leverages the Model Registry's archive: (1) Registry method: Find the previous Production model (now Archived) → click "Promote to Production" → KServe reconfigures the InferenceService with the old model URI. (2) Manual method: Find the old model's S3 path in the registry metadata → update the InferenceService's storageUri → KServe rolling update loads the old model. (3) Canary method: If using canaryTrafficPercent, set it to 0 (instant rollback to previous revision). Key: the old model's artifacts must still exist in S3/PVC. This is why Archived models are NEVER deleted — they're your rollback safety net. The registry tracks which models were Production and when, making rollback decisions data-driven.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Model Rollback Flow

  │  ROLLBACK:                                                                │
  │  ────────                                                                 │
  │  STEP 1: Check Model Registry                                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  job-matching/                                                     │    │
  │  │  ├─ v1  [🗄️ Archived]  accuracy: 89.2%  (2 months ago)          │    │

  │  │  └─ v3  [📦 Production] accuracy: 78.0%  ← BAD, DEMOTE           │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 2: Promote v2 → Production                                         │
  │  → Registry triggers KServe to update InferenceService                   │
  │  → KServe loads v2 model from S3                                         │
  │  → v3 moves to Archived (kept for investigation)                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RESULT: Service restored to 92.1% accuracy in ~2 minutes               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Sunday's pipeline produced a bad model (trained on corrupted data). Monday morning, users report terrible job matches. Alice checks the registry, sees V2 had 92% accuracy, promotes V2 back to Production. Service restored in 2 minutes. V3 is Archived and investigated — turns out the S3 data source had missing files.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Rollback via Model Registry: promote Archived version → Production. Or manually update InferenceService storageUri. Archived models = rollback safety net. Never delete old model artifacts.

Models Q128 of 200
What metadata should you track for each model version in the registry for production governance?
A) Only the model name and version number — all other information is in the training code repository
B) Model file size and storage location — governance only cares about cost and resource usage

Production model governance requires complete lineage. The registry stores: (1) Identity — name, version, author, timestamp, description. (2) Technical — framework (PyTorch 2.1), model format (safetensors), input/output shapes, artifacts URI. (3) Training provenance — dataset reference (S3 path + hash), hyperparameters (learning_rate=0.001, epochs=10), pipeline run ID (links back to KFP run). (5) Deployment — which InferenceServices use this model, deployment history (when deployed, when rolled back). (6) Compliance — license, ethical review status, bias audit results. Models Q129 of 200
How does KServe handle GPU memory when loading large models, and what is KV-cache management?
A) KServe loads the entire model into GPU VRAM and uses the remaining memory for KV-cache — if it doesn't fit, the deployment fails
B) KServe streams model weights from disk during inference — models never fully load into GPU memory, so VRAM size doesn't matter
C) KServe automatically splits models across all available GPUs in the cluster — no configuration is needed for multi-GPU serving
D) KServe loads model weights into GPU VRAM, then manages the KV-cache (Key-Value cache for attention) in remaining memory — vLLM's PagedAttention dynamically allocates KV-cache blocks like virtual memory pages, maximizing batch size without OOM
✅ Correct Answer: D

GPU memory management is critical for LLM serving. The GPU VRAM is divided into: (1) Model weights — the actual neural network parameters (~70% of VRAM for large models). (2) KV-cache — stores attention keys and values for each token in the context window; this grows linearly with sequence length and batch size (~25% of VRAM). (3) Overhead — CUDA context, intermediate activations (~5%). PagedAttention (vLLM) revolutionizes KV-cache management: instead of allocating contiguous memory for each sequence's KV-cache (which causes fragmentation and waste), it uses "pages" (blocks) like OS virtual memory. Blocks can be dynamically allocated, shared across sequences (for beam search), and moved between GPU and CPU memory. Result: 2-4x more sequences can fit in the same GPU VRAM, dramatically increasing throughput.

📝 Detailed Explanation
GPU VRAM Layout & PagedAttention
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GPU VRAM (80GB A100):                                                    │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  ████████████████████████████████████████████  Model Weights       │    │
  │  │  ████████████████████████████████████████████  (Llama-3-70B INT4)  │    │
  │  │  ████████████████████████████████████████████  ~35GB               │    │
  │  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                     │    │
  │  │  ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  KV-Cache (~35GB remaining)   │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  TRADITIONAL ALLOCATION:           PAGEDATTENTION (vLLM):          │    │

Models Q130 of 200
How do you configure GPU resource allocation for a KServe InferenceService and what are the best practices?
A) Always request 1 full GPU per replica — KServe cannot share GPUs between models or limit GPU memory
B) Use nvidia.com/gpu resource requests/limits in the predictor spec — for multi-model serving, use GPU time-slicing or MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) to share GPUs; set GPU memory limits via runtime args (e.g., --gpu-memory-utilization in vLLM)
C) GPU allocation is handled automatically by the NVIDIA GPU Operator — no configuration is needed in the InferenceService
D) Specify GPU requirements in the ServingRuntime only — InferenceService cannot override GPU settings from the runtime
✅ Correct Answer: B

GPU allocation for InferenceServices: (1) Basic — add nvidia.com/gpu: 1 to the predictor's resources.requests and resources.limits. (2) Fractional GPUs — use GPU time-slicing (NVIDIA GPU Operator feature) to share one GPU across multiple InferenceServices. (3) MIG — on A100/H100 GPUs, partition one physical GPU into isolated instances (e.g., 7×10GB slices), each assigned to a different InferenceService. (4) Memory limits — runtime-level flags like --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 (vLLM) prevent OOM. (5) Node scheduling — use nodeSelector/tolerations to ensure predictor pods land on GPU nodes. Best practice: for production LLMs, request full GPU; for lightweight models, use time-slicing or MIG to maximize GPU utilization across models.

Models Q131 of 200
What is model distillation and how does it differ from quantization?
A) Distillation trains a smaller "student" model to mimic a larger "teacher" model's outputs — unlike quantization (which reduces precision of the same model), distillation creates an entirely new, smaller architecture that learns to replicate the teacher's behavior
B) Distillation and quantization are the same thing — both reduce model size by lowering numerical precision
C) Distillation is a data preprocessing technique — it "distills" training data to remove noise and redundancy before training
D) Distillation splits a model across multiple GPUs — it's a model parallelism technique, not a compression technique
✅ Correct Answer: A

Knowledge distillation is fundamentally different from quantization. Quantization: same model architecture, lower precision weights (FP16→INT4). The model structure doesn't change — just the numerical representation. Distillation: completely different (smaller) architecture trained to imitate the teacher. Process: (1) Train large teacher model (e.g., Llama-3-70B). (2) Use teacher's output probabilities (not just the final answer) as "soft labels" to train a smaller student (e.g., a 7B model). (3) Student learns not just what the teacher predicts, but how confident it is about each option. Distillation can achieve 7B model quality approaching 70B model on specific tasks — far better than just training a 7B model from scratch. RHOAI's LLM Compressor supports distillation pipelines.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Quantization vs Distillation
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  QUANTIZATION:                         DISTILLATION:                      │
  │  ────────────                          ────────────                       │
  │  Llama-3-70B (FP16)                   Llama-3-70B (Teacher)             │
  │       │                                       │                           │
  │       │ INT4 conversion                       │ "teaches"                 │
  │       ▼                                       ▼                           │
  │  Llama-3-70B (INT4)                    TinyLlama-1.1B (Student)          │
  │  Same model, lower precision           Different model, learned behavior  │
  │  Size: 140GB → 35GB                   Size: 140GB → 2.2GB                │
  │  Quality: ~97% of original            Quality: ~85% of original          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WHEN TO USE EACH:                                                        │
  │  ────────────────                                                         │
  │  Quantization: You need the BIG model's quality but want to save VRAM    │
  │  Distillation: You can accept slightly lower quality for MUCH smaller    │
  │                model that runs on CPU or edge devices                    │
  │  Combined:     Quantize the teacher (INT4), then distill → tiny model   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The RAG LLM uses Llama-3-8B (quantized INT4). But the job-matching embedding model is tiny — it just needs to convert job descriptions to vectors. You distill a 7B embedding model into a 110M student model. The student runs on CPU with 95% of the teacher's matching quality, saving GPU resources for the RAG LLM.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Distillation = train small student from large teacher. Different from quantization (same model, lower precision). LLM Compressor supports both. Student models can run on CPU.

Models Q132 of 200
How do you monitor model drift in production and what actions should drift trigger?
A) Drift monitoring is optional — models in production don't drift if they were trained on good data
B) Manually check predictions once a month — drift happens slowly enough that monthly checks are sufficient
C) Use TrustyAI to continuously compare live prediction distributions against the reference (training) distribution — detect data drift (input features change), concept drift (input→output relationship changes), and prediction drift; trigger alerts → investigate → decide: retrain, rollback, or update model
D) Drift is automatically corrected by KServe — the InferenceService retrains itself when drift is detected
✅ Correct Answer: C

Model drift is inevitable in production — the world changes, and models become stale. Data drift: input features change distribution (e.g., job listings now use different vocabulary than 2024). Detected via KS-test or Wasserstein distance between reference and current feature distributions. Concept drift: same input means something different (e.g., "remote" in 2024 = work-from-home; in 2026 = AI-managed). Harder to detect — requires monitoring prediction accuracy against ground truth (when available). TrustyAI computes drift metrics continuously, stores them in Prometheus, and triggers alerts via Alertmanager when thresholds are exceeded. Actions: (1) Investigate cause. (2) If real drift: trigger pipeline retraining on recent data. (3) If unacceptable: rollback to previous model. (4) If expected seasonal change: document and adjust thresholds.

3.5 Model Optimization & EvaluationQ139-Q150

Models Q121 of 200
What is model quantization and why is it critical for LLM deployment in OpenShift AI?
A) Quantization converts models to a proprietary binary format — it's required for all KServe deployments regardless of model size
B) Quantization splits large models across multiple GPUs — it's a form of model parallelism, not compression
C) Quantization increases model precision from 16-bit to 32-bit — it improves accuracy at the cost of larger model size
D) Quantization reduces weight precision (FP16→INT8→INT4) to shrink model size and memory usage — a 70B model goes from 140GB to 35GB (INT4), enabling deployment on fewer/smaller GPUs with minimal accuracy loss (typically 1-3%)
✅ Correct Answer: D

Quantization is the most important optimization technique for LLM deployment. Neural network weights are stored as 16-bit floats (FP16) by default. Quantization converts them to lower precision: INT8 (8-bit, 2x smaller), INT4 (4-bit, 4x smaller). The key insight: LLM weights don't need 16-bit precision for inference — the accumulated error from rounding is negligible. Techniques: AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization — calibrates quantization per-channel), GPTQ (post-training quantization with gradient-based optimization), GGUF/GGML (llama.cpp format for CPU inference). RHOAI's LLM Compressor automates quantization pipelines. Result: Llama-3-70B (140GB, needs 4×A100) → 35GB INT4 (fits on 1×A100).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Model Quantization — FP16 → INT4
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PRECISION LEVELS:                                                        │
  │  ────────────────                                                         │
  │  FP32: 32 bits per weight → 280GB (Llama-3-70B)  [baseline, max quality]│
  │  FP16: 16 bits per weight → 140GB                 [standard training]    │
  │  INT8:  8 bits per weight →  70GB                 [2x compression]       │
  │  INT4:  4 bits per weight →  35GB                 [4x compression]       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  GPU REQUIREMENTS for 70B model:                                          │
  │  ──────────────────────────────                                           │
  │  FP16: 4× A100 (80GB each) = $40K/month cloud                           │
  │  INT4: 1× A100 (80GB)       = $10K/month cloud                          │
  │       or 1× L40S (48GB)     = $5K/month cloud  (with CPU offload)       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ACCURACY IMPACT:                                                         │
  │  ───────────────                                                          │
  │  INT8: ~0.5% accuracy drop (negligible for most use cases)               │
  │  INT4: ~1-3% accuracy drop (acceptable for chat/summarization)           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The RAG job description generator uses Llama-3-8B. FP16 requires a T4 (16GB) — but you only have one T4 shared with other workloads. INT4 quantization reduces the model to ~5GB, leaving 11GB for KV-cache and other serving overhead. Now the model fits comfortably on the shared T4.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Quantization = reduce precision to save VRAM. INT8 = 2x smaller, INT4 = 4x smaller. RHOAI tool: LLM Compressor (AWQ, GPTQ). Accuracy impact is minimal (1-3%).

Models Q122 of 200
What is continuous batching in vLLM and how does it improve LLM serving throughput?
A) Continuous batching means the server never stops accepting requests — it's just a fancy term for high availability
B) Unlike static batching (all requests in a batch must complete together), continuous batching allows new requests to join and completed requests to leave the batch dynamically — this eliminates "padding waste" where fast requests wait for slow ones, dramatically improving GPU utilization and throughput
C) Continuous batching splits each request into micro-batches — it processes requests one token at a time across all users
D) Continuous batching is a networking optimization that reduces TCP connection overhead — it has nothing to do with GPU compute
✅ Correct Answer: B

Continuous batching (also called "in-flight batching" or "iteration-level scheduling") is the key innovation in vLLM that makes LLM serving 10-30x more efficient than naive implementations. In static batching: 8 requests enter, the GPU processes all 8, and all 8 leave together. If one request generates 500 tokens and another generates 10, the 10-token request sits idle waiting. In continuous batching: requests join and leave the batch at every inference iteration. The GPU is always processing a full batch. Combined with PagedAttention (vLLM's KV-cache memory management inspired by OS virtual memory), continuous batching achieves near-optimal GPU utilization. Result: vLLM serves 10-30x more tokens/second than static batching at the same latency.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Static vs Continuous Batching for LLMs
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STATIC BATCHING:                    CONTINUOUS BATCHING (vLLM):          │
  │  ────────────────                    ──────────────────────────           │
  │  Iteration 1: [R1,R2,R3,R4]         Iteration 1: [R1,R2,R3,R4]          │
  │  Iteration 2: [R1,R2,R3,R4]         Iteration 2: [R1,R2,R3,R4,R5]←new   │
  │  ...                                 Iteration 3: [R1,R2,R4,R5,R6] ←R3   │
  │  Iteration 50:[R1,R2,R3,R4]         │             finished               │
  │  → 50 iterations, 4 sequences        │                                    │
  │  → R2 finishes at iter 10 but       Iteration 50: [R5,R6,R7,R8,R9,R10]  │
  │    stays in batch (padding)         → 50 iterations, 10 sequences        │
  │                                       → R2 left at iter 10 (no waste)    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  THROUGHPUT COMPARISON (Llama-3-8B on A100):                              │
  │  Static batching:    ~500 tokens/sec                                     │
  │  Continuous batching: ~5000 tokens/sec  (10x improvement)                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The RAG job description generator serves 50 concurrent users. With static batching, generating 10 descriptions takes 8 seconds (requests wait for each other). With vLLM's continuous batching, the same 10 descriptions complete in 2 seconds — each request leaves the batch as soon as its generation finishes.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: vLLM's continuous batching = dynamic batch membership. PagedAttention = efficient KV-cache memory. Together = 10-30x throughput. Use vLLM ServingRuntime for LLMs in production.

Models Q123 of 200
What is speculative decoding and how does it accelerate LLM inference?
A) A smaller "draft" model generates candidate tokens quickly, then the main model verifies them in parallel — accepting correct tokens and regenerating only incorrect ones, achieving 2-3x speedup without quality loss
B) The model guesses the user's intent and pre-computes likely responses — it's a caching strategy, not a model optimization technique
C) Tokens are generated randomly and filtered by quality — speculative decoding is a search algorithm, not a speed optimization
D) The model generates shorter responses by speculating what the minimum answer length should be — it's a response compression technique
✅ Correct Answer: A

Speculative decoding is an inference acceleration technique that uses two models: a small, fast "draft" model (e.g., Llama-3-68M) and the main "target" model (e.g., Llama-3-70B). Process: (1) Draft model generates K tokens (e.g., 5) quickly. (2) Target model verifies all K tokens in ONE forward pass (instead of K sequential passes). (3) Accepted tokens are kept; the first rejected token is regenerated by the target model. (4) Repeat. Since the target model's forward pass is the bottleneck, verifying 5 tokens in one pass vs. generating 1 token per pass = theoretical 5x speedup. In practice, 2-3x speedup with zero quality loss (output is identical to the target model alone). Supported by vLLM with draft model configuration.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Speculative Decoding
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STANDARD DECODING:                   SPECULATIVE DECODING:               │
  │  ─────────────────                    ──────────────────────              │
  │  │ Target: "The"    (1 pass)          │ Draft: "The cat sat on" (fast)   │
  │  │ Target: " cat"   (1 pass)          │ Target: verify all 4 tokens       │
  │  │ Target: " sat"   (1 pass)          │   in 1 pass → "cat sat on" ✓     │
  │  │ Target: " on"    (1 pass)          │                                 │
  │  │ Target: " the"   (1 pass)          │   Result: 4 tokens in 2 passes    │
  │  │                                     │   (1 draft + 1 verify)            │
  │  │  5 tokens = 5 passes               │   vs 4 tokens in 4 passes         │
  │  │                                     │   = 2x speedup                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  KEY: Draft model is ~100x faster than target. Verification is parallel. │
  │  Output is IDENTICAL to target model (no quality loss).                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The RAG job description generator uses Llama-3-70B (target) + Llama-3-68M (draft). Without speculative decoding: 15 seconds per description. With speculative decoding: 6 seconds per description. Same quality, 2.5x faster. User satisfaction improves significantly with lower latency.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Speculative decoding = draft model proposes, target model verifies in parallel. 2-3x speedup, zero quality loss. vLLM supports it natively. Requires a compatible draft model.

Models Q133 of 200
What is ONNX and why would you convert models to ONNX format for serving?
A) ONNX is a proprietary NVIDIA format — it only works with NVIDIA GPUs and Triton Inference Server
B) ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is an open standard format — converting models to ONNX enables serving with any ONNX-compatible runtime (OVMS, Triton, ONNX Runtime), provides hardware-agnostic deployment, and often includes graph optimizations that improve inference speed
C) ONNX is a training framework like PyTorch — it's an alternative to TensorFlow for building models from scratch
D) ONNX is a compression algorithm — converting to ONNX reduces model size by 90% without quality loss
✅ Correct Answer: B

ONNX is the lingua franca of model formats. Benefits: (1) Framework independence — train in PyTorch, serve with ONNX Runtime or OpenVINO (no PyTorch dependency at serving time). (2) Hardware portability — same ONNX model runs on NVIDIA GPU, Intel CPU (with OpenVINO optimizations), AMD GPU, or ARM edge devices. (3) Graph optimizations — ONNX Runtime applies operator fusion, constant folding, and dead code elimination automatically, often yielding 10-30% speedup vs native PyTorch serving. (4) Smaller serving images — PyTorch is ~2GB; ONNX Runtime is ~200MB. Conversion: torch.onnx.export(model, dummy_input, "model.onnx"). RHOAI's OVMS (OpenVINO Model Server) is optimized for ONNX + Intel CPUs. Not all models convert cleanly (custom ops may fail).

📝 Detailed Explanation
ONNX — Train Anywhere, Serve Everywhere
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TRAINING (flexible)                SERVING (optimized)                   │
  │  ──────────────────                 ────────────────────                  │
  │  ┌──────────┐                       ┌──────────────────────────┐        │
  │  │ PyTorch  │──┐                    │ ONNX RUNTIME (cross-plat)│        │
  │  └──────────┘  │    ┌──────────┐   │  • NVIDIA GPU (CUDA)     │        │

Models Q134 of 200
What is LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) and how does multi-LoRA serving work for LLMs?
A) LoRA adds small, trainable adapter matrices to a frozen base model — multi-LoRA serving loads one base model and multiple LoRA adapters, switching between them per-request without reloading, enabling one GPU to serve many fine-tuned variants simultaneously
B) LoRA is a model compression technique similar to quantization — it reduces model size by removing low-rank weights
C) LoRA is a distributed training strategy — it splits model layers across multiple GPUs for faster training
D) LoRA is a prompt engineering framework — it structures prompts to get better responses from the base model without any fine-tuning
✅ Correct Answer: A

LoRA is the most efficient fine-tuning method for LLMs. Instead of updating all 70B parameters (impossible on consumer GPUs), LoRA freezes the base model and adds small "adapter" matrices (typically 0.1-1% of the original parameters). These adapters capture task-specific knowledge. Multi-LoRA serving: vLLM loads one base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B at 5GB) plus multiple LoRA adapters (each ~10-50MB). Each inference request specifies which LoRA to use. The GPU switches adapters per-request with near-zero overhead. Use cases: one base model + LoRA for legal documents + LoRA for medical + LoRA for HR. One GPU serves all three domains. No need for 3 separate models occupying 3×5GB = 15GB VRAM.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Multi-LoRA Serving Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ONE GPU — ONE BASE MODEL — MANY ADAPTERS:                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │    │
  │  │  │  BASE MODEL: Llama-3-8B (frozen, 5GB)                    │    │    │
  │  │  │  ████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ │    │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  LORA ADAPTERS (loaded dynamically, ~10-50MB each):              │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐            │    │
  │  │  │ LoRA: HR     │ │ LoRA: Legal  │ │ LoRA: Medical│            │    │
  │  │  │ Job matching │ │ Contract     │ │ Research     │            │    │
  │  │  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘            │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  REQUEST: "lora_name: hr-jobs" → GPU switches to HR adapter     │    │
  │  │  REQUEST: "lora_name: legal"   → GPU switches to Legal adapter   │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: You have one Llama-3-8B base model. LoRA-HR is fine-tuned on job descriptions. LoRA-IT is fine-tuned on tech resumes. LoRA-MGMT is fine-tuned on management job postings. One T4 GPU serves all three domains — users specify which LoRA in their request. Without multi-LoRA, you'd need 3 GPUs or switch models with downtime.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: LoRA = small adapter on frozen base model. Multi-LoRA = one base + many adapters, switched per-request. vLLM supports it. Saves massive VRAM vs separate models.

Models Q135 of 200
What is model pruning and when should you use it instead of quantization?
A) Pruning removes entire layers from the model — it's a destructive process that always significantly reduces accuracy
B) Pruning is the same as dropout during training — it randomly disables neurons but doesn't change model size
C) Pruning removes individual weights (unstructured) or entire neurons/channels (structured) that contribute least to the model's output — it reduces compute (fewer operations) while quantization reduces memory; use pruning when inference speed matters, quantization when memory is the bottleneck
D) Pruning converts floating-point weights to sparse matrices — it's a storage format change, not a model modification
✅ Correct Answer: C

Pruning removes less important weights based on their magnitude (small weights = less impact). Unstructured pruning: zero out individual weights → sparse matrices → requires hardware/sparsity-aware runtime for speedup. Structured pruning: remove entire neurons, attention heads, or channels → smaller dense model → speedup on any hardware. Key difference from quantization: pruning reduces the NUMBER of operations (fewer weights to compute), while quantization reduces the SIZE of each operation (smaller precision). Combined approach: prune (remove 30% of weights) then quantize (INT4 on remaining) = ultra-compact model. SparseGPT and Wanda are popular LLM pruning algorithms. RHOAI's LLM Compressor supports both.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pruning vs Quantization
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ORIGINAL MODEL:          PRUNED (50% sparse):        QUANTIZED (INT4):   │
  │  ┌──┬──┬──┬──┐          ┌──┬──┬──┬──┐          ┌──┬──┬──┬──┐          │
  │  │W1│W2│W3│W4│          │W1│  │W3│  │          │▓▓│▓▓│▓▓│▓▓│          │
  │  ├──┼──┼──┼──┤          ├──┼──┼──┼──┤          ├──┼──┼──┼──┤          │
  │  │W5│W6│W7│W8│          │  │W6│  │W8│          │▓▓│▓▓│▓▓│▓▓│          │
  │  └──┴──┴──┴──┘          └──┴──┴──┴──┘          └──┴──┴──┴──┘          │
  │  8 weights × 2 bytes    4 weights × 2 bytes    8 weights × 0.5 bytes    │
  │  = 16 bytes             = 8 bytes (50% less)   = 4 bytes (75% less)    │
  │  Compute: 8 ops         Compute: 4 ops (faster) Compute: 8 ops          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WHEN TO PRUNE:             WHEN TO QUANTIZE:                            │
  │  ✅ Need faster inference   ✅ Need smaller memory                       │
  │  ✅ Have sparsity hardware  ✅ GPU VRAM is the limit                     │
  │  ✅ Structured pruning      ✅ Don't have sparsity support               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The salary predictor runs on CPU — memory isn't the issue, but inference speed matters (1000 req/min). Structured pruning removes 40% of neurons, reducing compute by 40% and latency from 15ms to 9ms per prediction. Quantization wouldn't help much (model is already small at 50MB).

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Pruning = fewer operations (faster compute). Quantization = smaller precision (less memory). Can be combined. Structured pruning gives speedup on all hardware. RHOAI: LLM Compressor.

How do you implement A/B testing between two model versions in production using KServe?
A) Deploy both models as separate InferenceServices and have the client randomly choose which one to call
B) KServe doesn't support A/B testing — you need a separate API gateway like Ambassador or Kong for traffic splitting
C) Use Kubernetes Ingress with weighted routing — A/B testing is a networking concern, not a KServe feature
D) Use canaryTrafficPercent for gradual traffic splitting, then compare metrics (latency, error rate, prediction distribution) between the two revisions in the KServe dashboard — this is native A/B testing at the model serving layer
✅ Correct Answer: D

KServe's canary rollout mechanism doubles as an A/B testing framework. Setup: Deploy the new model as a revision with canaryTrafficPercent: 50 (50% to new, 50% to old). Metrics comparison: Both revisions serve traffic simultaneously — compare latency (p50/p95/p99), error rate (4xx/5xx), throughput, and business metrics (prediction distribution, user engagement). Decision: If new model outperforms on all metrics, increase to 100%. If underperforms, set to 0 (instant rollback). Key difference from simple canary: A/B testing focuses on comparing business outcomes, not just "does it crash." You may run A/B for days to gather statistically significant results.

Models Q137 of 200
Your model endpoint returns 503 errors during traffic spikes. What is the most likely cause and fix?
A) The model is corrupted — delete and redeploy the InferenceService with a fresh model download
B) The HPA/KPA cannot scale fast enough — increase minReplicas to handle base load, reduce scale-down delay, or implement request queuing with a message broker to smooth traffic spikes
C) The S3 storage is throttling — model weights are being re-downloaded on every request, causing latency
D) The GPU is overheating — 503 errors are always caused by hardware thermal throttling on GPU nodes
✅ Correct Answer: B

503 errors during traffic spikes indicate the model server cannot accept new requests — typically because all replicas are at capacity and autoscaling hasn't caught up yet. Root causes: (1) minReplicas too low — baseline traffic already saturates available pods. (2) Scale-up delay — HPA checks every 15s by default; new pods take 30-60s to start and load the model. (3) Cold start — if using Knative scale-to-zero, the first request waits for a pod to boot (2+ minutes for GPU models). Fixes: Increase minReplicas to handle steady-state load. Implement request queuing (Redis/Kafka) to buffer spikes. Use "always-on" pods for GPU models (minReplicas ≥ 1). Configure HPA with faster polling (--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period) and lower thresholds (scale at 60% instead of 80%).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Traffic Spike Handling
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TRAFFIC SPIKE → 503s:                                                    │
  │  ──────────────────────                                                   │
  │  Requests/sec:  ▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁███▁▁▁▁                                         │
  │  Pods available:  ████████████████  (2 pods × 100 req/s cap = 200 max)  │
  │  Spike height:    ████████████████████████  (400 req/s → 200 rejected)  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  FIX 1: INCREASE minReplicas                                              │
  │  ─────────────────────────                                                │
  │  minReplicas: 2 → 4  (400 req/s capacity → no rejects)                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  FIX 2: REQUEST QUEUING                                                   │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                     │
  │  Client → Redis Queue → Model Server (smooth flow)                       │
  │  Spikes absorbed by queue, processed at steady rate                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  FIX 3: FASTER SCALING                                                    │
  │  ────────────────────                                                     │
  │  scaleTarget: 60 (scale at 60% CPU, not 80%)                             │
  │  HPA sync period: 15s → 5s (faster detection)                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Monday 9 AM: 500 users check new job matches simultaneously. The salary predictor (minReplicas=1) gets flooded with 400 req/s but can only handle 100 req/s. 300 requests get 503s. Fix: increase minReplicas to 3 (300 req/s capacity), add Redis queue for spike absorption. Monday 9 AM next week: zero 503s.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: 503 during spikes = autoscaling can't keep up. Fix: increase minReplicas, implement request queuing, reduce scale thresholds. GPU models: minReplicas ≥ 1 always.

What is the Model Registry API and how can you automate model promotion?
A) The Model Registry exposes a REST API (and Python SDK) for registering, versioning, and promoting models — pipelines can call the API to auto-register trained models, and CI/CD can auto-promote models that pass evaluation thresholds
B) The Model Registry has no API — all operations must be done manually through the OpenShift AI dashboard

Python SDK: from model_registry import ModelRegistry; registry = ModelRegistry(host=...); registry.register_model(name, version, metadata). REST API: Standard CRUD endpoints for models, versions, artifacts, and deployments. Automation patterns: (1) Pipeline auto-registration — the last step of a KFP pipeline calls the registry API to register the trained model. (2) CI/CD auto-promotion — if evaluation metrics exceed thresholds, automatically promote from Staging to Production via API call. What Grafana dashboards should you build for ML model monitoring in production?
A) Only a GPU utilization dashboard — infrastructure metrics are the only thing that matters for ML
B) A single dashboard showing model accuracy — if accuracy is stable, everything else is fine
C) Grafana is not suitable for ML monitoring — you need specialized ML observability tools
D) Build layered dashboards: Golden Signals (latency/errors/throughput), Model Quality (drift/bias/accuracy), Infrastructure (GPU/CPU/memory), and Business (prediction distribution/user impact) — each layer answers different questions for different stakeholders
✅ Correct Answer: D

Production ML requires layered observability: (1) Golden Signals — RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration). Prometheus metrics from KServe: request count, error rate (4xx/5xx), latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99). Answers: "Is the service healthy?" (2) Model Quality — TrustyAI metrics: drift (KS-test p-value), bias (demographic parity difference), accuracy/F1 (logged predictions vs ground truth). Answers: "Is the model still good?" (3) Infrastructure — Node exporter + DCGM: GPU utilization, GPU memory, CPU, disk I/O. Answers: "Do we have enough hardware?" (4) Business — Custom metrics: prediction distribution histogram, user-facing metric (e.g., "job match acceptance rate"). Answers: "Is the model driving business value?" Separate dashboards per persona: SREs → Golden Signals + Infra, Data Scientists → Model Quality, Product → Business.

Models Q141 of 200
What is a feature store and how does it improve ML model serving consistency?
A) A feature store is a database for model weights — it stores trained model parameters for fast retrieval during inference
B) A feature store is a GPU cache for embeddings — it pre-loads common feature vectors into GPU memory to reduce inference latency
C) A feature store is a centralized repository for ML features — it ensures the same feature transformations are applied during training AND serving, eliminating training-serving skew where different feature logic produces inconsistent predictions
D) A feature store is a version control system for Jupyter notebooks — it tracks feature engineering code changes across team members
✅ Correct Answer: C

Training-serving skew is one of the hardest ML bugs: the model was trained with features computed one way, but at serving time, features are computed differently (or with stale data). A feature store solves this by: (1) Centralized feature definitions — feature engineering code lives in one place, used by both training pipelines and serving endpoints. (2) Point-in-time correctness — when training on historical data, the feature store returns feature values AS THEY WERE at that point in time (not current values). (3) Online/offline consistency — same feature logic for batch training (offline) and real-time inference (online). (4) Feature reuse — teams share features instead of each team computing "user_age_days" independently. In OpenShift AI, Feast is commonly used as the feature store, integrated with KServe via transformers that fetch features before prediction.

📝 Detailed Explanation

  │  │ API:              │  ← DIFFERENT logic!                               │

  │  │   start_date)/365 │  ← Off by one? Leap year?                         │
  │  └──────────────────┘                                                    │
  │                                                                          │

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The salary predictor uses 15 features (years experience, skill count, certifications, etc.). Without a feature store, the training pipeline computes "years_experience" differently than the Django API serving code. A 0.2 year difference shifts salary predictions by $2,000 — noticeable to users. The feature store ensures identical computation everywhere.

Models Q142 of 200
What security considerations are unique to ML model serving compared to traditional API security?
A) Model extraction attacks (query the model to steal its weights), adversarial inputs (crafted inputs to cause misprediction), data poisoning through inference (inject malicious patterns), and model inversion (reconstruct training data from outputs) — these go beyond standard API security
B) ML models need the same security as any REST API — HTTPS, authentication, and rate limiting are sufficient
C) Model security is handled entirely by the GPU driver — NVIDIA's secure boot and encrypted memory protect models automatically
D) ML security is only relevant during training — once a model is deployed, its weights are read-only and cannot be attacked
✅ Correct Answer: A

ML serving introduces unique attack vectors beyond traditional API security: (1) Model extraction — attackers send thousands of queries to reconstruct model weights (especially dangerous for proprietary models trained on expensive data). Mitigation: rate limiting, query monitoring, output perturbation (add noise). (2) Adversarial inputs — carefully crafted inputs designed to cause misprediction (e.g., adding imperceptible noise to a resume to force a "no match" result). Mitigation: input validation, adversarial training, anomaly detection. (3) Model inversion — reconstruct training data from model outputs (privacy violation — extract resume text from job-matching scores). Mitigation: differential privacy, output clipping. (4) Membership inference — determine if a specific data point was in the training set. Mitigation: differential privacy during training. OpenShift AI mitigations: NetworkPolicy for model endpoints, OAuth proxy auth, audit logging of all inference requests.

📝 Detailed Explanation
ML-Specific Attack Vectors
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ATTACK                METHOD                    MITIGATION               │
  │  ──────                ──────                    ──────────               │
  │  Model Extraction      Query model 10K times     Rate limiting            │
  │                        → Reconstruct weights     Output perturbation      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Adversarial Input     Add crafted noise         Input validation         │
  │                        → Force wrong prediction  Adversarial training     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Model Inversion       Analyze outputs           Differential privacy     │
  │                        → Reconstruct training    Output clipping          │
  │                           data samples                                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Membership Inference  Test if X was in          Differential privacy     │
  │                        training data             during training          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  OPENSHIFT AI DEFENSE LAYERS:                                             │
  │  • NetworkPolicy (restrict endpoint access)                               │
  │  • OAuth Proxy (authenticate every request)                               │
  │  • Rate limiting (prevent extraction attacks)                             │
  │  • Audit logging (detect suspicious query patterns)                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: A competitor could query the job-matching API 100K times with synthetic resumes to steal the matching algorithm (model extraction). Rate limiting (100 req/min per user) + audit logging (detect pattern: all requests from one IP, systematic variation of inputs) prevents this. The model is proprietary IP — protecting it is as important as protecting source code.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: ML-specific threats: model extraction, adversarial inputs, model inversion. Beyond standard API security. Mitigate with rate limiting, input validation, audit logging, and differential privacy.

Models Q143 of 200
How do you optimize a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline for production serving on OpenShift AI?
A) RAG doesn't need optimization — the LLM handles retrieval and generation in one inference call automatically
B) Run everything on CPU to save GPU costs — RAG is primarily a CPU-bound text processing workload
C) Use a single large model for both retrieval and generation — splitting across models adds unnecessary latency
D) Deploy the embedding model (retrieval) and LLM (generation) as separate InferenceServices — the embedding model runs on CPU (small, fast), retrieves relevant documents from a vector DB (Milvus), then the LLM on GPU generates the final response using the retrieved context
✅ Correct Answer: D

RAG in production requires architectural optimization: (1) Embedding model (e.g., all-MiniLM-L6-v2, ~80MB) converts the user query to a vector. Runs on CPU via KServe — fast (~5ms), cheap, scales easily. (2) Vector database (Milvus, deployed as a separate service) stores pre-computed document embeddings. Searches for top-K similar documents (~10ms for 1M documents). (3) LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B INT4 on GPU) receives: system prompt + retrieved documents + user query → generates response. This separation means: the GPU LLM only runs when generating (not for every search), the embedding model is CPU-cheap, and the vector DB is independently scalable. Pipeline latency: embedding (5ms) + vector search (10ms) + LLM generation (2-8 seconds) = dominated by LLM, which is unavoidable.

📝 Detailed Explanation

  │       ▼                                                                    │

  │                               ▼                                           │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  STEP 2: VECTOR SEARCH (Milvus, 10ms)                              │    │
  │  │  Find top-3 similar job descriptions from 50K stored docs         │    │

  │                               ▼                                           │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  STEP 3: LLM GENERATION (GPU, 3s)                                  │    │
  │  │  KServe vLLM: system_prompt + retrieved_docs + user_query          │    │
  │  │  → "We are seeking a Senior Python Developer with 5+ years..."    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │

  │  • Embedding model: 1 CPU core, 512MB RAM (cheap, always-on)             │
  │  • Milvus: 2 CPU cores, 8GB RAM (indexes 50K docs)                       │
  │  • LLM: 1 GPU (T4), 8GB RAM (expensive, scale based on demand)          │
