Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The RAG job description generator splits into 3 InferenceServices: embedding (CPU, always-on), Milvus (indexes 10K job descriptions), Llama-3-8B (GPU, 2 replicas). GPU costs are 80% of the RAG budget — but the GPU only runs during generation (not for every page load). This architecture saves $2K/month vs running one monolithic GPU pod for everything.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: RAG = embedding model (CPU) + vector DB + LLM (GPU). Separate InferenceServices for each. GPU only for generation. Vector DB is independently scalable.

Models Q144 of 200
What strategies mitigate GPU model cold start problems in KServe?
A) Cold starts are unavoidable with GPU models — accept the 2-5 minute startup delay as a hardware limitation
B) Keep minReplicas ≥ 1 (warm pods always running), pre-load models into a shared PVC cache on GPU nodes, use model pre-warming (periodic health checks that keep models loaded), and for scale-to-zero scenarios, use smaller "standby" models that load faster
C) Use CPU-only models — GPU cold starts are the price of using accelerators and there are no workarounds
D) Store model weights in RAM instead of GPU VRAM — RAM is faster to load and avoids cold start delays entirely
✅ Correct Answer: B

GPU cold starts are 10-100x worse than CPU cold starts because model weights must be copied from storage → RAM → GPU VRAM. A 70B model (35GB INT4) takes 2-5 minutes to load even with fast SSDs. Mitigations: (1) minReplicas ≥ 1 — the simplest fix; keep at least one pod always warm. Cost: you pay for idle GPU time. (2) PVC cache — mount a fast local SSD PVC on GPU nodes; first pod loads model from S3→PVC; subsequent pods load from PVC (10x faster). (3) Model pre-warming — send periodic "health check" inference requests to keep the model loaded in VRAM. (4) Standby models — for scale-to-zero, deploy a tiny version (e.g., Llama-3-8B instead of 70B) that loads in 10 seconds and serves as a fallback while the full model warms up. (5) Node pinning — use nodeSelector to ensure GPU pods always land on the same node (leverages cached model in node-level storage).

📝 Detailed Explanation
GPU Cold Start Mitigation
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  COLD START TIMELINE (Llama-3-70B INT4, 35GB):                           │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                             │
  │  t=0s    Pod scheduled on GPU node                                        │
  │  t=5s    Init container: download from S3 (if no cache)                  │
  │  t=120s  S3 download complete (35GB @ 300MB/s)                           │
  │  t=125s  Load weights into RAM                                            │
  │  t=180s  Transfer RAM → GPU VRAM                                          │
  │  t=185s  Model ready! Total: ~3 minutes                                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  MITIGATION: PVC CACHE                                                    │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                     │
  │  t=0s    Pod scheduled on GPU node (PVC already has model)               │
  │  t=5s    Load from PVC (local SSD, 3GB/s)                                │
  │  t=17s   Transfer RAM → GPU VRAM                                          │
  │  t=22s   Model ready! Total: ~22 seconds (8x faster)                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  MITIGATION: WARM POD (minReplicas=1)                                     │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────                                      │
  │  t=0s    Pod already running, model in VRAM                               │
  │  t=1ms   Model ready! Total: ~1ms (instant)                               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The RAG LLM serves external users who expect sub-second first-token latency. With minReplicas=1 and PVC cache, requests never hit cold starts. Cost: ~$300/month for the idle GPU — acceptable vs losing users to 3-minute waits. For the internal salary predictor (used 9-5 only), scale-to-zero overnight with a standby tiny model for after-hours queries.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: GPU cold start = 2-5 min for large models. Fix: minReplicas ≥ 1 (warm pods), PVC cache (local SSD), model pre-warming, standby models for scale-to-zero. nodeSelector for cache locality.

Models Q145 of 200
A production model incident occurs — predictions are suddenly wrong for 30% of users. What is your incident response process?
A) Immediately roll back to the previous model version — speed is everything in incident response, diagnose later
B) Restart all InferenceService pods — most model issues are transient and fixed by restarting the serving infrastructure
C) Triage (check dashboards: drift/bias/latency/errors) → Mitigate (canary rollback to 0% or promote previous version) → Diagnose (check pipeline logs, training data, feature distributions) → Fix (retrain, correct data, or update feature logic) → Postmortem (document timeline, root cause, prevention)
D) Escalate to the data science team and wait — model issues require ML expertise and SREs shouldn't touch model serving
✅ Correct Answer: C

ML incident response follows a structured process because rolling back is fast (canaryTrafficPercent: 0 is instant) but understanding WHY prevents recurrence. (1) TRIAGE (first 5 min): Check TrustyAI dashboards — is drift detected? Are errors spiking? Is latency normal? Determine scope (30% of users — suggests canary issue or data segment problem). (2) MITIGATE (next 5 min): If model quality is the issue, instantly rollback (canary to 0%). If infrastructure (OOM, GPU failure), scale up or restart. Goal: stop user impact within 10 minutes. (3) DIAGNOSE (next 30 min): Check pipeline logs from the training run that produced this model. Compare feature distributions between training and current live data. Check if upstream data source changed. (4) FIX: Retrain on corrected data, update feature logic, or add validation checks to pipeline. (5) POSTMORTEM: Document timeline, root cause, detection time, mitigation time, and prevention (e.g., "add data validation step to pipeline before training").

📝 Detailed Explanation
ML Incident Response Timeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  T+0min   🚨 ALERT: TrustyAI drift p-value < 0.01                       │
  │  T+2min   📊 TRIAGE: Dashboard shows data drift in "job_title" feature  │
  │              30% of predictions affected (new job titles never seen)     │
  │  T+5min   🔄 MITIGATE: canaryTrafficPercent → 0 (rollback to V2)        │
  │              User impact stopped. Total downtime: 5 minutes.             │
  │  T+15min  🔍 DIAGNOSE: Pipeline logs show training data from May 2026   │
  │              Live data has "AI Prompt Engineer" titles (new in June)     │
  │  T+30min  🩹 FIX: Trigger pipeline retrain on June 2026 data             │
  │  T+2hrs   ✅ New V4 model trained, registered to Staging                 │
  │  T+4hrs   ✅ V4 validated, promoted to Production (canary 10%)           │
  │  T+24hrs  📝 POSTMORTEM: Root cause = training data staleness           │
  │              Prevention = weekly data freshness check in pipeline        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Tuesday 10 AM: job-matching quality drops. Triage shows drift in job titles (new AI roles). Mitigate in 5 minutes (rollback to V2). Diagnose: training data is 3 weeks stale. Fix: pipeline now includes a data freshness check — if training data is >7 days old, abort and alert. Postmortem shared with the whole team. Process turns a panic into a controlled response.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: ML incident = Triage (5min) → Mitigate (5min) → Diagnose (30min) → Fix → Postmortem. Canary rollback is instant mitigation. TrustyAI dashboards for triage. Postmortem prevents recurrence.

How do you deploy models across multiple OpenShift clusters for high availability and geographic distribution?
A) Deploy the same InferenceService on each cluster with identical configuration — use external DNS with geo-routing (Latency/GeoIP) to direct users to the nearest cluster; use the Model Registry to track which version is deployed where; use GitOps (ArgoCD) to keep configurations synchronized
B) KServe automatically replicates InferenceServices across all clusters in a fleet — no manual configuration is needed for multi-cluster serving
C) Use a single large cluster with nodes in multiple regions — multi-cluster deployment is unnecessary because OpenShift spans regions natively
D) Deploy the model on one cluster and use a CDN to cache predictions — inference results are cacheable like static web content
✅ Correct Answer: A

Multi-cluster model serving provides high availability and low latency for global users. Architecture: (1) Per-cluster deployment — each cluster gets its own InferenceService pointing to a replicated S3 bucket (or local MinIO with cross-cluster sync). (2) Global traffic management — external DNS (Route53, Cloudflare) with geo-routing sends US users to us-east cluster, EU users to eu-west cluster. (3) Configuration synchronization — GitOps with ArgoCD ensures all clusters deploy the same model version. The Model Registry is the source of truth for "which version is Production." (4) Cross-cluster model sync — S3 cross-region replication ensures model artifacts are available in all regions. Key consideration: KServe does NOT synchronize across clusters — multi-cluster is an architectural pattern you build on top, not a built-in feature.

Models Q147 of 200
What cost optimization strategies apply specifically to GPU model serving on OpenShift AI?
A) GPU costs are fixed — the only optimization is to use fewer models, which means sacrificing AI features
B) Use spot/preemptible instances for all GPU workloads — model serving can handle random pod terminations without user impact
C) Buy more GPUs — economies of scale reduce per-model costs, so the best optimization is to serve everything on GPU
D) Quantize models (INT4), use ModelMesh for multi-model GPU sharing, deploy CPU-suitable models without GPU (ONNX + OVMS), right-size minReplicas (avoid over-provisioning), use cluster autoscaling with GPU node scale-to-zero, and separate always-warm models from burstable ones on different node groups
✅ Correct Answer: D

GPU cost optimization is multi-layered: (1) Model optimization — quantize to INT4 (4x VRAM savings = smaller GPU needed). Smaller GPU = $5K/month vs $20K/month. (2) Multi-model sharing — ModelMesh packs 5-10 lightweight models on one GPU instead of 5-10 GPUs. (3) Right-model, right-hardware — simple regression/classification models → CPU (ONNX + OVMS, near-zero GPU cost). Only LLMs and deep models → GPU. (4) Right-sizing — minReplicas=1 (not 3 "just in case"), HPA scales up only during spikes. (5) Cluster autoscaling — GPU nodes scale to zero when idle (e.g., weekends for internal tools). (6) Tiered node groups — "always-warm" GPU pool (minReplicas models) + "burstable" GPU pool (spot instances for batch inference). Combined, these strategies can reduce GPU costs by 60-80% vs naive "one GPU per model, always on."

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Initial deployment plan: 5 models × 1 GPU each = $25K/month (cloud). After optimization: 1 GPU for the RAG LLM ($5K), 4 models on CPU ($200). Annual savings: ~$237K. This is the difference between AI being "too expensive" and a sustainable AI platform.

Models Q148 of 200
How does the KServe explainability feature differ from TrustyAI's monitoring, and when do you use each?
A) They are the same thing — both use LIME/SHAP and provide identical functionality
B) KServe Explainer provides per-request explanations (why THIS prediction?), while TrustyAI provides aggregate monitoring over time (is the model drifting? is it biased across demographic groups?) — use Explainer for real-time user-facing explanations, TrustyAI for ongoing governance and alerting
C) KServe Explainer is for model developers during training; TrustyAI is for SREs during production — they target different personas exclusively
D) Explainer is deprecated in favor of TrustyAI — all explainability functionality has moved to TrustyAI in RHOAI 3.x
✅ Correct Answer: B

KServe Explainer and TrustyAI are complementary, not redundant: KServe Explainer (per-request, real-time): When a user asks "why was my resume ranked #3?", the Explainer runs LIME/SHAP on that specific prediction and returns: "Python experience (+35%), missing AWS certification (-28%), etc." This is synchronous and user-facing. TrustyAI (aggregate, continuous): Monitors ALL predictions over time. Answers: "Over the last week, are female candidates receiving systematically lower scores than male candidates with identical qualifications?" This is asynchronous and governance-facing. Use BOTH: Explainer for transparency to users, TrustyAI for detecting systemic issues you might miss in individual explanations. They share the same underlying algorithms (LIME/SHAP) but serve different purposes and time horizons.

  │  WHEN: User clicks "Why?"              WHEN: Continuous background        │
  │  SCOPE: Single prediction              SCOPE: All predictions over time   │

  │  → Same underlying model, same algorithms, DIFFERENT PURPOSE             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: A job seeker clicks "Why am I ranked #3?" — KServe Explainer shows: "Skills match 85%, but 3 other candidates have AWS certification (weighted +15%)." Simultaneously, TrustyAI's weekly report shows no gender bias in rankings. The Explainer satisfies user curiosity; TrustyAI satisfies auditor requirements. Both are essential for a trustworthy AI system.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Explainer = per-request, real-time, user-facing. TrustyAI = aggregate, continuous, governance-facing. They complement each other — use both for responsible AI. Same algorithms (LIME/SHAP), different use cases.

Models Q150 of 200
How do you deploy a GenAI/LLM application end-to-end on OpenShift AI — from model selection to production serving?
A) Download the model from Hugging Face, wrap it in a Flask API, and deploy as a standard Kubernetes Deployment — LLMs are just bigger models and don't need special infrastructure
B) Browse Model Catalog → import model → quantize with LLM Compressor (INT4) → register in Model Registry → create InferenceService with vLLM ServingRuntime → configure GPU/minReplicas/canary → expose via Route → monitor with TrustyAI (drift/bias) → build RAG pipeline (embedding model + Milvus vector DB + LLM) → automate retraining via KFP pipeline
C) Use the RHOAI dashboard's "Deploy LLM" wizard — a single-click deployment that handles everything automatically without configuration
D) LLMs are too large for OpenShift AI — they require dedicated NVIDIA DGX systems and cannot run on standard Kubernetes clusters
✅ Correct Answer: B

The end-to-end GenAI deployment on OpenShift AI follows the full MLOps lifecycle: (1) DISCOVER — Model Catalog: browse Hugging Face or Red Hat curated models. (2) OPTIMIZE — LLM Compressor: quantize to INT4 (70B → 35GB, fits on single A100). (3) GOVERN — Model Registry: register with metadata (framework, metrics, license, training data reference). (4) DEPLOY — KServe InferenceService with vLLM ServingRuntime (PagedAttention, continuous batching for 10-30x throughput). Configure: nvidia.com/gpu: 1, minReplicas: 2, canaryTrafficPercent: 10 for rollout. (5) AUGMENT — RAG: deploy embedding model (CPU, ONNX) + Milvus vector DB + LLM (GPU) as separate InferenceServices. (6) MONITOR — TrustyAI: drift detection, bias monitoring, explainability. (7) AUTOMATE — KFP pipeline for periodic fine-tuning with LoRA adapters. This is the complete "GenAIOps" pattern.

4.1 Pipeline Architecture & KFP SDKQ151-Q160

Pipelines Q151 of 200
What is KubeFlow Pipelines (KFP) v2 and how does it compile Python code into executable workflows?
A) KFP is a visual drag-and-drop tool — you build pipelines in a GUI and it generates Python code from the diagram
B) KFP v2 is a Python SDK where you define pipelines using @dsl.pipeline decorators — the SDK compiles your Python DAG into an Argo Workflow YAML (IR), which Argo then executes as Kubernetes pods with artifact tracking in S3/MinIO and metadata in MariaDB
C) KFP converts Python directly to Kubernetes CronJobs — each pipeline step becomes a separate CronJob scheduled in sequence
D) KFP is a wrapper around Apache Airflow — it translates Python pipeline code into Airflow DAGs for execution
✅ Correct Answer: B

KFP v2 compilation flow: (1) Write — define pipeline with @dsl.pipeline, steps with @dsl.component or @dsl.container_component. (2) Compile — kfp.compiler.Compiler().compile(pipeline_func, 'pipeline.yaml') generates an Argo Workflow YAML (the Intermediate Representation). (3) Upload — via KFP UI or client.upload_pipeline(). (4) Execute — Argo Workflows reads the YAML, creates pods for each step, manages dependencies, handles retries. (5) Track — artifacts saved to S3/MinIO, run metadata to MariaDB, metrics to ML Metadata. The compilation step transforms Python semantics (loops, conditions, data passing) into Kubernetes-native constructs.

📝 Detailed Explanation
KFP v2 Compilation Pipeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PYTHON CODE (.py)                  ARGO YAML (.yaml)                     │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐            ┌────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ @dsl.pipeline       │            │ apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1│    │
  │  │ def my_pipeline():  │  COMPILE   │ kind: Workflow                  │    │
  │  │   step1 = load()    │──────────▶ │ spec:                           │    │
  │  │   step2 = train(    │            │   templates:                    │    │
  │  │     step1.output)   │            │   - name: load                  │    │
  │  │   step3 = eval(     │            │     container:                  │    │
  │  │     step2.output)   │            │       image: python:3.11        │    │
  │  └────────────────────┘            │       command: [python, -c]     │    │
  │                                     │   - name: train                  │    │
  │  STORAGE:                           │     dependencies: [load]         │    │
  │  ────────                           │     container: ...              │    │
  │  S3/MinIO ← artifacts              └────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │  MariaDB ← run metadata                                                   │
  │  ML Metadata ← lineage tracking                                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The anihpj training pipeline is a 20-line Python script using @dsl.pipeline. KFP compiles it to a 200-line Argo YAML. The team only maintains the readable Python; KFP handles all the Kubernetes complexity. When debugging, they can inspect the Argo YAML to understand exactly what pods will run.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: KFP v2 = Python DSL → compile → Argo Workflow YAML → execute as K8s pods. Key command: kfp.compiler.Compiler().compile(). Storage: S3 for artifacts, MariaDB for metadata.

Pipelines Q152 of 200
What infrastructure components does a pipeline server require and how do you configure them?
A) Only a Kubernetes cluster — the pipeline server runs entirely in-memory with no external dependencies
B) A separate OpenShift cluster dedicated to pipelines — pipelines cannot share a cluster with other OpenShift AI components
C) MariaDB/MySQL (pipeline run metadata, experiments), S3/MinIO (artifact storage), and the KFP API server — configured via a DataConnection to S3 and a database connection Secret in the Data Science Project
D) An external workflow engine (Jenkins, Airflow) — KFP requires a separate orchestrator and cannot run standalone
✅ Correct Answer: C

A pipeline server has three infrastructure dependencies: (1) MariaDB/MySQL — stores pipeline definitions, run status, experiment groupings. Created automatically when you enable pipelines in a Data Science Project, or connected via a database Secret. (2) S3-compatible storage (MinIO or AWS S3) — stores pipeline artifacts (datasets, models, metrics). Each pipeline step's outputs are serialized and saved here; downstream steps load from S3 URIs. Configured via a Data Connection in the project. (3) KFP API Server — the REST API and UI that data scientists interact with. Runs as a deployment in the project namespace. The dashboard shows pipeline runs, artifacts, and metrics. All three are provisioned automatically when you click "Configure pipeline server" in the OpenShift AI dashboard.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Server Infrastructure

  │  DATA SCIENCE PROJECT (anihpj):                                           │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  ┌────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐     │    │
  │  │  │ KFP API Server │  │   MariaDB      │  │  MinIO (S3)    │     │    │
  │  │  │ (UI + REST)    │  │   (metadata)   │  │  (artifacts)   │     │    │
  │  │  │                │  │                │  │                │     │    │
  │  │  │ Port: 8443     │  │ • pipelines    │  │ • datasets     │     │    │
  │  │  │ OAuth Proxy    │  │ • runs         │  │ • models       │     │    │
  │  │  │                │  │ • experiments  │  │ • metrics      │     │    │
  │  │  └────────────────┘  └────────────────┘  └────────────────┘     │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CONFIGURATION:                                                           │
  │  1. Data Connection → S3/MinIO endpoint + credentials                    │
  │  2. Database Secret → MariaDB connection string                          │
  │  3. Dashboard → "Configure pipeline server" → auto-provisions all        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The anihpj project uses MinIO (local S3, free) for artifact storage and the auto-provisioned MariaDB for metadata. When a pipeline run completes, Alice can see the trained model in MinIO and the accuracy metrics in the KFP UI — all in one project namespace.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Pipeline server = KFP API + MariaDB + S3/MinIO. Configured via Data Connection + database Secret. Dashboard auto-provisions. Artifacts in S3, metadata in MariaDB.

Pipelines Q153 of 200
What is the @dsl.pipeline decorator and how do you define pipeline parameters?
A) @dsl.pipeline marks a function as a pipeline entry point — parameters are typed function arguments (name: str, epochs: int = 10) that become configurable pipeline parameters with default values visible in the KFP UI
B) @dsl.pipeline is a class decorator — you define pipelines as classes with run/stop methods, not as functions
C) Parameters are defined in a separate YAML config file — @dsl.pipeline reads parameters from a ConfigMap at runtime
D) @dsl.pipeline is optional — any Python function can be uploaded as a pipeline without decorators
✅ Correct Answer: A

The @dsl.pipeline decorator transforms a Python function into a KFP pipeline definition. Parameters: function arguments with type annotations become pipeline parameters. Supported types: str, int, float, bool, dict, list. Default values become the default in the KFP UI. Complex types use dsl.Input[Dataset] and dsl.Output[Model] for artifact passing. Pipeline name/description: set via decorator args: @dsl.pipeline(name="anihpj-train", description="Weekly model retraining"). The function body defines the DAG by calling component functions — KFP infers dependencies from how outputs feed into inputs. DAG structure is implicit in the Python code, not declared separately.

📝 Detailed Explanation
@dsl.pipeline — Parameters and Structure
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @dsl.pipeline(                                                           │
  │      name="anihpj-training",          ← Visible in KFP UI                │
  │      description="Weekly job-matching model training"                    │
  │  )                                                                        │
  │  def training_pipeline(                                                   │
  │      learning_rate: float = 0.001,    ← Typed param with default         │
  │      epochs: int = 10,                ← Integer param                    │
  │      dataset_path: str = "s3://anihpj/jobs/",  ← String param           │
  │      use_gpu: bool = True             ← Boolean param                    │
  │  ):                                                                       │
  │      prep = data_prep(input_path=dataset_path)  ← Component call         │
  │      train = train_model(                        ← Dependency: prep→train│
  │          data=prep.outputs["dataset"],                                   │
  │          lr=learning_rate,                                               │
  │          epochs=epochs                                                   │
  │      )                                                                    │
  │      evaluate = eval_model(model=train.outputs["model"])                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The training pipeline has parameters like `learning_rate` and `epochs`. When Alice triggers a run, she can override defaults in the KFP UI — useful for experimentation without changing code. The pipeline auto-documents its parameters.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: @dsl.pipeline decorator marks entry point. Typed function args = pipeline parameters. Defaults appear in KFP UI. DAG structure is implicit from component call order.

Pipelines Q154 of 200
What is a KFP Experiment and how does it help organize pipeline runs?
A) An Experiment is a separate Kubernetes namespace — each experiment runs in its own isolated project
B) An Experiment is a debugging mode — it runs pipelines with verbose logging for troubleshooting
C) An Experiment is a logical grouping of pipeline runs for comparison — you create an experiment (e.g., "Salary Predictor Tuning"), submit multiple runs with different hyperparameters, and compare metrics side-by-side in the KFP UI
D) An Experiment is a sandbox environment — pipelines in experiments don't actually execute, they simulate results
✅ Correct Answer: C

A KFP Experiment is like a folder for pipeline runs. Create via client.create_experiment(name="salary-tuning"). All pipeline runs submitted to that experiment are grouped together. The KFP UI shows experiments as tabs, with each tab listing runs. You can compare runs within an experiment side-by-side: metrics, parameters, duration, status. Use cases: (1) Hyperparameter tuning — 50 runs with different learning rates, all in one experiment. (2) A/B testing — compare "model-v3" and "model-v4" runs. (3) Time-based grouping — "June 2026 Retraining" experiment for weekly runs. Experiments persist across pipeline versions — you can run different pipeline versions in the same experiment.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Experiments — Organizing Pipeline Runs
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  EXPERIMENTS (KFP UI):                                                    │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                    │

  │     ├─ Run #2: lr=0.0005, epochs=20 → MAE: $2,800                        │
  │     └─ Run #3: lr=0.01, epochs=5 → MAE: $4,100                           │
  │                                                                          │

  │     ├─ Run #142: Week 23, accuracy 92.1% (Production)                     │
  │     └─ Run #143: Week 24, accuracy 94.3% (Staging)                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CREATE: client.create_experiment(name="my-experiment")                   │
  │  SUBMIT: client.run_pipeline(experiment_id=exp.id, ...)                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: When tuning the salary predictor, Alice creates experiment "salary-hparam-search" and runs 20 pipelines with different learning rates. She compares all 20 runs side-by-side in the KFP UI, identifies the best parameters, and promotes that model. Without experiments, 20 runs would be scattered and hard to compare.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Experiment = logical grouping for comparing runs. Create via SDK or UI. Compare metrics side-by-side. All runs in one experiment are comparable.

Pipelines Q155 of 200
How do you trigger a pipeline run programmatically using the KFP client SDK?
A) Use kubectl apply on the pipeline YAML — KFP runs are standard Kubernetes resources
B) Pipeline runs can only be triggered from the KFP UI — there is no programmatic API
C) Use curl to POST to the pipeline server's /run endpoint with raw YAML body
D) Use kfp.Client(host=...).run_pipeline(experiment_id=..., job_name=..., params={...}) — the KFP SDK provides a Python client that authenticates via OpenShift OAuth, triggers runs, and returns a RunDetail object for monitoring
✅ Correct Answer: D

The KFP client SDK provides a full programmatic interface. Authentication: kfp.Client(host="https://ds-pipeline-anihpj.apps.cluster.com", namespace="anihpj") — uses the current OpenShift session token. Trigger run: client.run_pipeline(experiment_id=exp.id, job_name="salary-run-42", params={"learning_rate": 0.001, "epochs": 10}). Monitor: run_response = client.wait_for_run_completion(run_id, timeout=3600) — blocks until done or timeout. Get results: run_detail = client.get_run(run_id) — returns status, metrics, artifacts. This enables CI/CD integration: GitHub Actions can trigger a pipeline on PR merge, wait for completion, and report metrics as PR comments.

📝 Detailed Explanation
KFP Client SDK — Programmatic Pipeline Runs
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  from kfp import Client                                                   │
  │  client = Client(host="https://ds-pipeline-anihpj...", namespace="anihpj")│
  │                                                                          │
  │  # 1. Find/Create experiment                                              │
  │  exp = client.create_experiment(name="salary-tuning")                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  # 2. Run pipeline with params                                            │
  │  run = client.run_pipeline(                                               │
  │      experiment_id=exp.id,                                                │
  │      job_name="run-lr-0.001",                                            │
  │      pipeline_id=pipeline.id,                                             │
  │      params={"learning_rate": 0.001, "epochs": 10}                      │
  │  )                                                                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  # 3. Wait for completion                                                 │
  │  result = client.wait_for_run_completion(run.run_id, timeout=600)        │
  │  if result.run.status == "Succeeded":                                    │
  │      print(f"Accuracy: {result.run.metrics}")                           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The CI/CD pipeline (Tekton) calls the KFP client to trigger retraining on every merge to main. It passes parameters from a config file, waits for the pipeline to complete, and if accuracy > 90%, promotes the model via the Model Registry API. Fully automated — no human clicks.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: kfp.Client(host, namespace).run_pipeline(experiment_id, params). wait_for_run_completion(run_id, timeout). Use for CI/CD automation. Auth via OpenShift session.

Pipelines Q156 of 200
How do you collect and display metrics from pipeline steps in the KFP UI?
A) Print metrics to stdout — KFP parses log output for metric values automatically
B) Output a Metrics artifact with key-value pairs — KFP renders these as visualizations in the UI: scalar metrics show as numbers, ClassificationMetrics show as confusion matrices, and they're comparable across runs in the same experiment
C) Write metrics to a separate Prometheus endpoint — KFP scrapes Prometheus for pipeline metrics
D) Metrics are only available via the KFP SDK — the UI doesn't display pipeline metrics
✅ Correct Answer: B

KFP provides typed metric outputs: Scalar metrics: dsl.Output[Metrics] — key-value pairs like {"accuracy": 0.943, "loss": 0.12}. Rendered as numbers in the KFP UI Run Details. ClassificationMetrics: confusion matrix with rows/columns. HTML/Markdown: custom visualizations rendered inline. The key feature: metrics from different runs in the same experiment are automatically comparable. KFP UI shows a side-by-side comparison table of all runs' metrics. This is critical for hyperparameter tuning — you see at a glance which parameters produced the best metrics. Output metrics as: return dsl.Output[Metrics]({"accuracy": accuracy, "f1": f1_score}).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Metrics — Collection & Comparison

  │  COMPONENT OUTPUT:                                                        │
  │  ────────────────                                                         │

  │      accuracy = calculate_accuracy(model)                                 │
  │      return Output[Metrics]({"accuracy": accuracy, "f1": 0.91})          │
  │                                                                          │

  │  │ #2      0.0005  20       0.943      0.91   24m       ✅ Succeeded │    │
  │  │ #3      0.01    5        0.878      0.83   6m        ✅ Succeeded │    │
  │  │ → Best: #2 (highest accuracy)                                       │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice runs 20 hyperparameter experiments. Instead of manually collecting accuracy numbers from logs, she opens the KFP UI experiment view and sees all 20 runs' metrics in a sortable table. She sorts by accuracy, identifies the best parameters, and promotes that model.

Pipelines Q157 of 200
How do you compare pipeline runs and select the best model version?
A) Download all model artifacts and evaluate them manually — KFP has no comparison features
B) Only the latest run matters — previous runs are automatically archived and cannot be compared
C) Use KFP UI Experiment view to compare metrics side-by-side across runs, sort by any metric column, visualize metric trends over time, and select the best run — then register that run's model in the Model Registry for deployment
D) Pipeline runs are compared automatically — KFP promotes the best model to production without human review
✅ Correct Answer: C

The KFP UI experiment view is purpose-built for run comparison. Features: (1) Side-by-side metrics table — all runs in an experiment shown as rows with columns for parameters, metrics, duration, status. (2) Sortable columns — click "accuracy" to find the best run instantly. (3) Metric trends — line chart showing accuracy over successive runs (is the model improving?). (4) Run details — click any run to see the DAG visualization, step logs, and artifact outputs. (5) Model registration — from the best run, click "Register Model" to add it to the Model Registry. This closes the loop: experiment → compare → select best → register → deploy. The comparison view is the decision-making dashboard for model promotion.

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: After running 20 hyperparameter experiments, Alice opens the experiment view, sorts by F1 score, and immediately sees run #43 is best at 94.3% accuracy. She clicks "Register Model," and it appears in the Model Registry. This data-driven selection replaces "I think this one looks good" with metrics-based decisions.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: KFP Experiment view = run comparison dashboard. Sort by metrics, visualize trends, register best model. This is the bridge between pipelines (Cat 4) and model registry (Cat 3).

Pipelines Q158 of 200
What is the difference between a pipeline Run and a Recurring Run in KFP?
A) A Run is a one-time pipeline execution; a Recurring Run (Job) automatically triggers pipeline executions on a cron schedule — recurring runs create child runs on schedule, and each child run appears as a regular run in the experiment
B) Runs are for development; Recurring Runs are for production — they use different execution engines
C) Recurring Runs repeat the same run ID — they're identical executions of the same run, not new runs
D) Runs require manual approval; Recurring Runs auto-approve — the difference is only in approval workflow
✅ Correct Answer: A

Run: One-time execution. Created via client.run_pipeline() or "Create Run" in UI. Each run has a unique run_id. Use for: ad-hoc experimentation, manual triggers, CI/CD-triggered runs. Recurring Run (Job): Scheduled execution template. Created via client.create_recurring_run(cron_expression="0 2 * * 0"). KFP automatically creates a new child Run at each scheduled time. The parent Recurring Run tracks: schedule (cron expression), enabled/disabled status, catchup policy, and all child runs. You can pause/resume a recurring run without deleting it. Child runs appear in the same experiment as manual runs — they're indistinguishable once created. Both use the same execution engine (Argo Workflows).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Run vs Recurring Run
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RUN (one-time):                     RECURRING RUN (job):                │
  │  ──────────────                      ─────────────────────               │
  │  client.run_pipeline(                 client.create_recurring_run(       │
  │      experiment_id=exp.id,               experiment_id=exp.id,           │
  │      job_name="manual-test",             job_name="weekly-train",       │
  │      params={...}                        cron_expression="0 2 * * 0",   │
  │  )                                       params={...}                    │
  │  → Creates Run #42                   )                                   │
  │                                        → Creates Recurring Run           │
  │                                        → Every Sunday 2AM:                │
  │                                           → Auto-creates Run #43         │
  │                                           → Auto-creates Run #44         │
  │                                           → Auto-creates Run #45 ...     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The weekly retraining is a Recurring Run with cron "0 2 * * 0" (Sunday 2 AM). Each Sunday, KFP creates a new child run automatically. Monday morning, Alice checks the latest run's metrics in the experiment view. If the new model is better, she promotes it. No manual triggering needed — "set and forget" with oversight.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Run = one-time. Recurring Run = cron-scheduled, auto-creates child runs. create_recurring_run(cron_expression=...). Child runs appear in same experiment. Pause/resume without deleting.

Pipelines Q159 of 200
What is the KFP SDK client and how do you use it to manage pipelines programmatically?
A) The KFP client is a CLI tool installed via brew/apt — it has no Python SDK, only shell commands
B) kfp.Client(host=..., namespace=...) connects to the pipeline server — it provides methods for uploading pipelines, creating experiments, triggering runs, monitoring status, and managing recurring runs, all from Python code for CI/CD integration
C) The KFP client is embedded in the dashboard — all operations must be done through the UI, no programmatic access
D) The KFP client only reads pipeline data — it's read-only and cannot create or modify pipelines, runs, or experiments
✅ Correct Answer: B

The KFP Client SDK is the programmatic interface to the pipeline server. Key methods: Pipeline management — client.upload_pipeline(), client.list_pipelines(), client.get_pipeline(). Experiment management — client.create_experiment(), client.list_experiments(). Run management — client.run_pipeline(), client.list_runs(), client.get_run(), client.wait_for_run_completion(). Recurring runs — client.create_recurring_run(), client.list_recurring_runs(), enable/disable. Authentication: uses the OpenShift session token from oc whoami -t. The client is the bridge between CI/CD systems (Tekton, GitHub Actions, Jenkins) and the KFP server — every operation you can do in the UI has a corresponding SDK method. Use for: automated ML pipelines triggered by Git commits, data arrival events, or scheduled retraining.

KFP Client SDK — Full Management API
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  from kfp import Client                                                   │
  │  client = Client(host="https://ds-pipeline-anihpj...")                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  PIPELINES:                EXPERIMENTS:          RUNS:                    │

  │  upload_pipeline()        create_experiment()   run_pipeline()           │
  │  list_pipelines()         list_experiments()    list_runs()              │
