  │  delete_pipeline()        archive_experiment()  wait_for_run_completion()│
  │                                                                          │
  │  RECURRING RUNS:          ARTIFACTS:            AUTH:                     │
  │  ──────────────          ──────────            ────                     │
  │  create_recurring_run()  (via run detail)      OpenShift session token   │
  │  list_recurring_runs()                         Auto-detected from env    │
  │  enable/disable                                                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The CI/CD pipeline (Tekton) uses the KFP client to: upload new pipeline on Git push → create experiment if not exists → trigger run with production parameters → wait for completion → read metrics → if accuracy threshold met, call Model Registry API to promote. Zero manual steps from code commit to model in production.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: kfp.Client = full programmatic API. upload_pipeline, create_experiment, run_pipeline, wait_for_run_completion. Auth via OpenShift session. Enables CI/CD integration.

Pipelines Q160 of 200
A recurring pipeline has been running successfully for weeks but suddenly fails. What is the systematic troubleshooting approach?
A) Immediately delete and recreate the recurring run — stale schedules are the most common cause of pipeline failures
B) Restart the pipeline server pod — server-side issues cause 90% of recurring run failures
C) Increase all resource limits — pipeline failures after successful runs are always caused by resource exhaustion
D) Check the latest failed child run's details in KFP UI → identify which step failed → view step pod logs → check if input data changed (S3 path, schema), if credentials expired (Secret rotation), if resource limits hit (OOMKilled), or if external dependency changed (DB schema, API endpoint) — recurring runs fail when the WORLD changes, not the pipeline
✅ Correct Answer: D

Recurring run failures after a history of success are almost always caused by environmental changes: (1) Data changes — input data schema changed (new column, removed field), S3 path moved, data volume grew beyond memory limits. (2) Credential expiry — S3 access keys rotated, database password changed, API token expired. (3) Dependency changes — external API endpoint changed, database schema migration, package version incompatibility. (4) Resource limits — data grew from 100K to 1M rows, OOMKilled because memory limit unchanged. Debug: KFP UI → failed run → click failed step → Logs tab. The logs will tell you exactly what broke. The pipeline code didn't change — the world around it did. Fix the environmental issue, and the next scheduled run will succeed.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Recurring Run Failure — Environment Changed
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DEBUG FLOW:                                                              │
  │  ──────────                                                               │
  │  KFP UI → Recurring Runs → \"weekly-train\" → Latest child run (FAILED)   │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  Run graph: prep ✅ → train ❌ → eval (skipped)                            │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  Click \"train\" step → Logs tab:                                           │
  │  \"psycopg2.OperationalError: FATAL: password authentication failed\"     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ROOT CAUSE: Database password was rotated.                              │
  │  FIX: Update DB Secret → Next scheduled run auto-uses new password.      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  COMMON ENVIRONMENTAL FAILURES:                                            │
  │  ─────────────────────────────                                             │
  │  • \"AccessDenied\" → S3/DB credentials expired or rotated                │
  │  • \"No such key\" → S3 path changed or data moved                        │
  │  • \"OOMKilled\" → Data grew beyond memory limit                           │
  │  • \"Connection refused\" → Service endpoint changed                       │
  │  • \"ModuleNotFoundError\" → Package version pin removed from image       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Sunday's pipeline failed after 12 weeks of success. Alice checks the failed run: the data-prep step failed with "No such key: s3://anihpj/jobs/2026/june/" — the S3 path structure was reorganized by the data team. She updates the pipeline parameter from "2026/june/" to "2026/06/" and the pipeline runs successfully on retry. The pipeline code never changed — the data layout did.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Recurring run failures = environment changed (data, credentials, dependencies). Check the failed step's logs first. Don't delete/recreate — diagnose. The pipeline is fine; the world changed.

4.2 Building Pipeline ComponentsQ161-Q170

Pipelines Q161 of 200
How do you create a container component from an existing Docker image in KFP v2?
A) Container components are deprecated — you must rewrite all containers as Python function components
B) Push the Docker image to the pipeline server's internal registry — KFP auto-discovers images tagged with "kfp-component"
C) Use kubectl to create a ConfigMap describing the container — KFP reads ConfigMaps to discover available components
D) Use @dsl.container_component decorator returning a ContainerSpec with image, command, and args — KFP treats this as a black-box container step with typed inputs/outputs specified via dsl.Input/Output annotations
✅ Correct Answer: D

Container components wrap pre-existing Docker images as pipeline steps. Pattern: @dsl.container_component decorator on a function that returns dsl.ContainerSpec(image=..., command=..., args=...). Function parameters become component inputs (can reference as command arguments). Outputs declared via return type annotations using dsl.Output[Dataset], dsl.Output[Model], etc. KFP auto-generates the Argo container template from the spec. The image must exist in an accessible registry (with imagePullSecrets if private). Container components are best for: GPU-optimized training images, legacy codebases with complex dependencies, or when the step needs system packages not installable via pip.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Container Component Definition
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @dsl.container_component                                                  │
  │  def train_gpu(                                                            │
  │      training_data: dsl.Input[Dataset],                                   │
  │      epochs: int,                                                         │
  │      model: dsl.Output[Model]                                            │
  │  ):                                                                        │
  │      return dsl.ContainerSpec(                                             │
  │          image="quay.io/anihpj/train-gpu:v3.1",  ← Pre-built image      │
  │          command=["python", "train.py"],                                  │
  │          args=[                                                           │
  │              "--data-dir", training_data.path,                            │
  │              "--epochs", str(epochs),                                     │
  │              "--output", model.path                                       │
  │          ]                                                                │
  │      )                                                                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  KEY POINTS:                                                              │
  │  • Image must exist at runtime (pre-built + pushed)                      │
  │  • Inputs accessed via .path attribute (S3 URI or local path)            │
  │  • Outputs written to .path (KFP handles upload to S3)                   │
  │  • GPU: add .set_gpu_limit(1) on the component call                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The GPU training step uses a pre-built image with CUDA, PyTorch, and custom training scripts (2GB image). This image takes 10 minutes to build from scratch — using container components means the image is built once, cached in the registry, and the pipeline step starts in seconds. No pip install at runtime.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Container component = @dsl.container_component → dsl.ContainerSpec(image, command, args). Image must be pre-built. Use for GPU training, legacy code, system dependencies.

Pipelines Q162 of 200
How do Python function components work in KFP v2 and when should you use them?
A) They run locally in the Jupyter kernel — Python components are for development only and never run as pods
B) @dsl.component decorator wraps a Python function — KFP auto-containerizes it at compile time using a base image + packages_to_install; the function runs as a Kubernetes pod like any component, but without manual Dockerfile management
C) They are compiled to WebAssembly — Python components run in-browser for faster execution without container overhead
D) Python components can only use standard library — third-party packages require container components exclusively
✅ Correct Answer: B

Python function components are the simplest way to create pipeline steps. Decorated with @dsl.component, KFP automatically containerizes the function: it generates a Dockerfile using the specified base_image (default: python:3.11), adds packages_to_install via pip, and creates a container that runs the function. Key parameters: base_image (change for GPU support: nvidia/cuda:12.1-runtime-ubuntu22.04), packages_to_install (list of pip packages), pip_index_urls (private PyPI mirrors). Use when: rapid prototyping, simple transformations (pandas, numpy), you don't want Docker overhead. Don't use when: system packages needed (apt-get), strict dependency versioning required, or slow pip install is unacceptable for production speed.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Python Component — Auto-Containerization
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PYTHON CODE:                          KFP COMPILES TO:                   │
  │  ────────────                          ────────────────                   │
  │  @dsl.component(                                                        │
  │      base_image="python:3.11",         Dockerfile (auto-generated):     │
  │      packages_to_install=[             FROM python:3.11                  │
  │          "pandas==2.1.0",              RUN pip install pandas==2.1.0 \  │
  │          "scikit-learn==1.3.0"         scikit-learn==1.3.0              │
  │      ]                                  COPY component.py /              │
  │  )                                      ENTRYPOINT ["python", "-c", ...] │
  │  def prep_data(                                                          │
  │      input_csv: str,                  → Pod runs this container          │
  │  ) -> dsl.Output[Dataset]:             with the function code            │
  │      import pandas as pd                                                 │
  │      df = pd.read_csv(input_csv)                                        │
  │      return dsl.Output[Dataset](df)                                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice prototypes with Python components — she writes a 10-line function, specifies packages, and the pipeline runs. No Dockerfile. Once stable, Bob converts critical steps to container components with pre-built images for production speed. Best of both worlds: fast iteration → fast execution.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Python component = @dsl.component + packages_to_install. Auto-containerized. Runs as K8s pod (NOT local). Use for prototyping. Production steps → container components.

Pipelines Q163 of 200
How do artifacts differ from parameters in KFP and when should each be used?
A) Parameters are small values (str, int, float — max ~10KB) passed at pipeline start via the UI/SDK; Artifacts are large data objects (datasets, models, metrics) produced by steps and stored in S3/MinIO — use parameters for configuration, artifacts for data
B) Parameters and artifacts are interchangeable — any value can be passed as either without difference
C) Parameters are encrypted at rest; artifacts are plain text — use parameters for sensitive data
D) Parameters are persisted in MariaDB; artifacts are stored in etcd — they use different storage backends
✅ Correct Answer: A

Parameters: Small, simple values passed when starting a pipeline run. Types: str, int, float, bool. Stored in MariaDB as run metadata. Visible and editable in KFP UI when triggering runs. Use for: learning rate, epochs, dataset paths (strings), boolean flags. Max size ~10KB. Artifacts: Large data objects produced/consumed by pipeline steps. Types: Dataset, Model, Metrics, ClassificationMetrics, HTML, Markdown. Stored in S3/MinIO. Referenced by URI in MariaDB metadata. Use for: preprocessed datasets (parquet files), trained model weights (pickle/safetensors), evaluation metrics (JSON), visualizations (HTML). Artifacts survive step restarts and can be downloaded from KFP UI. Rule of thumb: if it's more than a config value, it's an artifact.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Parameters vs Artifacts
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PARAMETERS (small, config):          ARTIFACTS (large, data):            │
  │  ──────────────────────────          ──────────────────────────          │
  │  learning_rate: float = 0.001        Dataset: 100K rows (parquet, 50MB) │
  │  epochs: int = 10                    Model: weights file (safetensors)  │
  │  use_gpu: bool = True                Metrics: JSON (1KB)                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STORED IN: MariaDB                  STORED IN: S3/MinIO                │
  │  VISIBLE IN: KFP UI Run Details      VISIBLE IN: KFP UI Artifacts tab   │
  │  EDITABLE: Yes, when triggering      DOWNLOADABLE: Yes, from UI/CLI     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CODE:                                CODE:                              │
  │  def my_pipeline(lr: float):          def prep_data() -> Output[Dataset]:│
  │      train(lr=lr)                     def train(data: Input[Dataset])    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The pipeline has parameters (learning_rate=0.001, epochs=10) and artifacts (preprocessed dataset 50MB, trained model 200MB, metrics JSON). Parameters control HOW the pipeline runs; artifacts are WHAT it produces. Alice can change parameters in the KFP UI without recompiling the pipeline.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Parameters = small config values (str/int/float/bool), stored in MariaDB. Artifacts = large data (Dataset/Model/Metrics), stored in S3. Don't pass datasets as parameters.

Pipelines Q164 of 200
How do you configure resource requests and GPU allocation for pipeline steps?
A) Chain .set_cpu_limit(), .set_memory_limit(), .set_gpu_limit() on the component call — e.g., train_step(...).set_gpu_limit(1).set_memory_limit("16Gi") — KFP adds these as Kubernetes resource requests/limits in the step's pod spec
B) Resources are configured globally in the pipeline server — all steps get the same allocation
C) Add resource annotations to the component Python function — KFP reads @resource(gpu=1) decorators
D) Pipeline steps share the pipeline server's resources — you configure the server, not individual steps
✅ Correct Answer: A

KFP provides chained resource configuration methods on component calls: .set_cpu_limit(cpu) — CPU cores (e.g., "2" for 2 cores). .set_memory_limit(memory) — RAM (e.g., "16Gi"). .set_gpu_limit(gpu) — GPU count (e.g., 1). Optionally .set_cpu_request() and .set_memory_request() for guaranteed minimums. These are added to the pod spec that Argo Workflows generates. Example: train_step(data=prep.output).set_gpu_limit(1).set_memory_limit("32Gi") for GPU training. The GPU step will only schedule on nodes with available GPUs. Data prep steps typically use CPU only: prep_step().set_cpu_limit("4").set_memory_limit("8Gi"). Different steps = different resources = efficient cluster utilization.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Per-Step Resource Configuration
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @dsl.pipeline                                                            │
  │  def anihpj_pipeline():                                                   │
  │      # Data prep: CPU-intensive, no GPU needed                           │
  │      prep = data_prep().set_cpu_limit("4").set_memory_limit("8Gi")     │
  │                                                                          │
  │      # Training: GPU-intensive                                            │
  │      train = train_model(data=prep.outputs["dataset"])\
  │          .set_gpu_limit(1)\
  │          .set_memory_limit("32Gi")\
  │          .set_cpu_limit("8")                                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │      # Evaluation: lightweight, CPU only                                  │
  │      eval = evaluate(model=train.outputs["model"])\
  │          .set_cpu_limit("2").set_memory_limit("4Gi")                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The training step needs 1 GPU + 32GB (large dataset). The eval step only needs 2 CPUs. Without per-step resources, all steps would request 1 GPU — the eval step would block a GPU it doesn't use. Per-step config means GPU is only allocated where needed.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: .set_gpu_limit(n), .set_cpu_limit(s), .set_memory_limit(s) on component calls. Different resources per step. GPU only for training/inference steps.

Pipelines Q165 of 200
How do you configure retry policies and exit handling for pipeline steps?
A) Retries must be implemented inside the component code — KFP has no built-in retry mechanism for failed steps
B) Set a global retry count on the pipeline — all steps inherit the same retry policy
C) Use .set_retry(max_retries=3, backoff_duration="5s") on a step, and dsl.ExitHandler for cleanup — KFP retries failed steps automatically before marking the run as failed, and ExitHandler runs cleanup steps regardless of success/failure
D) Retry policy is configured in the pipeline server ConfigMap — all pipelines share the same retry settings
✅ Correct Answer: C

KFP provides granular retry and error handling: (1) Step retry: train_step(...).set_retry(max_retries=3, backoff_duration="30s") — KFP automatically retries the step up to 3 times with 30s between attempts. Common for network-dependent steps (database connections, API calls). (2) Exit handlers: with dsl.ExitHandler(cleanup_step(), name="cleanup"): ...main steps... — the cleanup step runs ALWAYS, even if main steps fail. Use for: deleting temporary resources, sending failure notifications, saving partial results. (3) Timeout: .set_timeout(3600) — fail the step after 1 hour. Prevents hung steps from consuming resources indefinitely. The retried step gets a fresh pod — no state is preserved between retries.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Retry & Exit Handler
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @dsl.pipeline                                                            │
  │  def robust_pipeline():                                                   │
  │      notify = notify_slack("Pipeline started")                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │      with dsl.ExitHandler(                                                │
  │          exit_task=notify_slack("Pipeline ended"),  ← Always runs      │
  │          name="notification"                                             │
  │      ):                                                                   │
  │          prep = data_prep()\.set_retry(max_retries=2)  ← Retries twice │
  │          train = train_model(prep.output)\.set_timeout(7200)             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RETRY FLOW:                                                              │
  │  Step fails → KFP retries (new pod) → fails again → KFP retries →       │
  │  → 3rd failure → step marked Failed → ExitHandler runs cleanup          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The database-connect step sometimes fails due to transient network issues. With set_retry(max_retries=2), it auto-retries instead of failing the entire pipeline. The ExitHandler sends a Slack notification on success OR failure — the team always knows the pipeline's final status.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: .set_retry(max_retries, backoff_duration) per step. dsl.ExitHandler for cleanup (always runs). .set_timeout for hung steps. Fresh pod per retry.

Pipelines Q166 of 200
How does KFP step caching work and when should you disable it?
A) Caching is always enabled — you cannot disable it; all successful steps are cached permanently
B) Caching saves step outputs in MariaDB — it's limited to 10MB per cached artifact
C) Caching is disabled by default — you must explicitly enable it on every step you want cached
D) Caching computes a hash of inputs + component spec — if a prior run with identical inputs exists, the step is skipped and cached outputs are reused; disable via .set_caching_options(enable_caching=False) for steps that must always run (data pulls, timestamped operations)
✅ Correct Answer: D

KFP caching is enabled by default for all steps. The cache key is a hash of: step inputs, component spec (image, command, args), and pipeline parameters. If you run the same pipeline twice with identical inputs, cached steps execute in milliseconds instead of minutes. Disable caching: step.set_caching_options(enable_caching=False) for: data ingestion steps (always fetch latest data), steps with non-deterministic outputs (random sampling), steps that depend on external state (API calls that return different results each time). Cache staleness: cache never expires automatically — if your data in S3 changes but the URI stays the same, KFP uses stale cache. Workaround: include a timestamp or data version parameter in the step inputs to invalidate cache when data changes.

📝 Detailed Explanation
KFP Step Caching — When to Disable
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ENABLE CACHING (default):           DISABLE CACHING:                     │
  │  ────────────────────────             ────────────────                    │
  │  ✅ Preprocessing (same dataset)      ❌ Data ingestion (fetch latest)    │
  │  ✅ Model training (same hyperparams) ❌ API calls (external state)       │
  │  ✅ Evaluation (same model+data)      ❌ Timestamp generation             │
  │                                        ❌ Random sampling                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  DISABLE: step.set_caching_options(enable_caching=False)                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CACHE INVALIDATION TRICK:                                                │
  │  Include data_version="2026-06-14" as parameter → new hash each day     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The weekly pipeline's data-prep step processes the same 100K job listings. With caching, only the first run takes 2 hours — subsequent runs skip data-prep (same inputs). The data-fetch step has caching disabled — it always pulls the latest job listings. Combined: fetch fresh data (no cache) + prep stable data (cache) + train (cache if same hyperparams).

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Caching = ON by default. Hash of inputs + spec. Disable for data ingestion, API calls, non-deterministic steps. set_caching_options(enable_caching=False).

Pipelines Q167 of 200
How do you test a pipeline component before deploying the full pipeline?
A) You can't — components only run as part of a full pipeline execution on the KFP server
B) Run the Python function directly in a Jupyter notebook or local script with mock inputs — Python function components are just Python functions; test them locally, then verify in a minimal 1-step pipeline in dev before adding to the full DAG
C) Use kubectl exec into the pipeline server pod and run component code manually
D) KFP provides a built-in component test runner — use kfp test-component my_component.py
✅ Correct Answer: B

Testing pipeline components follows a progressive approach: (1) Unit test — Python function components are just Python functions. Call them directly in a notebook: result = prep_data(input_csv="test.csv"). Verify the output shape, types, and values. (2) Integration test — create a minimal 1-step pipeline with only the component you're testing. Upload to KFP, run with test data, verify the step completes and artifact is correct. (3) Full pipeline test — run the complete pipeline in a dev experiment with a small dataset (100 rows instead of 100K). (4) Container components — test the Docker image locally first: docker run my-image python train.py --epochs 1, then as a 1-step pipeline. Pipeline testing is iterative — fix issues at the simplest level before testing in the full DAG.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Progressive Component Testing
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LAYER 1: LOCAL FUNCTION TEST (seconds)                                   │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────                                     │
  │  # In Jupyter notebook                                                    │
  │  result = prep_data(input_csv="test_10rows.csv")                         │
  │  assert len(result.df) == 10                                              │
  │  assert "cleaned_text" in result.df.columns                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  LAYER 2: 1-STEP PIPELINE (1-2 minutes)                                   │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────                                    │
  │  @dsl.pipeline                                                             │
  │  def test_prep():                                                         │
  │      prep_data(input_csv="s3://test/10rows.csv")                         │
  │  → Upload → Run → Verify artifact in S3                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  LAYER 3: FULL PIPELINE (5-30 minutes)                                    │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────                                     │
  │  Run complete 4-step pipeline with small dataset                          │
  │  → Verify end-to-end: data→train→eval→register                           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice tests her new "skill-extractor" component locally in Jupyter with 10 sample resumes. Works perfectly. She creates a 1-step pipeline to test with S3 data — the pod fails because pandas version mismatch. She fixes packages_to_install, re-tests, and only then adds the component to the full 4-step pipeline. This saves hours vs debugging in the full pipeline.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Test Python components locally first (just call the function). Then 1-step pipeline. Then full DAG. Container components: docker run locally, then pipeline test.

Pipelines Q168 of 200
How do you share and reuse pipeline components across multiple pipelines and projects?
A) Components cannot be shared — each pipeline must define all its components inline
B) Package components as a Python library (pip installable), store component YAML in a shared Git repo, or publish to a component registry — then import them in any pipeline using standard Python imports or kfp.components.load_component_from_url()
C) Use kubectl to copy component pods between namespaces — shared components run as cluster-scoped resources
D) KFP automatically discovers components across all projects in the cluster — no sharing configuration needed
✅ Correct Answer: B

Component reuse strategies: (1) Python package — extract component functions into a pip-installable package (anihpj-components). Import in any pipeline: from anihpj_components import data_prep, train_model. (2) Component YAML — compile a component to YAML, store in Git, load at runtime: kfp.components.load_component_from_url("https://github.com/anihpj/components/data-prep.yaml"). (3) Container images — publish component images to a shared registry; any pipeline can reference them. (4) Git submodule — maintain a shared components repo as a Git submodule in each pipeline project. Best practice: one component library (anihpj-ml-components) with versioned releases (v1.0, v1.1). All pipelines import the same version for consistency. Update the library → all pipelines get improvements on next run.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Component Sharing Patterns
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SHARED COMPONENT LIBRARY (anihpj-ml-components v1.2):                   │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  ├─ data_prep.py       # Standard data cleaning for anihpj       │    │
  │  │  ├─ train_model.py     # GPU training with best practices        │    │
  │  │  ├─ evaluate.py        # Model evaluation with anihpj metrics    │    │
  │  │  └─ register.py        # Model Registry integration              │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │       │                          │                          │            │
  │       ▼                          ▼                          ▼            │
  │  ┌──────────┐            ┌──────────┐            ┌──────────┐          │
  │  │Pipeline A│            │Pipeline B│            │Pipeline C│          │
  │  │salary    │            │job-match │            │skill-ext │          │
  │  │predictor │            │training  │            │training  │          │
  │  └──────────┘            └──────────┘            └──────────┘          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The data-prep component is used in 3 pipelines (salary predictor, job matching, skill extraction). Instead of copy-pasting the same 50-line function, it's in anihpj-ml-components. When Alice fixes a bug in data-prep, all 3 pipelines get the fix on their next run. DRY principle for ML pipelines.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Share components via Python packages, component YAML in Git, or shared container images. load_component_from_url() for YAML. Version your component library.

Pipelines Q169 of 200
A compiled pipeline YAML fails to upload with a validation error. What's the systematic debugging approach?
A) Re-write the pipeline from scratch — compilation errors are usually unfixable bugs in the KFP compiler
B) Ignore the error and use kubectl apply instead — KFP upload validation is overly strict
C) Check component decorators for missing required fields, verify all type annotations are from dsl module (not plain Python types for complex objects), ensure component functions are pure Python (no closures, no external state), and validate the generated YAML with a YAML linter for syntax errors
D) Delete the pipeline server and recreate it — upload errors are always caused by server-side corruption
✅ Correct Answer: C

Pipeline compilation/upload debugging checklist: (1) Component decorators — @dsl.component missing required parameter? All inputs must have type annotations. (2) Type annotations — complex types (Dataset, Model) must be imported from kfp.dsl, not plain Python types. (3) Pure functions — components must be pure (no global variables, no file I/O at definition time, no closures capturing mutable state). (4) YAML validation — check generated YAML with python -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(open('pipeline.yaml'))". (5) KFP version — ensure SDK version matches server version (pip show kfp vs server API version). (6) Step-by-step — comment out all steps, add back one at a time to isolate the problematic component. Most errors are simple: typo in decorator, missing type annotation, or SDK/server version mismatch.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Compilation Debugging
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DEBUG FLOW:                                                              │
  │  ──────────                                                               │
  │  1. SYNTAX CHECK                                                          │
  │     $ python -m py_compile pipeline.py                                   │
  │     → Syntax errors? Fix Python first.                                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  2. MINIMAL PIPELINE                                                      │
  │     @dsl.pipeline                                                          │
  │     def test(): pass                                                      │
  │     → Compiles? If not: KFP SDK installation issue.                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  3. ADD STEPS ONE AT A TIME                                               │
  │     Add prep → compile → OK                                               │
  │     Add train → compile → FAIL ← THIS STEP IS THE PROBLEM                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  4. INSPECT THE FAILING COMPONENT                                         │
  │     • Missing type annotation?                                            │
  │     • Wrong import (plain dict vs dsl.Input)?                            │
  │     • Closure capturing external variable?                                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice adds a new component that imports pandas at the module level. Pipeline compilation fails with a cryptic error. She isolates the problem by commenting out steps, finds the issue (module-level import in a component function), moves the import inside the function body, and the pipeline compiles successfully.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Compilation errors: check decorators, type annotations (use dsl types), pure functions (no globals/closures). Isolate by commenting out steps. Verify KFP SDK version matches server.

Pipelines Q170 of 200
What is the complete data science pipeline workflow on OpenShift AI — from notebook to automated production?
A) Write code in Jupyter → manually run each cell → copy results to production — pipelines are optional automation
B) Define pipeline in YAML → kubectl apply → Argo Workflows runs it — Python SDK is only for prototyping
C) Pipelines only handle training — data prep and deployment are separate manual processes outside the pipeline
D) Prototype in Workbench (Jupyter/VS Code) → codify as KFP pipeline (@dsl.pipeline with components) → compile to Argo YAML → upload to pipeline server → create Recurring Run (cron schedule) → each run: data prep → train → evaluate → register model → trigger KServe deployment → monitor with TrustyAI → drift triggers retraining — the full closed-loop MLOps cycle
✅ Correct Answer: D

The complete pipeline workflow closes the MLOps loop: (1) EXPERIMENT — Data scientist prototypes in JupyterLab workbench, exploring data, testing model architectures. (2) CODIFY — Working code becomes KFP components (@dsl.component / @dsl.container_component), composed into a pipeline with @dsl.pipeline. (3) AUTOMATE — Pipeline compiled, uploaded, configured as a Recurring Run (e.g., weekly). (4) EXECUTE — Each scheduled run: data ingestion → preprocessing → training → evaluation → model registration. (5) DEPLOY — Registered model promoted to Production → KServe InferenceService updated (canary rollout). (6) MONITOR — TrustyAI tracks drift, bias, performance metrics. (7) CLOSE LOOP — Drift alert → trigger pipeline retraining on fresh data. This is the "AI factory" — models continuously improve without manual intervention. The pipeline is the automation backbone connecting workbenches (Cat 2), models (Cat 3), and serving (Cat 3) into a self-improving system.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Complete Pipeline Workflow — The AI Factory
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                         THE AI FACTORY                                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐          │
  │  │WORKBENCH │───▶│PIPELINE  │───▶│REGISTRY  │───▶│KSERVE    │          │
  │  │(Cat 2)   │    │(Cat 4)   │    │(Cat 3)   │    │(Cat 3)   │          │
  │  │Prototype │    │Automate  │    │Govern    │    │Deploy    │          │
  │  └──────────┘    └────┬─────┘    └──────────┘    └────┬─────┘          │
  │       ▲               │                                │                │
  │       │               │  SCHEDULE:                     ▼                │
  │       │               │  cron "0 2 * * 0"      ┌──────────┐           │
  │       │               │  (every Sunday)        │TRUSTYAI  │           │
  │       │               │                        │(Cat 3)   │           │
  │       │               │                        │Monitor   │           │
  │       │               │                        └────┬─────┘           │
  │       │               │                             │                  │
  │       └───────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘                  │
  │                    DRIFT DETECTED → RETRIGGER PIPELINE                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: This is the anihpj AI platform in one diagram. Alice prototypes the salary predictor in Jupyter (Cat 2). Bob codifies it as a KFP pipeline with weekly scheduling (Cat 4). Each run registers a new model version in the Registry (Cat 3). KServe deploys with canary (Cat 3). TrustyAI monitors for drift (Cat 3). When drift is detected, the pipeline auto-retrains. The AI factory runs itself — humans only intervene when metrics degrade beyond thresholds.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Complete pipeline workflow = Workbench (Cat 2) → KFP Pipeline (Cat 4) → Model Registry (Cat 3) → KServe (Cat 3) → TrustyAI (Cat 3) → Retrigger. This is the "big picture" connecting all 4 exam domains.

4.3 Elyra & Visual Pipeline DesignQ171-Q178

Pipelines Q171 of 200
What is Elyra and how does it enable visual pipeline building without coding?
A) Elyra is a standalone desktop application — you install it locally and upload pipeline YAML to OpenShift separately
B) Elyra is a JupyterLab extension providing a visual canvas — drag notebooks/Python scripts onto a canvas, connect them with arrows to define execution order, configure each node's properties (runtime image, env vars, resources), and export as KFP YAML ready for upload to any pipeline server
C) Elyra is a CLI tool that generates pipeline code from natural language descriptions — you describe what you want in English
D) Elyra replaces JupyterLab entirely — it's a separate IDE for pipeline development with no notebook support
✅ Correct Answer: B

Elyra democratizes pipeline creation. Data scientists who don't know Python/KFP SDK can still build production pipelines visually. Workflow: (1) Create notebooks — each notebook does one pipeline step (data-prep.ipynb, train.ipynb, evaluate.ipynb). (2) Open Elyra canvas — JupyterLab sidebar → Elyra → Pipeline Editor. (3) Drag and connect — drag notebook files onto canvas, draw arrows to define dependencies. (4) Configure properties — each node: runtime image (container to run the notebook), environment variables, CPU/memory, output files. (5) Export — generates KFP YAML that can be uploaded to any KFP server. Elyra is built into the ODH workbench images — no separate installation. The generated YAML is standard KFP — can be version-controlled, shared, and runs identically to hand-coded pipelines.

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice the data scientist doesn't need to learn KFP SDK. She creates 4 notebooks for her workflow, opens Elyra, drags them onto the canvas, connects them, configures GPU for the training node, and exports. The ML engineer reviews the generated YAML and deploys it. Elyra bridges the gap between data scientists (notebooks) and ML engineers (production pipelines).

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Elyra = visual pipeline builder in JupyterLab. Drag notebooks → connect → configure → export KFP YAML. Built into ODH workbench images. No coding required.

Pipelines Q172 of 200
How do you configure Elyra runtime images and what are the common pitfalls?
A) Configure a Runtime Configuration pointing to the pipeline server URL — each node then needs a Runtime Image (container image that executes the notebook); common pitfalls: forgetting to specify the runtime image (export fails), using an image without papermill installed (notebook execution fails), or pointing to an inaccessible registry
B) Runtime images are auto-detected from the notebook metadata — Elyra reads the kernel spec and selects the matching image automatically
C) Runtime images are configured globally in the pipeline server — all Elyra pipelines share the same execution image
D) Elyra only works with the default ODH workbench image — custom images are not supported for notebook execution
✅ Correct Answer: A

Elyra requires two configurations: (1) Runtime Configuration — the connection to your pipeline server. Set in JupyterLab Settings → Elyra → Runtime Configurations. Specify: KFP API endpoint URL, authentication type (DEX or OAuth), namespace. (2) Node Runtime Image — each node in the canvas needs a container image that will execute the notebook. The image MUST have papermill installed (Elyra uses papermill to execute notebooks programmatically). Common ODH images already include it. If you use a custom image, ensure papermill is in requirements.txt. Pitfall #1: empty runtime image field → export fails with validation error. Pitfall #2: image exists but no papermill → notebook step fails with "papermill: command not found." Pitfall #3: image from private registry but no imagePullSecrets → ImagePullBackOff.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Elyra Runtime Configuration
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RUNTIME CONFIGURATION (global):                                          │
  │  ──────────────────────────────                                            │
  │  Name: anihpj-pipeline-server                                             │
  │  URL: https://ds-pipeline-anihpj.apps.cluster.com                        │
  │  Auth: DEX / OAuth                                                        │
  │  Namespace: anihpj                                                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  NODE PROPERTIES (per node):                                              │
  │  ──────────────────────────                                                │
  │  Runtime Image: quay.io/opendatahub/workbench-images:2024a               │
  │  ← MUST include papermill!                                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Env Vars:                                                                │
  │  POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret123                                              │
  │  AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAXXXX                                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CPU: 2    Memory: 8Gi    GPU: 0                                         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice's first Elyra export failed because she left the Runtime Image field empty on the evaluate node. After adding the ODH workbench image, the export succeeded. Second attempt: the pipeline ran but the train step failed — her custom image didn't have papermill. She added papermill to the Dockerfile, rebuilt, and the pipeline ran flawlessly.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Elyra needs: Runtime Config (pipeline server URL) + Runtime Image per node (must have papermill). Empty runtime image = export failure. Missing papermill = step failure.

Pipelines Q173 of 200
How does Elyra handle data passing between notebook steps in a visual pipeline?
A) Elyra passes data through shared memory between pods — notebooks share a common filesystem managed by Elyra
B) Data is embedded in the pipeline YAML — Elyra serializes notebook outputs directly into the workflow definition
C) Each notebook reads inputs from environment variables or S3 paths set by Elyra, and writes outputs to S3 — Elyra configures the KFP artifacts system so downstream notebooks access upstream outputs via S3 URIs passed as pipeline parameters
D) Elyra doesn't support data passing — each notebook is independent and must handle its own data I/O
✅ Correct Answer: C

Elyra leverages KFP's artifact system for data passing between notebook steps. When you connect notebook A → notebook B in Elyra: (1) Execution — notebook A runs in its pod, reads input from S3 (via env vars), produces output files. (2) Artifact storage — Elyra/KFP stores A's output files in S3/MinIO as pipeline artifacts. (3) Passing — Elyra passes the S3 URIs of A's outputs as environment variables to notebook B's pod. (4) Consumption — notebook B reads the S3 paths from environment variables and loads the data. Notebook authors use os.getenv("INPUT_DATA") to get upstream outputs. The actual data files are in S3 — only URIs are passed between steps. This is the same mechanism as KFP SDK pipelines — Elyra just automates the artifact wiring.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Data Passing in Elyra Pipelines
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Notebook A (data-prep.ipynb):           Notebook B (train.ipynb):        │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ df = pd.read_csv(...)       │         │ ds_path = os.getenv(        │  │
  │  │ df.to_parquet("/tmp/out")  │         │   "INPUT_DATA")  ← Elyra   │  │
  │  │ ← Elyra uploads to S3     │         │ df = pd.read_parquet(       │  │
  │  └────────────┬───────────────┘         │   ds_path)                   │  │
  │               │                          └────────────────────────────┘  │
  │               │  S3 URI passed as env var                                 │
  │               └──────────────────────────▶                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ELYRA AUTO-GENERATES:                                                    │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                     │
  │  Node A output → S3: s3://anihpj/artifacts/run-42/prep-output.parquet   │
  │  Node B env: INPUT_DATA=s3://anihpj/artifacts/run-42/prep-output.parquet │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice's data-prep notebook outputs a cleaned parquet file. She doesn't need to worry about how the train notebook gets it — Elyra handles the S3 upload and passes the URI automatically. She just uses os.getenv("INPUT_DATA") in her train notebook and it works. This abstraction lets her focus on ML, not data plumbing.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Elyra passes S3 URIs as env vars between notebook steps. Same mechanism as KFP artifacts. Notebooks use os.getenv() to read upstream outputs. Data files in S3, URIs in env vars.

Pipelines Q174 of 200
What are common Elyra export errors and how do you resolve them?
A) Elyra export always succeeds — errors only occur at pipeline runtime, never at export time
B) All Elyra errors are caused by network issues — check your internet connection and retry the export
C) Export errors require reinstalling the Elyra extension — they're always caused by corrupted JupyterLab extensions
D) Missing Runtime Image (most common), invalid env var format (must be KEY=VALUE per line), missing output file paths, circular dependencies (A→B→A), and incompatible node types — check each node's property inspector; the error message typically identifies which node has the problem
✅ Correct Answer: D

Elyra export errors by frequency: (1) Missing Runtime Image (60% of errors) — at least one node has an empty Runtime Image field. Check each node's properties. (2) Invalid env var format (20%) — env vars must be "KEY=VALUE" one per line. "KEY VALUE" (space, no equals) or "KEY: VALUE" (colon) will fail. (3) Missing output files (10%) — every node needs at least one output file specified. (4) Circular dependencies (5%) — A depends on B, B depends on A. Elyra detects this and shows an error. (5) Incompatible node types (5%) — mixing Python scripts and notebooks incorrectly. Fix approach: read the error message (it names the problematic node), open that node's properties, fix the issue, re-export. Export errors are almost always configuration, not code.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Elyra Export Error Troubleshooting
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ERROR: "Failed to export pipeline: Node 'train-model.ipynb' has        │
  │          invalid runtime image configuration"                           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  FIX: Click train-model.ipynb node → Properties → Runtime Image         │
  │       → Fill in: quay.io/opendatahub/workbench-images:2024a            │
  │       → Re-export → Success!                                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  QUICK CHECKLIST PER NODE:                                                │
  │  ✅ Runtime Image: filled in                                             │
  │  ✅ Output Files: at least one specified                                  │
  │  ✅ Env Vars: KEY=VALUE format (one per line)                            │
  │  ✅ Dependencies: no cycles (A→B→A)                                      │
  │  ✅ Node type: matches file extension (.ipynb for notebooks)             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice's first pipeline export fails. She reads the error: "Node 'evaluate-model.ipynb' has missing output files." She opens the node properties, adds "evaluate-output.ipynb" as the output file, re-exports — success. The error message told her exactly what to fix.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Elyra export errors = config issues, not code. Check: Runtime Image, Output Files, Env Var format (KEY=VALUE), no cycles. Error message names the failing node.

Pipelines Q175 of 200
When should you use Elyra vs writing KFP SDK Python code directly?
A) Elyra: rapid prototyping, data scientists who prefer visual tools, notebook-based workflows, simple linear/conditional DAGs. KFP SDK: complex pipelines with loops (ParallelFor), dynamic DAGs, programmatic parameter logic, CI/CD integration, reusable component libraries — both produce the same KFP YAML and can coexist
B) Elyra is always better — visual tools replace coding entirely for all pipeline complexity levels
C) KFP SDK is always better — visual tools are toys and cannot be used for production pipelines
D) Use Elyra for training pipelines only — deployment pipelines must use the KFP SDK because Elyra can't handle GPU configuration
✅ Correct Answer: A

Elyra and KFP SDK are complementary, not competing. Elyra strengths: zero-code pipeline creation, ideal for data scientists, notebook-centric workflows, quick prototyping. Limitation: limited support for complex control flow (nested loops, dynamic DAG branching). KFP SDK strengths: full Python expressiveness (dsl.ParallelFor, dsl.Condition, dsl.ExitHandler), dynamic parameter logic, reusable components as Python packages, Git-friendly (text files). Limitation: steeper learning curve. Coexistence: Alice prototypes in Elyra, exports YAML. Bob reviews the YAML, may convert to KFP SDK for complex additions while keeping simple steps as Elyra-generated. Both produce standard KFP YAML that runs on the same pipeline server. Choose based on complexity and team skills, not ideology.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Elyra vs KFP SDK — Decision Guide
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  USE ELYRA WHEN:                     USE KFP SDK WHEN:                    │
  │  ──────────────                      ────────────────                     │
  │  ✅ Notebook-based workflow          ✅ Complex control flow              │
  │  ✅ Data scientist is the author     ✅ ML engineer is the author         │
  │  ✅ Simple DAG (linear/conditional)  ✅ dsl.ParallelFor (loop steps)     │
  │  ✅ Rapid prototyping                ✅ CI/CD integration needed          │
  │  ✅ Visual design preference         ✅ Reusable component library        │
  │  ✅ Team without Python expertise    ✅ Dynamic parameter logic           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BOTH produce valid KFP YAML → runs on same pipeline server              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice builds 80% of pipelines in Elyra (data cleaning, simple training DAGs). Bob handles the 20% complex cases in KFP SDK (hyperparameter grid search with ParallelFor, dynamic model selection). Both pipelines run on the same server, in the same project. The team uses the right tool for each job.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Elyra = visual, notebook-based, simple DAGs. KFP SDK = code, complex DAGs (loops/conditions), CI/CD. Both produce KFP YAML. Choose by complexity and team skills.

Pipelines Q176 of 200
How does papermill integrate with Elyra for parameterized notebook execution?
A) Papermill is an alternative to Elyra — you use one or the other, not both together
B) Papermill converts notebooks to Python scripts before execution — Elyra pipelines run .py files, not .ipynb
C) Elyra uses papermill under the hood to execute notebooks with injected parameters — you tag a notebook cell with "parameters", and Elyra/papermill injects values (from env vars or pipeline parameters) into that cell before executing the notebook as a pipeline step
D) Papermill is only needed for JupyterLab — Elyra doesn't use papermill; it has its own notebook execution engine
✅ Correct Answer: C

Papermill is the execution engine Elyra uses to run notebooks in pipeline steps. Workflow: (1) Tag a cell — in your notebook, add a cell and tag it as "parameters" (JupyterLab → Property Inspector → Cell Tags). (2) Define parameters — in that cell, set variables with defaults: input_path = "s3://default/", learning_rate = 0.001. (3) Elyra injects — when the pipeline runs, Elyra/papermill creates a copy of the notebook with the parameters cell overwritten with actual runtime values (from pipeline parameters or upstream outputs). (4) Execute — papermill runs the modified notebook from top to bottom. This enables the same notebook to work with different parameters per run without modification. The runtime image MUST have papermill installed (pip install papermill).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Papermill Parameter Injection
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  NOTEBOOK (train-model.ipynb):                                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ [Cell 1 — tagged "parameters"]                                    │    │
  │  │ learning_rate = 0.001    ← Default value                         │    │
  │  │ epochs = 10                                                       │    │
  │  │ data_path = "s3://default/"                                       │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │ [Cell 2]                                                          │    │
  │  │ model = train_model(data_path, learning_rate, epochs)            │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  PIPELINE RUN (papermill injects):                                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ [Cell 1 — OVERWRITTEN by papermill]                               │    │
  │  │ learning_rate = 0.0005   ← From pipeline param                   │    │
  │  │ epochs = 20               ← From pipeline param                   │    │
  │  │ data_path = "s3://anihpj/jobs/june/"  ← From upstream step       │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice's train-model.ipynb has a parameters cell with defaults. When the pipeline runs with learning_rate=0.0005, papermill injects this value before execution. She can run the same notebook with 20 different parameter sets without editing a single cell.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Elyra uses papermill for notebook execution. Tag a cell "parameters" with defaults. Papermill overwrites it with runtime values. Runtime image must include papermill.

Pipelines Q177 of 200
How should you version-control Elyra pipelines for team collaboration?
A) Elyra pipelines are stored in the pipeline server database — version control happens automatically
B) Export the pipeline as KFP YAML and commit both the .pipeline file (Elyra canvas) AND the generated YAML to Git — this gives you visual editing history AND deployable artifacts; use branches for experimenting with pipeline variations
C) Elyra pipelines cannot be version-controlled — they exist only in the JupyterLab interface
D) Use the Elyra built-in version history — it tracks all changes automatically like Google Docs
✅ Correct Answer: B

Elyra pipeline version control workflow: (1) Save canvas — Elyra saves the visual layout as a .pipeline file (JSON format, describes nodes and connections). (2) Export YAML — generate the deployable KFP YAML. (3) Commit both — .pipeline file (visual editing history, diffable JSON) + compiled YAML (deployable artifact). (4) Collaborate — team members clone the repo, open .pipeline in their Elyra, modify visually, re-export YAML, commit changes. Git diff on .pipeline shows which nodes were added/removed/changed. The generated YAML diff shows the actual pipeline changes. This dual-file approach gives both human-readable and machine-executable version history.

Elyra Pipeline Version Control

  │  GIT REPO: pipelines/                                                     │
  │  ─────────────                                                             │
  │  ├─ job-matching/                                                         │
