  │  │  ├─ pipeline.yaml          ← Compiled KFP YAML (deployable)           │
  │  │  ├─ data-prep.ipynb        ← Notebook step 1                          │
  │  │  ├─ train-model.ipynb      ← Notebook step 2                          │
  │  │  └─ evaluate.ipynb         ← Notebook step 3                          │
  │  │                                                                       │
  │  WORKFLOW:                                                                 │
  │  git pull → open .pipeline in Elyra → edit → export YAML →               │
  │  git add .pipeline pipeline.yaml → git commit → git push                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice and Bob collaborate on the job-matching pipeline. Alice adds a validation step in Elyra, exports YAML, commits both files. Bob pulls, sees the .pipeline diff (new validation node added), reviews the YAML diff, approves. The pipeline evolves with full Git history — who changed what, when, and why.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Version-control both .pipeline (Elyra canvas) AND compiled YAML in Git. .pipeline diffs show visual changes. YAML diffs show actual pipeline changes.

Pipelines Q178 of 200
What is the complete Elyra-to-production workflow — from canvas to automated pipeline?
A) Draw pipeline on canvas → click "Run" → it goes to production. Elyra handles deployment automatically.
B) Export YAML → kubectl apply → done. No further steps needed for production pipeline management.
C) Design on Elyra canvas → export KFP YAML → commit YAML + .pipeline to Git → upload to pipeline server (UI or SDK) → create Experiment → test with small dataset → create Recurring Run (cron schedule) → monitor runs in KFP UI → iterate by editing in Elyra, re-exporting, committing, and re-uploading new versions
D) Elyra pipelines are for prototyping only — production pipelines must be rewritten in KFP SDK from scratch
✅ Correct Answer: C

The Elyra-to-production lifecycle: (1) Design — drag notebooks onto canvas, connect, configure properties (runtime image, env vars, resources). (2) Export — generate KFP YAML from the visual design. (3) Version — commit .pipeline + .yaml to Git for team review and history. (4) Upload — via KFP UI (Upload Pipeline button) or SDK (client.upload_pipeline()). (5) Test — create Experiment, run with small test dataset, verify outputs. (6) Schedule — if tests pass, create Recurring Run with production cron schedule. (7) Monitor — watch runs in KFP UI, check metrics, inspect artifacts. (8) Iterate — when changes needed, edit in Elyra, re-export, commit new version, upload as new pipeline version. The Elyra-generated YAML is production-grade — it runs the same Argo Workflows engine as hand-coded pipelines.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Elyra → Production Workflow
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DESIGN ──▶ EXPORT ──▶ GIT ──▶ UPLOAD ──▶ TEST ──▶ SCHEDULE ──▶ MONITOR│
  │  (Elyra)    (YAML)    (commit)  (KFP)     (dev)    (cron)      (UI)    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ITERATE: Edit Elyra → Re-export → Git commit → Upload new version      │
  │  Each iteration tracked in Git with visual (.pipeline) + code (YAML)    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice designs the job-matching pipeline in Elyra, exports YAML, commits to Git. Bob reviews the PR, approves, uploads to the production pipeline server, creates a Recurring Run. The pipeline runs every Sunday. When Alice wants to add a validation step, she opens the .pipeline in Elyra, adds the node, re-exports, commits. The new version is uploaded and the Recurring Run uses it next Sunday.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Elyra→production: Design→Export→Git→Upload→Test→Schedule→Monitor. Elyra YAML is production-grade. Iterate by editing canvas, re-exporting, uploading new version.

4.4 Pipeline Execution & SchedulingQ179-Q190

Pipelines Q179 of 200
What happens during a pipeline run lifecycle — from trigger to completion?
A) The pipeline runs synchronously in the client process — triggering code blocks until the pipeline completes
B) KFP converts the pipeline to a single Kubernetes Job — all steps run sequentially in one pod
C) Pipeline runs are simulated first — KFP dry-runs the DAG, then executes only if all steps pass validation
D) Trigger → KFP creates a Run record in MariaDB → Argo parses the Workflow YAML → creates pods for each step respecting DAG dependencies → each step pod runs its container → outputs saved to S3/MinIO → on step completion, Argo triggers downstream steps → Run status updated → metrics/artifacts recorded → Run marked Succeeded/Failed
✅ Correct Answer: D

The pipeline run lifecycle: (1) Trigger — UI click, SDK call, or cron schedule creates a Run record in MariaDB with status "Pending." (2) Argo submission — KFP submits the compiled Argo Workflow YAML to Argo. (3) Pod creation — Argo creates pods for steps with no dependencies (first tier of DAG). Each pod gets: container spec, env vars, resource limits, S3 credentials. (4) Step execution — pod runs the container (component image + command). Container writes outputs to local path; KFP agent uploads to S3/MinIO as artifacts. (5) Dependency resolution — when a step's upstream dependencies complete, Argo creates the downstream step's pod with input artifact URIs injected. (6) Completion — all steps done → Run status "Succeeded." Any step fails → downstream skipped → Run "Failed." Entire lifecycle visible in KFP UI with real-time DAG status coloring.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Run Lifecycle
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TRIGGER ──▶ PENDING ──▶ RUNNING ──▶ SUCCEEDED / FAILED                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  PENDING:                                                                 │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ MariaDB: Run #143, status=Pending, params={lr:0.001}              │    │
  │  │ Argo: Workflow submitted, pods not yet created                    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RUNNING:                                                                 │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  [prep ████████████] ✅ Done (45s)                                 │    │
  │  │  [train ████████████████████] ⏳ Running (est. 10m)               │    │
  │  │  [evaluate] ⏸ Pending (waiting for train)                        │    │
  │  │  [register] ⏸ Pending (waiting for evaluate)                     │    │
  │  │  S3: prep-output.parquet uploaded ✅                              │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SUCCEEDED:                                                               │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ All steps ✅ → metrics recorded → artifacts saved → Run green    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice triggers a pipeline run and watches the DAG in KFP UI. The prep step finishes in 45 seconds (green), training starts (spinning), eval and register are gray (waiting). After 12 minutes, all steps are green and the model is registered. She can see exactly where time is spent and which step failed if something goes wrong.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Pipeline lifecycle: Trigger → Pending → Running → Succeeded/Failed. Argo manages pod creation respecting DAG. KFP UI shows real-time status. Artifacts in S3, metadata in MariaDB.

Pipelines Q180 of 200
How do you pass different parameter values to each pipeline run without modifying the pipeline code?
A) Edit the pipeline Python file and recompile before each run — parameters are hardcoded in the pipeline definition
B) Define typed parameters in @dsl.pipeline function signature with defaults — when triggering a run (UI or SDK), override any parameter value; KFP injects the overridden values at runtime without recompiling the pipeline
C) Use environment variables in the container spec — parameters are passed through Kubernetes ConfigMaps
D) Parameters are fixed at upload time — once a pipeline is uploaded, parameters cannot be changed per run
✅ Correct Answer: B

KFP parameters enable "compile once, run many times with different settings." The pipeline function signature defines parameters: def my_pipeline(learning_rate: float = 0.001, epochs: int = 10, data_path: str = "s3://default/"). These become a form in the KFP UI — each field shows the default value, editable before triggering. Via SDK: client.run_pipeline(params={"learning_rate": 0.0005, "epochs": 20}). The pipeline YAML is compiled once, uploaded once, but run with infinite parameter combinations. This is how hyperparameter tuning works: same pipeline, 50 runs, each with different learning rates and epochs. Parameters appear in the KFP UI Run Details for comparison. You can also set parameters in Recurring Runs — each scheduled execution uses the configured parameters.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Parameters — Compile Once, Run Many
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  COMPILE & UPLOAD (once):                                                 │
  │  ────────────────────────                                                  │
  │  @dsl.pipeline                                                             │
  │  def train_pipeline(                                                      │
  │      learning_rate: float = 0.001,   ← Default                           │
  │      epochs: int = 10,               ← Default                           │
  │      use_gpu: bool = True                                                 │
  │  ):                                                                        │
  │      ...                                                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RUNS (many, different params):                                           │
  │  ──────────────────────────────                                            │
  │  Run #1: lr=0.001, epochs=10  (defaults)                                  │
  │  Run #2: lr=0.0005, epochs=20 (overridden)                               │
  │  Run #3: lr=0.01, epochs=5     (overridden)                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  All runs use the same pipeline YAML — only params differ.               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice compiles the training pipeline once. She runs it 20 times with different learning rates for hyperparameter tuning — each run in the same experiment, parameters visible in the comparison table. She finds the best parameters without ever modifying or recompiling the pipeline.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Pipeline parameters = typed function args with defaults. Override per run via UI or SDK. Compile once, run many. Parameters visible in Run Details for comparison.

Pipelines Q181 of 200
How do you implement parallel execution of independent pipeline steps?
A) KFP pipelines are always sequential — parallel execution requires manually creating multiple pipelines
B) Add a "parallel: true" flag to each step decorator — KFP automatically parallelizes all flagged steps
C) Steps without dependencies on each other are automatically parallelized by Argo — if step A and step B both depend on prep but not on each other, Argo runs them simultaneously as separate pods; use dsl.ParallelFor for dynamic fan-out parallelism over a list
D) Parallel execution requires a special pipeline server configuration — it's opt-in at the server level
✅ Correct Answer: C

KFP/Ago automatically parallelizes independent steps. In the pipeline DAG, if step A and step B both depend on `prep` but not on each other, Argo creates pods for both simultaneously. This is implicit parallelism — you don't need to declare it. dsl.ParallelFor enables explicit dynamic parallelism: loop over a list and run a step for each item in parallel. Example: train 5 models with different architectures simultaneously. with dsl.ParallelFor(items=["resnet", "bert", "xgboost"]): train_model(architecture=item) — Argo creates 3 pods running in parallel, each training a different model. Results are collected as a list. This is critical for hyperparameter tuning: run 50 training jobs in parallel instead of sequentially (50x speedup). Configure parallelism parameter on ParallelFor to limit concurrent executions.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Parallelism
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  IMPLICIT PARALLELISM:               EXPLICIT (ParallelFor):              │
  │  ────────────────────                ────────────────────────             │
  │         ┌───┐                              ┌───┐                          │
  │    ┌───▶│ A │                        ┌───▶│lr=0.001│                     │
  │    │    └───┘                        │    └───┘                          │
  │  ┌─┴─┐                               │                                    │
  │  │prep│  A and B run simultaneously   │    ┌───┐                          │
  │  └─┬─┘                               ├───▶│lr=0.01│                      │
  │    │    ┌───┐                        │    └───┘                          │
  │    └───▶│ B │                        │                                    │
  │         └───┘                        │    ┌───┐                          │
  │                                       └───▶│lr=0.1│                       │
  │                                            └───┘                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ParallelFor(items=[0.001, 0.01, 0.1]): 3 parallel pods                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The hyperparameter tuning pipeline uses ParallelFor to train 20 models simultaneously (different learning rates). Instead of 20 × 15 min = 5 hours sequential, all 20 run in parallel finishing in ~20 minutes. The cluster scales up GPU nodes to handle the load, then scales down when done.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Independent steps = auto-parallel (implicit). dsl.ParallelFor = dynamic fan-out over list. Use for hyperparameter tuning, cross-validation, ensemble training. parallelism param limits concurrency.

Pipelines Q182 of 200
How do you implement conditional branching in a KFP pipeline for ML-specific logic?
A) Use dsl.Condition with a runtime-evaluated expression referencing step outputs — if accuracy > threshold, deploy; elif accuracy > minimum, canary at 10%; else abort and notify — conditions evaluate actual run values, not compile-time constants
B) Use Python if/elif/else in the pipeline function — KFP executes the Python code at compile time, so conditions must be statically resolvable
C) Create three separate pipelines for each branch and manually choose which to run — KFP doesn't support branching
D) Use Kubernetes labels to control execution — label pods with the branch name and use nodeSelector to route execution
✅ Correct Answer: A

dsl.Condition enables runtime branching based on actual step outputs. The condition expression references step outputs (e.g., eval.outputs["accuracy"] > 0.85) and evaluates at runtime when the step completes. Multi-branch: use nested Conditions or elif-style chaining. Key distinction: Python if/else in the pipeline function body runs at COMPILE time (determines DAG structure). dsl.Condition runs at RUNTIME (determines execution path). You can combine them: use Python if to optionally include steps in the DAG (different pipeline versions), use dsl.Condition for runtime ML gating. For ML: if accuracy > 0.90 → full deploy, elif > 0.80 → canary 10%, else → notify and stop.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Conditional Branching for ML Gating
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @dsl.pipeline                                                            │
  │  def ml_pipeline():                                                       │
  │      eval = evaluate(train.outputs["model"])                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │      with dsl.Condition(eval.outputs["accuracy"] > 0.90, "full-deploy"):│
  │          deploy_full(train.outputs["model"])   ← >90%: go to prod       │
  │                                                                          │
  │      with dsl.Condition(eval.outputs["accuracy"] <= 0.90, "check-min"): │
  │          with dsl.Condition(eval.outputs["accuracy"] > 0.80, "canary"): │
  │              deploy_canary(train.outputs["model"])  ← 80-90%: canary   │
  │          with dsl.Condition(eval.outputs["accuracy"] <= 0.80, "abort"): │
  │              notify_abort()  ← <80%: reject                             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Three-tier deployment gating: accuracy > 90% → full production deploy. 80-90% → canary at 10% (monitor before promoting). < 80% → abort and notify. This prevents marginal models from reaching users while still allowing good-but-not-great models to be tested via canary.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: dsl.Condition = runtime branching (evaluates step outputs). Python if = compile-time branching (determines DAG). Use dsl.Condition for ML quality gates. Nested conditions for multi-tier logic.

Pipelines Q183 of 200
How do you inspect pipeline artifacts after a run completes?
A) Artifacts are internal to KFP — they can only be accessed by downstream pipeline steps, not by users
B) Download the entire S3 bucket — artifacts are not organized by run and must be found manually
C) KFP UI → Run Details → Artifacts tab shows all input/output artifacts with names, types, and download links; or use the SDK: run = client.get_run(run_id); for artifact in run.outputs: download from S3 URI — artifacts are organized by run for easy inspection
D) Artifacts are only accessible during the run — they're deleted when the run completes to save storage
✅ Correct Answer: C

Artifact inspection is critical for debugging and model selection. KFP UI: Open a completed run → Artifacts tab → each step's inputs and outputs listed with: artifact name, type (Dataset/Model/Metrics), preview (first few rows of Dataset), and download button. SDK: run = client.get_run(run_id); run.outputs.artifacts returns artifact metadata including S3 URIs. Direct S3: artifacts stored at s3://bucket/artifacts/{pipeline-name}/{run-id}/{step-name}/{artifact-name}. Metrics: rendered as charts in UI (scalar = number, ClassificationMetrics = confusion matrix, HTML = inline). Artifacts persist after run completion — you can compare artifacts from runs months apart. This is how you verify: "did the preprocessing step actually output the right columns?"

📝 Detailed Explanation
Artifact Inspection Paths
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S3 ARTIFACT STRUCTURE:                                                   │
  │  ──────────────────────                                                    │
  │  s3://anihpj-pipelines/artifacts/                                         │
  │  ├─ job-matching-weekly/                                                  │
  │  │  └─ run-143/                                                           │
  │  │     ├─ data-prep/                                                      │
  │  │     │  └─ output_dataset.parquet    ← Cleaned data                    │
  │  │     ├─ train-model/                                                    │
  │  │     │  └─ model.safetensors         ← Trained weights                 │
  │  │     └─ evaluate/                                                       │
  │  │        └─ metrics.json              ← Accuracy, F1, etc               │
  │  │                                                                       │
  │  SDK: run.outputs.artifacts[0].uri → s3://.../run-143/.../model.safetensors│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice wants to verify the data-prep step's output before trusting the trained model. She opens run #143 in KFP UI, clicks the data-prep step's output artifact, and sees the first 10 rows of the cleaned dataset. Columns look correct, no nulls. She downloads the metrics.json and confirms accuracy: 94.3%. She's confident in promoting this model.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Artifacts: KFP UI Run Details → Artifacts tab → download/view. SDK: run.outputs.artifacts. S3: organized by pipeline/run/step. Persist after run completion.

Pipelines Q184 of 200
How do you integrate KFP pipelines with CI/CD systems like Tekton or GitHub Actions?
A) KFP pipelines replace CI/CD — you don't need Tekton or GitHub Actions when using KFP
B) CI/CD pipeline (Tekton/GitHub Actions) triggers KFP operations via the SDK: on Git push → compile & upload pipeline → create experiment → trigger run with test params → wait for completion → read metrics → if metrics pass threshold, promote model via Registry API — CI/CD orchestrates the MLOps workflow; KFP executes the ML steps
C) CI/CD integration requires a special plugin — KFP doesn't have a standard API for external systems to call
D) Use webhooks to trigger pipeline runs — CI/CD sends HTTP POST to the pipeline server's webhook endpoint
✅ Correct Answer: B

CI/CD + KFP integration pattern: CI/CD (Tekton/GitHub Actions) acts as the outer orchestration loop — it responds to Git events, manages approvals, and coordinates across systems. KFP acts as the inner ML execution loop — it runs the actual data processing and training. Flow: (1) Git push triggers CI/CD. (2) CI/CD installs kfp SDK, authenticates to pipeline server. (3) CI/CD calls client.upload_pipeline() to register new version. (4) CI/CD creates experiment, triggers run with test parameters. (5) CI/CD calls client.wait_for_run_completion(). (6) CI/CD reads run metrics via SDK. (7) If accuracy > threshold, CI/CD calls Model Registry API to promote. (8) CI/CD sends Slack notification with results. This separates concerns: CI/CD handles Git→KFP→Registry orchestration; KFP handles data→train→eval.

📝 Detailed Explanation
CI/CD + KFP Integration
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GIT PUSH                                                                 │
  │     │                                                                      │
  │     ▼                                                                      │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │

  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Every push to main triggers the CI/CD pipeline: upload new pipeline → run with test data → check accuracy → if > 90%, auto-promote to Production. No human clicks. From code commit to model in production in under 30 minutes. This is GitOps for ML.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: CI/CD orchestrates; KFP executes ML. SDK methods: upload_pipeline, run_pipeline, wait_for_run_completion. CI/CD reads metrics, calls Registry API. GitOps for ML.

Pipelines Q185 of 200
What strategies should you use for pipeline failure recovery in production?
A) Delete the failed run and re-trigger — pipeline failures are always transient and fixed by retrying
B) Manually fix the error and resume from the failed step — KFP supports run resumption from failure points
C) Pipeline failures require full pipeline rewrite — there's no recovery mechanism for failed runs
D) Per-step retry with backoff (set_retry), idempotent step design (same input = same output), artifact-based recovery (cached steps skip), ExitHandler notifications, and cluster autoscaling to handle resource exhaustion — most failures are environmental, not code bugs
✅ Correct Answer: D

Production pipeline failure recovery is multi-layered: (1) Automatic retry — .set_retry(max_retries=3, backoff_duration="30s") handles transient failures (network blips, DB timeouts). (2) Idempotency — design steps so running twice with same inputs produces same result and doesn't corrupt state. (3) Caching — if a step succeeded previously with identical inputs, KFP uses cached output (zero cost retry). (4) ExitHandler — always-run cleanup/notification step that alerts the team with: failed step name, error log excerpt, run ID link. (5) Cluster autoscaling — if failure is OOMKilled (data grew), cluster auto-adds larger nodes for next run. (6) Manual intervention — fix root cause (update credential, increase memory limit, correct S3 path), then re-trigger the run. KFP does not support resuming from failed step — the entire run retries.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Failure Recovery Layers
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LAYER 1: AUTO-RETRY (transient failures)                                │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────                                  │
  │  step.set_retry(max_retries=3).set_timeout(3600)                         │
  │  → Network timeout? Retry. DB connection refused? Retry.                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  LAYER 2: CACHING (skip successful steps)                                 │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────                                  │
  │  Step succeeded in previous run → cached output → skip on retry          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  LAYER 3: NOTIFICATION (ExitHandler)                                      │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────                                      │
  │  dsl.ExitHandler(notify_slack()) → team alerted on ANY outcome          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  LAYER 4: MANUAL FIX + RE-TRIGGER                                         │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────                                      │
  │  Fix root cause → client.run_pipeline() with same params → succeeds     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Sunday's pipeline fails with OOMKilled on the training step (data grew from 100K to 500K rows). Retry doesn't help. ExitHandler sends Slack alert. Bob increases memory limit to 64Gi, re-triggers. Cached data-prep and eval steps skip. Only training re-runs — 15 min instead of 25 min. Pipeline succeeds.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Recovery: retry (transient) → caching (skip done) → notify (ExitHandler) → fix + re-trigger. KFP cannot resume from failed step — entire run retries. Idempotent steps prevent corruption.

Pipelines Q186 of 200
How do you manage pipeline versions when you have dev, staging, and production environments?
A) Use separate pipeline servers per environment, Git branches for pipeline code (dev→staging→main), and promote pipeline YAML through environments via CI/CD — each environment has its own pipeline server, experiments, and recurring runs; the Model Registry tracks which pipeline version produced each model
B) Use one pipeline server for all environments — KFP namespaces runs by environment tag automatically
C) Pipeline versioning is handled by the pipeline name — append "-dev" or "-prod" to the pipeline name for each environment
D) KFP has built-in environment support — set KFP_ENV=production and it auto-routes to the correct server
✅ Correct Answer: A

Pipeline environment strategy mirrors application deployment: (1) Pipeline servers — one per environment. Dev server for experimentation, staging for pre-production validation, production for scheduled runs. (2) Git branches — dev branch (experimental changes), staging (validated), main (production-ready). (3) CI/CD promotion — merge dev→staging triggers upload to staging server + test run. Merge staging→main triggers upload to production server + create/update Recurring Run. (4) Model lineage — Model Registry metadata includes pipeline_run_id, linking each model to the exact pipeline version and environment that produced it. This enables answering: "Which pipeline version trained the production model?"

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Environment Strategy
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GIT BRANCHES:          PIPELINE SERVERS:          MODEL REGISTRY:        │
  │  ────────────          ────────────────          ──────────────          │
  │  dev ──────▶ dev server (experiment)                                     │
  │   │           • Ad-hoc runs                                              │
  │   │           • Test with sample data                                    │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │  staging ──▶ staging server (validate)                                   │
  │   │           • Test with full data                                      │
  │   │           • Compare vs current prod                                  │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │  main ─────▶ production server (live)                                    │
  │              • Recurring Run (cron)                                      │
  │              • Auto-register to Registry                                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Alice experiments on the dev server (branch: dev). When ready, she opens PR to staging. CI/CD uploads to staging server, runs with full dataset. Metrics look good → merge to main → CI/CD uploads to production server, updates Recurring Run. Next Sunday, production runs the new pipeline version. Full traceability: which Git commit → which pipeline version → which model.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Pipeline versioning: separate servers per env, Git branches promote via CI/CD. Model Registry tracks pipeline_run_id for lineage. Dev→Staging→Prod promotion flow.

Pipelines Q187 of 200
How do pipeline templates accelerate ML workflow creation across teams?
A) KFP has a built-in template gallery — browse and one-click deploy pre-built pipelines from the UI
B) Templates are not supported — each pipeline must be written from scratch for its specific use case
C) Create a base pipeline class/factory function with common steps (data validation, training loop, evaluation, registration) — teams extend it with their specific model logic; store in a shared component library; parameterize everything so the same template serves classification, regression, and NLP use cases
D) Use Elyra templates — save a .pipeline file as a template and reuse it by changing notebook references
✅ Correct Answer: C

Pipeline templates standardize ML workflows across teams. Pattern: (1) Base pipeline factory — def create_training_pipeline(data_source, model_trainer, eval_metrics, deploy_target) returns a configured @dsl.pipeline. (2) Common steps — data validation, preprocessing, training loop, evaluation, conditional deployment gate. These are the same for 90% of ML projects. (3) Extension points — teams inject their specific: data source (S3 path, DB query), model trainer (PyTorch, TensorFlow, XGBoost), evaluation metrics (accuracy, MAE, F1), deployment target (KServe InferenceService name). (4) Shared library — template in anihpj-ml-components, all teams import it. Benefits: consistency (all pipelines have validation gates, notifications, versioning), reduced onboarding (new team = new model_trainer implementation), compliance (audit trail built into template).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Template Pattern
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TEMPLATE (anihpj-ml-components):                                         │
  │  ────────────────────────────────                                          │
  │  def ml_training_pipeline(                                                │
  │      data_source: Callable,       ← Team-specific data fetcher           │
  │      model_trainer: Callable,     ← Team-specific training logic         │
  │      eval_metrics: List[str],     ← [\"accuracy\", \"f1\"] or [\"mae\"]    │
  │      deploy_target: str           ← KServe InferenceService name         │
  │  ) -> dsl.Pipeline:                                                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │      # COMMON STEPS (same for all teams):                                 │
  │      validate = validate_data(data_source())                             │
  │      train = model_trainer(validate.output)                               │
  │      eval = evaluate(train.output, metrics=eval_metrics)                 │
  │      with dsl.Condition(eval.outputs[\"score\"] > threshold):             │
  │          register(train.output)                                           │
  │          deploy(deploy_target)                                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  TEAM-SPECIFIC (just implement callbacks):                                │
  │  salary_team: ml_training_pipeline(                                       │
  │      data_source=fetch_salary_data,                                       │
  │      model_trainer=train_xgboost_regressor,                              │
  │      eval_metrics=[\"mae\", \"rmse\"],                                     │
  │      deploy_target=\"salary-predictor\"                                   │
  │  )                                                                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Three teams need pipelines: salary prediction, job matching, skill extraction. Instead of 3 completely different pipelines, they use the same template with different callbacks. When Bob improves the validation step in the template, ALL three teams get the improvement on their next pipeline upload. Standardized quality, reduced maintenance.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Pipeline templates = factory functions with callbacks for team-specific logic. Common steps: validate→train→eval→gate→deploy. Share via component library. DRY for ML pipelines.

Pipelines Q188 of 200
How do you orchestrate multiple pipelines that depend on each other?
A) Pipelines cannot depend on each other — each pipeline is independent and isolated
B) Use the KFP SDK in a parent pipeline or external orchestrator — Pipeline A's completion triggers Pipeline B via SDK call; pass data through S3 artifacts with known paths; use Model Registry events (\"model registered\" → trigger deployment pipeline); or use Argo Workflows' DAG-of-DAGs pattern
C) Nest pipelines inside each other — KFP supports sub-pipeline composition natively with dsl.SubPipeline
D) Use a single monolithic pipeline — splitting into multiple pipelines is an anti-pattern
✅ Correct Answer: B

Multi-pipeline orchestration patterns: (1) SDK chaining — CI/CD or parent pipeline calls client.run_pipeline() for Pipeline A, waits for completion, then triggers Pipeline B with A's output artifacts. (2) S3 contract — Pipeline A writes outputs to known S3 path; Pipeline B reads from that path (configured as parameter). (3) Event-driven — Model Registry event (\"new model registered\") triggers deployment pipeline. (4) Argo DAG-of-DAGs — Argo Workflows natively supports submitting child workflows from parent workflows. KFP pipelines ARE Argo workflows — you can submit one pipeline from another using Argo's workflow template reference. KFP does NOT have a built-in sub-pipeline feature in v2. The recommended pattern: use CI/CD (Tekton) as the top-level orchestrator that chains multiple KFP pipeline executions with dependency management.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Multi-Pipeline Orchestration
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n  │  CI/CD ORCHESTRATOR (Tekton):                                             │\n  │  ───────────────────────────                                               │\n  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │\n  │  │  Step 1: Run data-pipeline (fetch + clean + validate)             │    │\n  │  │         → Output: s3://anihpj/processed/2026-06-14/              │    │\n  │  │                                                                    │    │\n  │  │  Step 2: Run training-pipeline (with data from Step 1)            │    │\n  │  │         → Output: model registered as \"salary-predictor/v4\"      │    │\n  │  │                                                                    │    │\n  │  │  Step 3: Run evaluation-pipeline (with model from Step 2)         │    │\n  │  │         → Metrics: accuracy 94.3%                                 │    │\n  │  │                                                                    │    │\n  │  │  Step 4: If metrics > threshold → promote model → deploy          │    │\n  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │\n  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
\n

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The data engineering team maintains a data-pipeline (daily S3 cleanup). The ML team's training-pipeline depends on fresh data. CI/CD orchestrates: run data-pipeline → wait → run training-pipeline with fresh data path. If data-pipeline fails, training-pipeline never runs. Dependency management without monolithic pipelines.

\n

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Multi-pipeline orchestration: CI/CD chains pipelines via SDK. No built-in sub-pipeline in KFP v2. Use S3 contracts or Model Registry events for coupling. Tekton/Argo for top-level orchestration.

Pipelines Q189 of 200
What are the top 5 pipeline execution best practices for production reliability?
A) (1) Idempotent steps (same input = same output), (2) Data validation BEFORE expensive training, (3) Per-step retry with backoff for transient failures, (4) ExitHandler notifications for all outcomes, (5) Caching-enabled for repeated steps but disabled for data ingestion — these 5 prevent the most common production pipeline failures
B) Use the largest possible GPU for all steps, run as root for fewer permission issues, hardcode credentials for simplicity
C) Best practices don't matter — pipelines either work or they don't; there's no middle ground
D) Run everything in one monolithic step to avoid inter-step communication failures
✅ Correct Answer: A

Production pipeline reliability comes from defensive design: (1) Idempotency — steps produce the same output given the same input. Critical for retries: if a step partially completed (wrote some data to S3) then crashed, the retry must not corrupt data. (2) Early validation — catch bad data BEFORE spending GPU hours. Schema checks, row counts, distribution tests. Fail in 5 seconds, not 30 minutes. (3) Retry with backoff — network blips, DB timeouts, API rate limits are transient. set_retry(max_retries=3, backoff=\"30s\") recovers automatically. (4) ExitHandler notifications — always know pipeline status. Success: metrics summary. Failure: step name + error log. Never silently fail. (5) Selective caching — cache deterministic, expensive steps (preprocessing with same data). Don't cache data ingestion (must be fresh) or API calls (different results each time).

📝 Detailed Explanation
Production Pipeline Reliability Checklist
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ✅ IDEMPOTENT:     f(x) = f(f(x)). Same input → same output.            │
  │  ✅ VALIDATE EARLY: Check data BEFORE GPU. 5s failure > 30min failure.  │
  │  ✅ RETRY:          .set_retry(3) with backoff. Transient errors auto-fix│
  │  ✅ NOTIFY:         ExitHandler → Slack/email on ALL outcomes.          │
  │  ✅ CACHE SMART:    Cache deterministic steps. Don't cache data pulls.   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BONUS:                                                                   │
  │  ✅ TIMEOUT:        .set_timeout(3600). No hung steps burning GPU $$.   │
  │  ✅ RESOURCES:      GPU only for training. CPU for prep/eval.            │
  │  ✅ SECRETS:        K8s Secrets, never pipeline params.                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The weekly pipeline has been running for 6 months with zero unplanned failures because it follows all 5 practices. When the DB password rotated (transient auth failure), retry handled it. When data was accidentally truncated, validation caught it before training. The team sleeps soundly on Saturday nights.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Top 5: Idempotency, Early Validation, Retry with Backoff, ExitHandler Notifications, Smart Caching. These prevent 90% of production pipeline incidents.

Pipelines Q190 of 200
What is the most important mindset shift when moving from notebook-based ML to production KFP pipelines?
A) Pipelines are just automated notebooks — the mindset is the same, just scheduled
B) Production ML requires learning a completely new skillset — discard everything you know about notebooks
C) The only difference is that pipelines run on GPU — everything else works the same as Jupyter
D) Shift from interactive exploration to deterministic automation — every step must be idempotent, parameterized, and independently testable; data passes through artifacts (S3) not memory; failures must be handled gracefully (retry/notify); and the pipeline is a living artifact that evolves via Git version control, not a one-off notebook cell execution
✅ Correct Answer: D

The notebook-to-pipeline mindset shift bridges Cat 2 (Workbenches) and Cat 4 (Pipelines). Notebook thinking: interactive, exploratory, state in memory, manual re-runs. Pipeline thinking: deterministic, automated, state in S3 artifacts, automatic retry/notify. Every step must be idempotent, parameterized, independently testable. The pipeline is a version-controlled living artifact in Git, not a one-off .ipynb file. This mindset shift is what the EX267 exam tests — can you think in production ML patterns?

📝 Detailed Explanation
Notebook vs Pipeline Mindset
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  NOTEBOOK THINKING              PIPELINE THINKING                         │
  │  ────────────────              ────────────────                           │
  │  "Let me try this..."          "This step is tested and versioned"       │
  │  State in memory (df)          State in S3 artifacts                     │
  │  Run top-to-bottom manually    Run automatically on schedule             │
  │  Errors → fix → re-run cell    Errors → retry → notify → fix → re-run   │
  │  Visual inspection             Metrics + artifact comparison             │
  │  One .ipynb file               Git versioned .py + .yaml                 │
  │  "Works on my laptop"          "Works on any K8s pod"                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters: Final question of Cat 4 — the bridge between experimentation (Cat 2) and automation (Cat 4). Alice prototypes in Jupyter, extracts code into KFP components, composes a pipeline, and schedules it. Her notebook was the blueprint; the pipeline is the factory.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Notebook → Pipeline = interactive → deterministic, memory → artifacts, manual → automated, visual → metrics. This mindset shift is the core of MLOps maturity from Cat 2 to Cat 4.

4.5 anihpj Pipeline Scenarios & MLOps IntegrationQ191-Q200

Pipelines Q191 of 200
You need to build an end-to-end pipeline for the anihpj job-matching model that runs weekly. What components should it include?
A) Just a training step — the model can be trained on raw data directly without preprocessing
B) Data ingestion (pull latest job listings from PostgreSQL) → Preprocessing (clean text, extract skills, normalize) → Training (fine-tune sentence transformer on GPU) → Evaluation (compute accuracy vs test set) → Conditional gate (if accuracy > 85%, register in Model Registry and trigger KServe canary deployment; else notify and abort)
C) Download model from Hugging Face → deploy to KServe — pipeline only handles deployment, not training
D) A single notebook that does everything in one cell — pipelines are overkill for weekly retraining
✅ Correct Answer: B

The anihpj job-matching pipeline follows the standard ML training DAG: (1) Ingest — psycopg2 connects to PostgreSQL, pulls job listings with labels (matched/not matched). Uses Data Connection for credentials. (2) Preprocess — pandas cleans text (remove HTML, lowercase), extracts skills via regex, normalizes salary ranges. Outputs: cleaned parquet dataset. (3) Train — loads sentence-transformer base model, fine-tunes on anihpj job pairs. GPU step with .set_gpu_limit(1).set_memory_limit("32Gi"). Outputs: model safetensors. (4) Evaluate — computes accuracy, precision, recall, F1 on held-out test set. Outputs: Metrics artifact. (5) Gate — dsl.Condition(eval.outputs["accuracy"] > 0.85): if true → register model + trigger KServe canary; if false → send Slack notification (ExitHandler) + stop. This DAG runs every Sunday at 2 AM via Recurring Run.

📝 Detailed Explanation
anihpj Job-Matching Pipeline DAG
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  [ingest]──▶[preprocess]──▶[train (GPU)]──▶[evaluate]──▶ accuracy>85%?  │
  │    2m            5m              15m             3m           │          │
  │                                                               ├─YES──▶   │
  │                                                               │ [register]│
  │                                                               │ [deploy]  │
  │                                                               └─NO───▶   │
  │                                                                 [notify] │
  │                                                                  STOP    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SCHEDULE: Recurring Run, cron "0 2 * * 0" (Sunday 2 AM)                │
  │  EXPERIMENT: "job-matching-weekly"                                       │
  │  TOTAL: ~25 minutes per run                                              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters: This is the production anihpj pipeline. Every Sunday, it pulls the latest job listings, retrains the matching model, evaluates quality, and only deploys if accuracy improved. If the new model is worse (bad data week), the pipeline stops and notifies the team. This prevents bad models from reaching production automatically.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Production pipeline = Ingest → Preprocess → Train(GPU) → Evaluate → Conditional Gate → Register → Deploy. dsl.Condition for quality gating. Recurring Run for scheduling.

Pipelines Q192 of 200
How do you implement a RAG pipeline on OpenShift AI that generates job descriptions using the anihpj dataset?
A) The LLM generates everything from memory — no retrieval step is needed for job descriptions
B) RAG runs entirely in one pod — the embedding model, vector database, and LLM are in a single container for simplicity
C) Separate the pipeline into three InferenceServices: (1) Embedding model (CPU, ONNX) converts query to vector, (2) Milvus vector DB retrieves top-3 similar job descriptions, (3) LLM (GPU, vLLM) generates the new description using the retrieved context — orchestrated by a lightweight KFP pipeline that chains these API calls
D) Use Elyra to build the RAG visually — drag a "RAG" node onto the canvas and Elyra auto-configures all components
✅ Correct Answer: C

The anihpj RAG pipeline for job description generation is a multi-service architecture: (1) Embedding Service — KServe InferenceService with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (ONNX, CPU, 500MB). Converts "Senior Python Developer" → 384-dim vector. Latency: 5ms. (2) Vector Database — Milvus standalone deployment with 10K indexed job descriptions. Searches for top-3 most similar descriptions. Latency: 10ms. (3) LLM Service — KServe vLLM with Llama-3-8B (INT4, GPU). Receives: system prompt + 3 retrieved examples + user query → generates tailored job description. Latency: 2-8 seconds. (4) Orchestration — KFP pipeline step that calls embedding API → Milvus API → LLM API, assembles the final response. Each service independently scalable: embedding model always-on (cheap CPU), LLM has minReplicas=2 for GPU throughput.

📝 Detailed Explanation
anihpj RAG Pipeline Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  USER: "Write a JD for Senior Python Developer"                          │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │

  │  │  │ "Senior Python Developer" → [0.12, -0.34, ..., 0.87]    │    │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │    │
  │  │                              │                                     │    │
  │  │                              ▼                                     │    │
  │  │  Step 2: Vector Search (Milvus, 10ms)                              │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │    │
  │  │  │ Top-3 matches:                                              │    │    │
  │  │  │  1. "Senior Software Engineer" (similarity: 0.94)          │    │    │
  │  │  │  2. "Python Backend Developer" (similarity: 0.91)         │    │    │
  │  │  │  3. "Lead Developer" (similarity: 0.88)                   │    │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │    │

  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │    │
  │  │  │ Llama-3-8B: system_prompt + 3 examples + user_query       │    │    │
  │  │  │ → Generated job description (200 words)                   │    │    │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters: This is the anihpj RAG in production. Separating embedding (CPU), vector search (Milvus), and generation (GPU) means each component uses the right hardware. The embedding model costs $30/month (CPU), Milvus $50/month, and the LLM $300/month (GPU). If you ran everything on GPU, it would cost $600/month with no benefit — the embedding step doesn't need GPU.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: RAG pipeline = Embedding (CPU, KServe) → Vector DB (Milvus) → LLM (GPU, vLLM). Separate InferenceServices for each. KFP orchestrates the API calls. Right hardware for each step.

Pipelines Q193 of 200
How should you add data validation to a pipeline to prevent training on corrupted data?
A) Add a validation step after ingestion that checks: schema (columns and types match expected), completeness (no nulls in critical columns, row count within expected range), distribution (feature statistics not drifted from baseline), and data freshness (timestamp of latest record) — if validation fails, the pipeline stops BEFORE training, saving GPU hours and preventing bad models
B) Data validation happens implicitly during training — the model will produce low accuracy if data is bad, which the evaluation gate catches
C) Validation is the data engineer's responsibility — pipelines should trust that data in S3/DB is always clean
D) Use a try/except in the training code — if the model fails to train, catch the error and skip to the next step
✅ Correct Answer: A

Data validation should happen early in the pipeline — before expensive GPU training. A validation step checks: (1) Schema — columns exist, types match (e.g., salary is numeric, not string). Use Great Expectations or simple pandas assertions. (2) Completeness — null percentage per column, minimum row count (e.g., "at least 10K rows — if only 50 rows, something's wrong"). (3) Distribution — compare feature statistics (mean, std, histogram) against a stored baseline. KS-test p-value < 0.05 → possible data issue. (4) Freshness — max(timestamp) should be within expected range (e.g., data from last 7 days). If any check fails: raise ValueError("Data validation failed: ...") → pipeline stops with clear error message. This prevents the most expensive failure mode: training for 30 minutes on bad data, producing a bad model, then catching it at evaluation. Validating upfront saves GPU hours.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Data Validation Gate
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  [ingest]──▶[VALIDATE]──▶[preprocess]──▶[train]──▶[evaluate]            │
  │                │                                                          │
  │                ├─ Schema check: ✅ columns match                          │
  │                ├─ Null check: ✅ < 5% nulls                               │
  │                ├─ Row count: ❌ 50 rows (expected 10K+)                  │
  │                ├─ Distribution: ❌ salary mean shifted +40%               │
  │                └─ Freshness: ✅ data from today                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  → VALIDATION FAILED: Pipeline stops. No GPU time wasted.                │
  │  → Notification: "Data validation failed: only 50 rows. Check S3 path."  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Last month, the data team accidentally overwrote the 100K-row jobs dataset with a 50-row test file. The pipeline trained for 30 minutes on 50 rows, produced a terrible model, and deployed it. Result: 4 hours of bad predictions before rollback. With validation: the pipeline would have stopped in 5 seconds with "Validation failed: only 50 rows." $50 in GPU costs saved, zero bad predictions.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Add data validation step BEFORE training. Check schema, completeness, distribution, freshness. Fail fast — don't train on bad data. Saves GPU hours and prevents bad model deployment.

Pipelines Q194 of 200
How should the anihpj pipeline notify the team on success or failure?
A) Pipelines can't send notifications — the team must manually check the KFP UI for run status
B) KFP has built-in email alerts — configure SMTP settings in the pipeline server and it auto-emails on completion
C) Write status to a log file — the team monitors logs with a separate tool for pipeline notifications
D) Use an ExitHandler step that calls a notification API (Slack webhook, email service, PagerDuty) — the ExitHandler runs regardless of success/failure, so it always sends status; include run ID, metrics summary, and a direct link to the KFP run
✅ Correct Answer: D

Pipeline notifications use dsl.ExitHandler — the exit step runs ALWAYS, whether the pipeline succeeds or fails. Pattern: (1) Create notification component — a Python component that takes status and metrics as input, calls Slack/email/PagerDuty API. (2) Wrap main DAG — with dsl.ExitHandler(exit_task=notify(status="success", metrics=...)). (3) Pass context — the exit task receives the pipeline status and key metrics. The notification should include: pipeline name, run ID (link to KFP UI), status, key metric (accuracy), duration, and which step failed (if applicable). This is more reliable than having each step send its own notification — one centralized notification point ensures exactly one message per run.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Notifications with ExitHandler
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @dsl.pipeline                                                            │
  │  def anihpj_pipeline_with_alerts():                                       │
  │      notify_success = notify_slack("✅ Pipeline SUCCEEDED")              │
  │      notify_failure = notify_slack("❌ Pipeline FAILED")                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │      with dsl.ExitHandler(                                                │
  │          exit_task=notify_success,   ← Runs on success                   │
  │          name="notification"                                              │
  │      ):                                                                   │
  │          ingest = fetch_data()                                            │
  │          train = train_model(ingest.output)                               │
  │          ...                                                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  SLACK MESSAGE (auto-generated):                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │ 🤖 Pipeline: job-matching-weekly                                   │    │
  │  │ ✅ Status: SUCCEEDED                                               │    │
  │  │ 📊 Accuracy: 94.3% (▲ +2.2% vs last week)                         │    │
  │  │ ⏱️ Duration: 25 minutes                                            │    │
  │  │ 🔗 Run: https://kfp.apps.cluster.com/#/runs/details/143           │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: Every Sunday at 2:30 AM, the Slack #ml-pipeline channel gets a message: "✅ job-matching-weekly SUCCEEDED. Accuracy: 94.3% (▲2.2%). Model registered and canary at 10%." Monday morning, Alice checks Slack from her phone — she knows the pipeline ran successfully before she even opens her laptop.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: ExitHandler for notifications — runs always. Call Slack/email/PagerDuty API. Include: run ID (link), status, metrics, duration. One centralized notification per run.

Pipelines Q195 of 200
How do you optimize pipeline costs when running on expensive GPU nodes?
A) Only request GPU for steps that need it (training, not data prep), use nodeSelector to run CPU steps on cheap nodes, set step timeouts to prevent runaway costs, use spot/preemptible instances for non-critical pipelines, enable caching for repeated steps, and scale GPU nodes to zero when pipelines aren't running via cluster autoscaler
B) Run everything on GPU — the cost difference between CPU and GPU nodes is negligible at pipeline scale
C) Use smaller models — pipeline costs are dominated by model size, not infrastructure choices
D) Run pipelines less frequently — cost optimization is about scheduling, not resource allocation
✅ Correct Answer: A

Pipeline cost optimization strategies: (1) GPU only where needed — data prep and evaluation steps run on CPU (cheap). Only training uses GPU. A pipeline with 1 GPU step + 3 CPU steps costs ~$2/run vs $8/run if everything used GPU. (2) Node affinity — nodeSelector: {node-type: cpu} on CPU steps ensures they never waste GPU nodes. (3) Timeouts — .set_timeout(3600) prevents hung steps from running for hours. (4) Spot instances — dev/test pipelines run on spot/preemptible GPU nodes (70% cheaper). Production uses on-demand. (5) Caching — repeated steps with same inputs skip execution (zero cost). (6) Cluster autoscaler — GPU nodes scale to zero when no pipelines are running (nights, weekends). Combined savings: 60-80% vs naive all-GPU all-the-time approach.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Cost Optimization
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  COST BREAKDOWN (per weekly run):                                         │
  │  ────────────────────────────────                                          │
  │  Step         Node Type    Duration    Cost                               │
  │  ────         ─────────    ────────    ────                               │
  │  Data prep    CPU ($0.1/h)  5 min      $0.01                              │
  │  Training     GPU ($3/h)   15 min      $0.75                              │
  │  Evaluation   CPU ($0.1/h)  3 min      $0.01                              │
  │  Register     CPU ($0.1/h)  1 min      $0.01                              │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────                                │
  │  Total per run: ~$0.78 (4 runs/month = $3.12/month)                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  VS NAIVE ALL-GPU: 4 steps × GPU = $3.12/run = $12.48/month             │
  │  SAVINGS: $9.36/month (75% reduction)                                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The weekly pipeline costs $3.12/month optimized vs $12.48/month naive. Annual savings: $112. For 5 pipelines: $560/year. This is the difference between AI being a cost center and being cost-effective. Every GPU step that can run on CPU is pure savings.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: GPU only for training/inference. CPU for data prep/eval. nodeSelector for hardware targeting. Spot instances for dev. Caching for repeated steps. Cluster autoscaler for scale-to-zero.

Pipelines Q196 of 200
What security best practices apply to KFP pipelines handling sensitive data?
A) Pipeline security is handled by OpenShift — no additional configuration is needed beyond cluster defaults
B) Never pass secrets as pipeline parameters (stored plaintext in MariaDB), use Kubernetes Secrets mounted as env vars, encrypt S3 artifacts with KMS, use NetworkPolicy to restrict pipeline pod egress, run pipeline steps with non-root SCC, and audit all pipeline run access via OpenShift audit logs
C) Store all data in the pipeline server database — MariaDB encrypts data at rest and is the most secure storage option
D) Pipeline security is the data scientist's responsibility — add encryption/decryption code in each notebook cell
✅ Correct Answer: B

Pipeline security layers: (1) Secrets — NEVER as pipeline parameters (visible in UI, stored plaintext). Use set_env_variable(secret_key_ref=...) to inject from K8s Secrets. (2) S3 encryption — enable S3 server-side encryption (SSE-KMS) for artifacts. MinIO supports SSE as well. (3) NetworkPolicy — restrict pipeline step pods from accessing unapproved services. (4) SCC — run pipeline pods with restricted SCC (non-root). (5) Audit — all Run creations, parameter changes, and pipeline uploads are logged via OpenShift audit. (6) Image scanning — scan component container images for vulnerabilities before use. (7) RBAC — limit who can create/run pipelines in each project. Pipelines have the same security surface as any Kubernetes workload — apply standard K8s security practices.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Security Checklist
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ❌ DON'T:                               ✅ DO:                           │
  │  ────────                                ──────                           │
  │  pipeline_param("password")              Secret → env var                │
  │  Hardcoded credentials in code           .set_env_variable(secret_ref=)  │
  │  S3 bucket with public access            S3 with SSE-KMS encryption      │
  │  Pipeline pods: allow-all egress         NetworkPolicy: deny-all + allow │
  │  Container runs as root                  SCC: restricted (non-root)      │
  │  No audit trail                          OpenShift audit logging enabled │
  │  Unscanned community images              Scan images before pipeline use  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The pipeline processes real job listings with salary data (PII). Secrets for S3 and DB are never in code or parameters. S3 artifacts are encrypted. NetworkPolicy ensures pipeline pods only talk to anihpj-db and anihpj-s3. Audit logs show who triggered each run and with what parameters.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Never pipeline parameters for secrets. Use K8s Secrets via set_env_variable. Encrypt S3 artifacts. NetworkPolicy for pod egress. SCC restricted (non-root). Audit logging.

Pipelines Q197 of 200
A pipeline server fails completely. How do you recover pipeline definitions and resume scheduled runs?
A) Pipeline definitions are lost — you must rewrite all pipelines from scratch when the server fails
B) Restore from the nightly OpenShift etcd backup — pipeline definitions are stored in etcd alongside cluster state
C) Pipelines auto-recover — the KFP operator automatically recreates all pipelines and runs after a server failure
D) Pipeline source code (Python) should be version-controlled in Git — recompile and re-upload to a new pipeline server; artifact data in S3 survives independently; MariaDB can be restored from backup for run history; Recurring Runs must be recreated via SDK/UI
✅ Correct Answer: D

Pipeline disaster recovery relies on separation of concerns: (1) Code — pipeline Python files in Git. Recompile and re-upload to new server. Never lost. (2) Compiled YAML — optionally store compiled YAML in Git for faster recovery. (3) Artifacts — stored in S3/MinIO, independent of pipeline server. All historical model artifacts, datasets, and metrics survive server failure. (4) Metadata — MariaDB should be backed up regularly. Restore from backup for run history, experiment structure, and recurring run definitions. (5) Recurring Runs — recreate via SDK script that re-registers all cron schedules. Recovery time: ~30 minutes (new server provision + re-upload pipelines + recreate schedules). The pipeline server is cattle, not a pet — treat it as replaceable infrastructure.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Pipeline Disaster Recovery
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  WHAT SURVIVES SERVER FAILURE:          WHAT NEEDS RECOVERY:              │
  │  ────────────────────────────          ────────────────────              │
  │  ✅ Git: pipeline source code           ❌ MariaDB: run history          │
  │  ✅ S3/MinIO: all artifacts             → Restore from backup            │
  │  ✅ Container registry: images          ❌ Recurring Runs: schedules      │
  │  ✅ KServe: InferenceServices           → Recreate via SDK script        │
  │  ✅ Model Registry: model versions      ❌ KFP UI: web interface          │
  │                                          → New server = new UI            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RECOVERY STEPS:                                                          │
  │  1. Provision new pipeline server (dashboard or CLI)                     │
  │  2. Restore MariaDB from backup (if available)                           │
  │  3. Re-upload pipelines from Git: kfp.Client().upload_pipeline()        │
  │  4. Recreate recurring runs: client.create_recurring_run(...)            │
  │  5. Verify: trigger test run → check artifacts in S3                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The anihpj pipeline server's MariaDB pod crashes and the PVC is corrupted. Recovery: new pipeline server provisioned (dashboard, 5 min) → pipelines re-uploaded from Git (2 min) → recurring runs recreated via script (1 min) → test run triggers and succeeds (25 min). Total downtime: ~30 minutes. All artifacts and models in S3 and Registry are untouched.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Pipeline code in Git (never lost). Artifacts in S3 (independent). MariaDB needs backup. Recurring runs must be recreated. Pipeline server is replaceable — treat as cattle.

Pipelines Q198 of 200
How do you build a multi-model pipeline that trains and deploys several models simultaneously?
A) Use dsl.ParallelFor over a list of model configs — each iteration trains a different model in parallel; after all complete, evaluate each model, select the best via metrics comparison, register the winner, and deploy — all in one pipeline DAG
B) Create one pipeline per model — KFP cannot train multiple models in a single pipeline run
C) Train models sequentially to avoid GPU contention — parallel training on shared GPU nodes causes OOM errors
D) Use Elyra to drag multiple train nodes — Elyra auto-handles multi-model orchestration without code
✅ Correct Answer: A

Multi-model pipelines use ParallelFor for concurrent training. Pattern: (1) Define models — list of configs: [{"name": "xgboost", "lr": 0.1}, {"name": "randomforest", "n_estimators": 100}]. (2) ParallelFor training — with dsl.ParallelFor(items=model_configs): train_one_model(config=item). Each model trains in its own pod, potentially on different GPU nodes. (3) Collect results — each iteration outputs a Model artifact. (4) Evaluate all — fan-in: run evaluation on each model. (5) Select best — compare metrics, determine winner. (6) Deploy winner — register and deploy the best model. All models train simultaneously — total time = slowest model, not sum of all. This is the ensemble/autoML pattern: try many architectures, keep the best.

📝 Detailed Explanation
Multi-Model Training Pipeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                              ┌──────────┐                                │
  │                         ┌───▶│ XGBoost  │──┐                             │
  │                         │    └──────────┘  │                             │
  │  ┌──────┐    ┌────────┐ │    ┌──────────┐  │    ┌────────┐   ┌────────┐ │
  │  │prep  │───▶│Parallel│─┼───▶│LightGBM  │──┼───▶│Compare │──▶│Deploy  │ │
  │  │data  │    │For     │ │    └──────────┘  │    │Metrics │   │Best    │ │
  │  └──────┘    └────────┘ │    ┌──────────┐  │    └────────┘   └────────┘ │
  │                         └───▶│CatBoost  │──┘                             │
  │                              └──────────┘                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  3 models train in parallel → compare → deploy best → archive others     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why this matters for anihpj/jobpost: The team isn't sure which algorithm works best for salary prediction. They run a multi-model pipeline with XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost in parallel. After 20 minutes, all three are trained. Evaluation shows CatBoost has the lowest MAE ($2,800). It's automatically registered and deployed. The other two models are archived for comparison. Data-driven model selection, not guesswork.

💡 EX267 Exam Tip: Multi-model pipeline = ParallelFor over model configs. All train simultaneously. Fan-in to compare metrics. Deploy best. AutoML pattern on KFP.

Pipelines Q199 of 200
What is the complete anihpj MLOps architecture connecting all OpenShift AI components?
A) Each OpenShift AI component operates independently — there is no integration between workbenches, pipelines, registry, and serving
B) The architecture is a simple pipeline: train → deploy — everything else is optional monitoring
C) OpenShift AI is just a collection of tools — each team uses whatever they want without a unified architecture
D) Workbench (prototype) → KFP Pipeline (automate: data prep→train→evaluate→register) → Model Registry (version+metadata+stage) → KServe (deploy with canary+GPU+autoscaling) → TrustyAI (monitor drift+bias) → drift alert triggers pipeline retraining — a closed-loop AI factory where models continuously improve without manual intervention
✅ Correct Answer: D

The anihpj MLOps architecture is the integration of all four EX267 domains: Cat 2 (Workbenches) — JupyterLab/VS Code for experimentation and prototyping. Data scientists explore data, test models, build notebooks. Cat 4 (Pipelines) — KFP automates the training workflow. Elyra for visual design, KFP SDK for complex DAGs. Recurring Runs on cron schedules. Cat 3 (Models) — Model Registry governs versions, metadata, stages. KServe deploys with canary rollouts, GPU autoscaling, vLLM for LLMs. TrustyAI monitors drift, bias, and performance. Cat 1 (Platform) — RHOAI Operator manages everything. GPU Operator provides acceleration. OLM handles upgrades. The "AI factory" pattern: data flows from workbench prototypes → automated pipelines → governed registry → monitored serving → retraining triggers. Each component feeds the next in a continuous improvement loop.

A) (1) Create pipeline: @dsl.pipeline with typed params → compile → upload. (2) Run pipeline: client.run_pipeline(experiment_id, params={...}) or UI trigger.
